en: *Sādhananidānaśrīcakrasaṃvara-nāma-pañjikā* (The Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Glorious Cakrasaṃvara Entitled "The Introduction to the Means for Achievement").
Toh. no. 1401. Derge Tanjur, vol. BA, folios 1v.1–78r.7.
Translated by Sūryagupta and ’Gos Lhas btsas. Kambala’s *Sādhananidhi*, a commentary on the *Herukābhidhāna*.
The manuscript transcribed here:
NAK 4-122/vi. bauddhatantra 87 NGMPP B 31/20.
*Herukāvidhāna*, fols. 73, palm leaf, 33.5 x 5.5 cm.

A considerable amount of text survives in Göttingen Xc 14/30 (though apparently unnoticed by Bandurski; perhaps this is what Shukla refers to), although in that manuscript the text is attributed to Devagupta (in fact, this commentary was apparently translated twice).
The Tibetan Translation:
*Sādhananidāna-śrīcakrasaṃvara-nāma-pañjikā*, titled *The Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Glorious Cakrasaṃvara: The Introduction to the Means for Achievement*.
Toh. no. 1401. Derge Tanjur, vol. BA, folios 1v.1–78r.7. Translated by Sūryagupta and ’Gos Lhas btsas. % define commands
The opening quotation,
as corrected, emended, and conjectured by the editor, according to the reading of the manuscript.
Homage to the Buddha.

The Commentary on the Tantra Resides Here. In the language of India: *Śrīcakrasaṃvarapañjikā-nāma-sādhanopāyikoddeśa*. In the language of Tibet: *Dpal 'khor lo sdom pa'i dka' 'grel sgrub pa'i thabs kyi gleṅ gźi* (The Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Glorious Cakrasaṃvara, titled "The Basis for the Method of Accomplishment"). Homage to the Blessed One, the Glorious Vajra Ḍākinī!

Having paid homage to the Lord Śrī Heruka, who is the nature of the three bodies and bliss, I shall write down, with faith, a small portion of that which has come down through the succession of the lineage of gurus.
Having prostrated to the glorious Heruka, the blissful lord of the three bodies,
I shall [explain] that which has descended from the lineage of gurus.
Now,
beginning with the words "Then" (*atha*) and so forth, this tantra is joined with other tantras.
Regarding the phrase "Then" (*atha*) and so forth: this tantra is perfectly connected with the conclusion of other tantras;
thus, the word "then" (*atha*) is in reference to the preceding tantra. It indicates the immediate succession of this tantra [from that previous one].
Therefore, this word "then" (*atha*)...
"By this, this tantra is made clear without interruption;
for it was said, 'Thus have I [heard],' precisely at the proclamation of the three hundred thousand [stanzas].
(Note: G reads *trilakṣābhidhāne*.)
Thus have I [said];
for this reason it is called the *Triśatikā*, as it was spoken thus by me.
For this very reason, the introductory statement (*nidānavākya*) has not been employed at the beginning of this [work], because it was already employed previously.
For this very reason, there is no initial introductory statement at the beginning, because it was already introduced previously.
*Tantram* means a continuous connection (*prabandha*).
"Tantra" refers to a continuous sequence.
The tantra of the cause,
the tantra of the means, and the tantra of the result.
The causal continuum, the method continuum, and the resultant continuum.
The cause is the lineage (*gotra*). In this very context, practitioners are even more difficult to find.
Regarding that, the cause...
The *hetu-tantra* (cause-tantra) is the logical reason; here it refers to the practitioner who is extremely difficult to find.
"Method-tantra" refers to the practices such as meditation, recitation, offerings, diagrams, and the application of mantras, following the sequence beginning with entry into the frontal maṇḍala;
[namely,] the application of mantras and so forth,
preceded by the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*).

Regarding that which is called the *Upāya-tantra* (Method Tantra): it consists of the sequence of entering the maṇḍala first, followed by meditation (*bhāvanā*), recitation (*japa*), ritual offerings (*bali*), magical diagrams (*yantra*), the application of mantras (*mantra-prayoga*), and so forth.

*Phalam* means: non-dual, resting solely in luminosity; beyond the sphere of speech; and far removed from the fluctuations of the mind. *Advayam* [is] non-dual; *prakāśaikaniṣṭham* [is] resting solely in luminosity; *advayam* [is] non-dual; *avāggocaram* [is] beyond the sphere of speech; *dūram eva cittavṛtteḥ* [is] far indeed from the fluctuations of the mind.
That which is called the "Continuum of the Fruit" abides as a single, non-dual clarity; it is beyond the sphere of speech and remote from the domain of the mind.
How, then, is there a continuity?
What is that connection like?
The meaning is that by means of this, the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma) abide here. "Gang 'dir sangs rgyas kyi chos rnams gnas pa'o" means this;
its seal (mudrā) is the syllable *a*.
The mudrā of this is the syllable ĀḤ.
The meaning is that, in terms of conventional appearance, all phonemes and letters arise from this. This is the sense of the statement: "All letters arise from A."
It is also stated in the *Śrīvajramaṇḍālaṃkāra*: [as evidenced by the testimony of the *Vajragarbhālaṃkāratantrodbhavakalparāja* (Toh. 490), fol. 42a].
Also, from the *Śrīvajrahṛdayālaṃkāratantro*:
"The unstruck (*anāhata*), supreme, subtle, and imperishable syllable, like a blazing lamp, resides in the center of the heart; it is the supreme form, the Lord."
"Madhyama... the syllable *a* is the supreme lord," as quoted in Raviśrījñāna’s *Amṛtakaṇikā* and also quoted in Āryadeva’s *Caryāmelāpakapradīpa*.
"In the center of the heart, indestructible, blazing like a lamp,
unchanging and supremely subtle— this is the supreme lord.
Thus it was said, and furthermore, it is stated in the *Dvikalparāja*:
From the second *Viniścaya-rāja*: "Mahāmudrā abides at the navel, having the form of a blazing lamp-flame;
she is of the nature of the primordial vowel (*ādi-svara*), and is thus conceived by the wise."
"Imagined," as stated in *Hevajratantra* II.iv.40cd–41ab, also cited in Raviśrījñāna’s *Amṛtakaṇikā*.
G: *prakalpita iti*.

It is said: "The syllable *ata* is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) abiding in the throat; it is like the tip of a flickering lamp, the nature of the first vowel. The Buddhas have analyzed this as 'intellect' (*buddhi*).
Regarding the word *ata*: the connection is that "everything shall be explained" starting from the letter *a*.
It will be explained:
the word "therefore" (tasmāt) is to be construed as "all explanations arise from the letter A.
What is that?
What is it? It is called "the secret" (*rahasya*). That is to say, it is not to be disclosed to those who do not belong to the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
Regarding the term "Secret" (*gsang ba*), it refers to those classes [of teachings] that have not been made manifest.
What is it that is not to be revealed? It is the seven things to be concealed. (G adds:
*tadyathā* or something similar)
What is that which has not been made manifest? It is the seven secrets (*saptarahasya*): "In the secret [place], in the teaching of reality (*tattva*), and in the wheel...
[The commentary continues: "In the secret [place], in the teaching of reality, in the ten [stages], and in the fivefold seed-syllables."
And in the secret [teaching], which is the true nature of the hidden; in the secret,
the secret lotus.
In the *Rahasyavijayānanda*: "In the secret [teaching], *sa-v-...*; in the *Sarvasaṃgama*, ...
the end..."
Regarding the phrase "the uninterrupted bliss of the secret": it is stated in the *Sampuṭatilaka* (or the *Tattvavibhāṣā*):

"The Secret Reality is the object, The Secret King’s Wheel, The Secret Hidden Truth, The Secret Secret Lotus, The Secret Seed-Syllable Joy, The Secret Assembly of All, The Secret Uninterrupted Bliss."

Regarding the term *saṃkṣepāt* ("in brief"): it refers to the measure of the text (*granthapramāṇa*), not to the meaning (*artha*). This is because it is a compendium (*saṃgraha*) that encompasses all the qualities of a Buddha.
Therefore, it is called *saṃvara*. It is so named because it covers (*saṃvṛṇoti*) and gathers (*saṃgṛhṇāti*), [bringing about] union (*saṃyoga*).
That is to say, it is the "union with Śrī Heruka. This is the designation *saṃvara*. The meaning is that it covers everything and grasps [it]; [it brings about] union with Śrī Heruka.
This very [state] is the *saṃvara*; "saṃvara" means the sense of "holding everything.
*Śrīheruka* is the self (*ātman*). The *mudrā* is Vajravārāhī. The union of these two is the characteristic of the *mahāmudrā*.

Regarding the phrase "The glorious Heruka, the perfect union": the glorious Heruka is oneself; Vajravārāhī is the mudrā; their perfect union is the defining characteristic of the Great Mudrā (*mahāmudrā*). *Kāmyante* means "desired objects" (*kāmāḥ*), which refers to the attainment of one's wished-for aims.
Because they are desired, they are called "desires," meaning the excellence of the objects of desire.

It accomplishes the state of being a Vajradhara. [The phrase] "the accomplisher of all desired aims" means that by this very [means], one accomplishes both Buddhahood and the state of being a Vajradhara; therefore, it is "the accomplisher of all desired aims."
What is that?
It is "even higher than the high. Here, "high" (uttara) means superior (utkṛṣṭa).
The "excellent" has its meaning already explained.
Regarding the phrase "the Guru is also the Guru," the meaning of "Guru" (bla ma) is spoken of as follows:

for the sake of leading [beings] up the staircase by means of the power of the various inclinations and the differences in the mental dispositions of sentient beings, there is the teaching of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma; yet even higher than that is the unsurpassed reality residing in the heart. This is not grasped by the path of speech, which consists of what is to be individually realized by all the Buddhas together with the Vajra-holders.

... by means of differentiation, for the sake of purifying the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) ... because of the teaching ... and the subsequent [teaching]. The unsurpassed state of being present in the heart ... by way of being that which is to be experienced ...?

In order to purify the views of transitory collections (satkāyadṛṣṭi) through the power of the distinctions among the various inclinations and intentions of sentient beings, eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma were taught. Furthermore, the supreme reality itself, which dwells within the hearts of those who have become superior, is unsurpassed; it is the very nature of self-cognizing awareness (*pratyātmavedya*) belonging to the Buddhas together with the Vajra-holders, which transcends the path of words.
Therefore...
For this very reason: "Those devoid of reality do not achieve success even in hundreds of millions of eons.
(Quoted in Āryadeva’s *Caryāmelāpakapradīpa* as scriptural authority.)
"Even in hundreds of millions of eons,
one who is deficient in reality will not attain accomplishment.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Regarding the title *Ḍākinījālasamvara*, he speaks of the perfection of the assembly. "The *Ḍākinījālasamvara*" refers to the excellence of the retinue.

[The root] *ḍai* means "to move through the air. Because of the substitution of *ai* for *ā*, there is the form *ḍā*. The meaning is "movement through space. From the word *ḍā*, the third case ending is applied. *Aka* [is used in the sense of] going; *kuṭilā* means "crooked" or "winding" movement. A *ḍākinī* is one whose nature (*śīla*) is not blunt (*akuṇṭha*) in this [movement]. By means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), [she moves] with thousands of millions of billions of bodies simultaneously; that is the meaning. (2v) [In every way].

Now, regarding *ḍākinī*: it is derived from the syllables *a* and *ār*. Because she moves (*gati*), there is *ḍā*; thus, the meaning is "one who moves through space" (*nam mkhar 'gro ba*). The term *ḍā* is spoken as a designation for sound. *Ākāśa* means moving through the sky; here, moving everywhere is "moving through the sky. Since this nature of moving through the sky exists in her, she is called a *ḍākinī* (Sky-Goer). [There are] hundreds of billions of them.
The meaning is that, through the miraculous power of the empty body, one travels everywhere simultaneously.
"Their net" (*tāsāṃ jālam*) means a collection; it is a term signifying a multitude.

The vow (*saṃvara*) is the supreme bliss, because it is perfectly satiated by bliss with them in every single moment. By the word "secret" (*rahasya*) and so forth, the void consisting of sixteen syllables is indicated; by the word "all" (*sarva*), these very [deities] are meant.
The passage beginning with "Secret" (*gsang ba*) and so forth consists of symbolic syllables that are the nature of the sixteen emptinesses; all these sounds are what he spoke.
In the syllable *ra*, there is the element of blood (*raktadhātu*).
*Ra* is the great element of copper.

By the syllable *ha*, [there is] the one born from the mountain (*girija*); thus, "born from the head" (*śiroja*). By the syllable *sya*, there is the vessel of fragrance, just as fragrance [resides] within the body.
The vessel is the leaf;
it is the container for the scent. Just as there is fragrance upon the body, the syllable *pa* is taught to signify the force (*vega*).
The syllable *pa* is spoken of as wind; the syllable *ra* is said to be fragrance itself.
It is taught that the syllable *me* is fragrance itself;
by the syllable *me*, there is a flower. The syllable *me* is the flower.
The letter *ra* followed by the suffix *ṇat* [is used]; *ṇa* is likewise *lañtsva'o*;
it is considered that *mye* is the flesh (*pisita*) with the letter *ka*.
I also desire the great meat;
*sakāraṃ* and *kunduraṃ* indeed,
*sakāraṃ* is the very application.
The syllable *rvā* is said to be the head; the syllable *tma*,
O Goddess, is the stalk of the lotus.
The syllable *me* is the goddess Me;
the syllable *ni* is scented oil.
*ni ni dri yi mar khu'o*, *sakāra* is the tooth-dust;
*sa ni so dang sen mo ste*.
The letter *dā* was produced by Sāgaraja;
let it be the essence of the essence.
The syllable *sthi* is the essence of space;
the syllable *taṃ* is considered to be camphor.
This is the teaching on *taṅkāra* (or *tagāra*).
Alternatively:
Alternatively,
she is the knowledge of the all-in-one-form, omnipresent and subtle.
The nature of form is emptiness, [which is] the heart, the secret, and so forth;
it is omniscience, all-pervading,
and exceedingly subtle.
The secret essence of the heart is equality; its illusory nature is emptiness itself. The form of the mind is inconceivable, like another wish-fulfilling jewel.
It is known as "Non-conceptual Wisdom" and is renowned as the "Secret.
The nature of the mind is inconceivable and all-pervading, just like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
It is designated by the name "Wisdom," and it is also explained as "Secret.
By means of that which is the Dharmakāya in terms of both the ultimate and the non-ultimate [truth]...
And it is said that they are delightful because of the wisdom of the omniscient one.
The supreme [body] is by way of the ultimate itself;
it is described as the *dharmakāya*.
It is the wisdom of omniscience through insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This is explained as "joyful.
It is inconceivable, stable, immovable, and all-pervasive by its very nature; it is the lamp of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).

As for the phrase "in the self of all," this refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*) together with the mind (*citta*) and all the sense faculties. It is known as the "all-encompassing" and is remembered as wisdom (*prajñā*), intelligence, and discernment.
The nature that is coemergent with all stable and mobile phenomena, Which is steadfast and inconceivable—
Blazing with intense joy and bliss,
that which is called "the self of all" consists of all the sense faculties,
consciousnesses, and the mind.
In every respect and in every way,
it is explained as "mental consciousness," and it is also called "wisdom," "intellect," and "cognition."

"Always" (*sadā*) means that which is supreme, consisting of the past, future, and present; by this, it is devoid of arising and destruction. It possesses pervasiveness, the nature of a vajra-body, [the quality of being] *ta* + + + + + + + + + +, the state of *tvaṃ*, and the state of *kārālikatvaṃ* + + + + + +.
"Always" refers to the past and the future...
This supreme one,
whose nature is suchness, has abandoned arising and ceasing;
this pervasive vajra body is that very state.
It is explained as being sovereign, eternally present in the east, and existing at all times. *Sthita* (is situated/abiding) [3 recto missing].

Regarding the term "abides": it abides perfectly as the very continuum of mind, pervading equally throughout all bodies, in all realms, and for all sentient beings everywhere. It is untainted and inconceivable; stainless and devoid of self. Because it is itself empty and equal to space, it is utterly free from both existence and non-existence. It is peaceful, without beginning or end—the [nature] of all phenomena.

"Because the body of the Lord (Īśvara) maintains the nature of all, it perfectly relies upon the two truths. Just as the seed of fire resides well-supported within wood, and just as sesame oil resides within sesame seeds, so too is that which resides within the three realms to be known as Mahāmudrā. This is the intended meaning. "The *ḍākinī* is the actual *sattva*... [is said].

In this context, "the voice of all ḍākinīs" is held to be [the goddesses] such as Rab tu gtum mo (Pracaṇḍā) and others; since [the world] is thoroughly constructed from the subtlest particles of these [elements], it is their actual nature. If one asks who they are, they are called "beings" (*sattva*), which are twofold according to the distinction between the mobile and the immobile. It is said: "Sentient beings are explained as the mobile, while the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is the immobile."
Regarding the phrase "Vajrasattva Supreme Bliss": it is called "vajra" because it is indivisible, and because it possesses qualities similar to a vajra, it shatters all other things.

From below, he is the *sattva*, the state of all things being one. Because he is both *vajra* and *sattva*, he is Vajrasattva—the bliss of existence and non-existence. "Vajrasattva" is expressed as bliss. The phrase "this is" refers to that which is clearly apprehended; he himself is the Blessed One, the Self-Arisen (*svayambhū*). All stable and moving things, and all those who are liberated, [are] himself...

"Because he is self-arisen, he is the Bhagavān (Self-Arisen Blessed One). He is called Bhagavān because he possesses *bhaga*; by the term *bhaga*, one should understand the six qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and so forth. Alternatively, it is understood as 'conquering' (*bhagna*), because he has conquered the Māras of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. Furthermore, since the afflictions are conquered by wisdom (*prajñā*), it is said that he 'conquers through wisdom. [The afflictions...]"

"Because he is free from fear, he is a hero (*vīra*). Because he is bound by the form of the channel-wheel (*nāḍī-cakra*), it is the binding of the ḍākinīs’ net. It is explained that the supreme bliss is the wheel of the *samaya*. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "even more than the guru" (*bla ma las kyang*) and so forth: the "guru" refers to the sixteen elements (*dhātu*). Even more venerable (*bla ma*) than those are the twenty-four ḍākinīs. Their assembly is the *samaya*.

Alternatively, because these very [teachings] are bound by way of the fundamental wheel (*mūlacakra*), they are called "vows" (*samvara*). In order to clarify the introductory words that are to be kept strictly secret, he spoke as follows regarding what occurred: "The Secret," which means this: "Supreme" refers to myself; "Delight" refers to having heard it; "All as my own self" is the seventh case used in the sense of the third case, meaning "not by another, nor through another."

This is the meaning of "No. At what time? It is at the time of eternal abiding. Where? In the state of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Furthermore, what is that? It should be applied as "this is the Self-Arisen Blessed One" (*svayambhū bhagavān*). Alternatively, the secret is the element of space; likewise, the supreme is water, and joy is explained as fire. The self of all, which is eternally moving, is eternal.

"Abiding in the expanse of space," it is said. Furthermore, the entire realm of sentient beings is the nature of all ḍākinīs; that very [nature] is Vajrasattva. "Bliss" refers to great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and "supreme" means preeminent. This should be construed as: "The Blessed One has explained how it is. Regarding the word "arisen" (*bhūta*): "earth" is bliss, and its great passion—

It arises for the purpose of subsequent inference. Therefore, regarding the phrase "the manner of sound": the emergence of the sound of the syllable *hūṃ* as it enters into the interior of the vajra-jewel is the entirety of the heroes (*vīra*) and yoginīs of the three times and the three realms. Their commitment (*samaya*) is held to be the assembly, because of the union in equanimity with the vajra and the lotus. The object...

"Conduct" (*caryā*) refers to the enjoyment by the twelve sovereign lords (*daśendra*). "Sphere of activity" (*gocara*) is the characteristic of consciousness that attains the domain of one's own mind through the mode of individual self-cognition (*pratyātmavedya*). "Beginning" refers to the non-delusion regarding the primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) that is utterly established as stainless in its center and periphery, pure like space, having abandoned the five obscurations of secrecy.

It must be suppressed for a time; otherwise, it would be [permanently] pure by its very nature. Just as in the case of the application of the two rubbing sticks, so it is: from the friction of the fire-drill, the wood, and the human effort, smoke arises and fire is produced; yet, when sought thoroughly, that fire does not exist in the fire-drill, nor in the wood, nor even in both together.
It does not abide in the wood, nor in the fire, nor in the friction, nor in the hands of the person; when thoroughly examined, it does not reside in any one of these.

Now, this fire is as follows: the churning stick (*mantha*) is said to be the arising of *dharma*, while the churning rod (*manthāna*) is called the *vajra*. Through their union, the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) is extracted, which brings about the state of Buddhahood as it is known. Gnosis arising from the body of wisdom (*prajñā*) is equal to space; when conjoined with skillful means (*upāya*), the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is properly born. It is a single form, great bliss, arising from mantra-recitation and meditation. Listen, O Lord of Guhyakas, for the Tantra of Wisdom (*prajñātantra*) has been proclaimed by these three. Thus spoke the Blessed One.

Just as it was in that [previous] case, here too, the "elements to be churned" are said to be the *dharmodaya*, and the "churning" is designated as the vajra. Furthermore, from their perfect union, the emergence of nectar-like gnosis (*jñāna*) is the agent of manifest enlightenment itself. Thus: "The gnosis arising from the body of wisdom (*prajñā*) is coextensive with space and simultaneous with skillful means; it is the singular form of great bliss."

"O you who are to be known through the authentic empowerment, endowed with mantra recitation, meditative concentration, and so forth—listen as this tantra is explained! Thus spoke the Blessed One to the Lord of Secrets.
By the word "tantra," this proclamation is made through the etymological definition of "vajra" (diamond/thunderbolt) in its entirety.
The word *tantra* (*rgyud*) here refers to the entirety of the vajra definitive expressions as they are proclaimed;

that is, from the beginning with "Then" (*atha*) until the very end of the completion. "Sealing" (*mudraṇa*) means the intended meaning. Thus, the meaning is the summary of the intended meaning [of the tantra] starting from "Then" and ending with its final conclusion.

Because it serves as a protection for the mind, mantra is gnosis (*jñāna*); because it protects the mind, it is called *mantra*, which is gnosis. Meditation (*dhyāna*) is characterized by one-pointedness of mind.
Meditative concentration has the characteristic of one-pointedness of mind.
Alternatively, by the word "mantra," recitation is indicated through the vocalization of the *āli* and *kāli*. Furthermore, the meaning of *āli* and *kāli* is explained as the recitation of mantra.
Through great exertion for the sake of the mind of awakening, he himself became the sovereign lord of yogic powers;
this mind of awakening is the vajra, because it is the intrinsic nature of all buddhas.
If one is firmly established in the bodhicitta,
one is oneself the sovereign of yogins;
this bodhicitta is the vajra.

"It is the nature of all Buddhas" refers to the "supreme breath. The first [type of woman], eleven years of age, is beneficial for alchemy (*rasāyana*) by opening the lotus. The second, twelve years of age, is for the sake of the *surata-samaya* (the pledge of sexual union). The third, sixteen years of age, possesses flowers [of youth] through constant practice of the mantra. The fourth, twenty years of age, is supreme for the accomplishment of the *khecarī* (sky-farer). The fifth, twenty-five years of age, is for the purpose of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Thus it is shown according to the sequence of the five wisdoms through the purity of the mirror and so forth. "By the breath" means this.

Accompanied by his consort, who follows him in her practice, and preceded by his own tutelary deity and others, he should take hold of the *kulikā*, the daughter of the *kula*, and other women, and consecrate them by the deposition of the *bodhicitta*.

Regarding the phrase "and the supreme speech from which the *dbugs* arise": first, for the purpose of taking the essence (*sāra*), one should exhorted by Padma at the age of eleven; second, at the age of twelve, one should take great delight for the sake of the commitment (*samaya*); third, at the age of sixteen and possessing flowers, one should first practice recitation for the sake of the accomplishments (*siddhi*); fourth, at the age of twenty, [one practices] wisdom (*prajñā*).

"By means of the nature of Kyi (the syllable *kyi*), one accomplishes the practice of moving through the sky (*khecarī*). By means of the nature of the twenty-fifth year, it is for the purpose of empowerment"—up to this point, the sequence of the purification of the five wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and so forth, has been shown. "The emission of breath" refers to [the practitioner] together with the consort who has been thoroughly purified by the principal deity.

This is the engagement in conduct. A "noble one" (rigs ldan) is a daughter of noble family; if she is not available, another may also be taken, provided that the bodhicitta is firmly established within the well-ordained assembly.

"With fragrance" means having adorned [the deity] with various flowers, garments, ornaments, and so forth. "With water" refers to all kinds of things to be known. Having offered these—which counteract, in due order, the afflictions born of wind, bile, and phlegm—and having performed worship, one should become the embodiment of worship itself. One should perceive oneself as the state of omniscience (sarvabuddhatva), illuminating the ten directions with the lamp of the light of gnosis, which is the form of supreme bliss and brings about perfect awakening. The word "tu" (but/then) is for the purpose of indicating a restriction. "Constantly" means without interruption. "Devoted to the reality of cultivation" means intent upon the essence of meditative practice.

The term "dri" (fragrance) refers to adorning [the deities] with various flowers and the like, as well as garments, ornaments, and so forth. The term "chu" (water) should be understood as various kinds of liquor; it is an offering consisting of gifts that accord with what is beneficial for those afflicted by wind, bile, and phlegm. Having become the very essence of the offering, one becomes the essence of the Buddhas.

The body of supreme joy illuminates the ten directions, and through the lamp of primordial wisdom (*jñāna-pradīpa*), one brings about manifest enlightenment. Furthermore, the word "also" (*api*) has the sense of causing certain knowledge. "Always" means to be continuously devoted to the meditation on suchness (*tattva*).

Alternatively, "exhalation" refers to the breath that enters evenly through both the left and right nostrils; at the time when those breaths correctly converge at the navel channel, it is the supreme unchanging mudrā. Where there is another phrase, "the intermediate supreme," it should be stated as being between the first and the last—that is, between the young girl (*kumārī*) and the old woman (*vṛddhā*).

The powder of pāṭalī is called "intermediate. The supreme intermediate and the collections of compendiums are indicated by that. For this very reason, it is said: "even with fragrant water," where "fragrant water" refers to *śilākāṣṭha* (camphor). Together with that is *guggulu*. Being such as this, one should make offerings to the *kulikas* (those of noble family). Regarding the phrase "by way of the distinction of time," the determination of time shall now be explained.

Furthermore, in order to enter [the practice] without being distracted by desire and so forth, one should first clearly distinguish the six seasons from the time of midday: winter, summer, autumn, the early winter, the late winter, and spring. These are the times when the gods of desire arrive together; having thus clearly understood these seasons, one should perform all activities with diligence. From the late winter at dawn...

It is said: "In the spring and summer, there are two parts of the day; the wise should apply midday to the *sa-gar*. Likewise, evening is the autumn, and the first part of winter is the night. Having fully understood the nature of these [times], they should be correlated with Vajrasattva and the others: "Vajrasattva is the latter part of winter, and Vairocana, the Sage, is the spring. O!

Ho! The supreme *ṛta* is the spring; likewise, summer is *heruka*. The Vajra Sun is at mid-autumn; Padmanarteśvara is early winter. In the spring, one should consume honey; likewise, in summer, water. At the time of autumn, clarified butter; likewise, in early winter, flowers. Ho! Late winter is *karpūra*; likewise, summer is the four equal [seasons]. These are the great medicines; know them as the six seasons.

"Par bya, this time is peerless; it is the most sublime of all applications. When those yogins have realized their own nature, they will delight all the yoginīs; this is the assembly of the yoginī ḍākinīs. Thus it was said. "Messengers" (pho nya) refers to those who are delighted by offerings. "Supreme" and so forth refers to those previously explained.

That which arises simultaneously with the *des ni* (by that) is internalized by the mind; "to be meditated upon" means to always act in accordance with its nature. "The accomplishment of the desired object" is the accomplishment of the Vajradhara.

The word "ni" (and) has the sense of a term of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). "Self-nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to camphor. "Should be offered" and so forth are to be taken according to the literal meaning of the words. "Honey" refers to *mahāmākṣika* honey. "Blood" refers to flowers. "Together with camphor" means flowers that exist together with camphor, by way of their indivisibility. "Red sandalwood" refers to meat. "Combined" (*sambhṛta*)...

"Action" refers to the extraction of the essence of the six incomparable [substances] together with excrement and so forth. "The vajra sign" arises from the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*). Alternatively, "all-vajra" is the Blessed One, the glorious Heruka; his "sign" is the skull-cup, and "holding" it means grasping it with one's own hand. Taking the ring finger as the base and the thumb as Mount Meru—

It is to be prepared like the nectar churned from the ocean; it should be understood through three conceptualizations: *oṃ ha hoḥ hrīḥ*. In that regard, by the syllable *ha*, the dregs are extracted; by the syllable *hoḥ*, impurities are destroyed. That which is the blazing fire-syllable *hrīḥ* is proclaimed as *pavaka*. The wise one should taste the nectar thus prepared.
Having first offered it to the Guru, and thereafter to the Vajrin named Heruka, and having presented the mudrā, one should consume it oneself.
First, one should offer to the Guru; following that, one should offer the *heruka*. Having offered it to the mudrā, one should experience perfect bliss oneself.
Through this yoga, which is the essence of the five nectars, one becomes equal to the Holder of the Vajra.
Göttingen: The essence of the five nectars is produced through their combination; by means of this very preparation, one becomes equal to Vajrasattva.

"Or else, together with the *ga-pura*, it is accompanied by the *bodhicitta*; it should be placed in the midst of the *tsogs*. Regarding this, the *tsogs* refers to the assembly of all the sense faculties, such as the eyes and so forth; having become sevenfold, they are distinguished into two types of *tsogs*, which are their gathering. What are those two? They are described as "the thumb, ring finger, and little finger joined," and so on. Here, the "thumb" (*mthe bong*) is the *vajra*.

The *yoni* is the *śṛṅkhala*, and the *śṛṅkhala* is the *padma*. Their union is the joining of the tips of the thumb and the *śṛṅkhala*. "To taste" (*myang*) means "to be known. Regarding the phrase "the four offerings and likewise the yoginīs," it refers to the four vajras: first, the awakening of emptiness; second, the gathering of the seed-syllables; third, the completion of the image; and fourth, the arrangement of the syllables. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that one should worship the four skull-cups atop the *bya ba* (the ritual vessel) and likewise the yoginīs, such as the ḍākinīs and so forth, who constitute the nature of the maṇḍala wheel. By that very [means], it is said: "The hero, entering into non-dual union, maintains that very meditative absorption. In this context, "hero" (*vīra*) refers to the twenty [deities].

Together with the four mudrās, there is the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Here, [the faces] such as the face of the sky are the purities of faith and so forth. The word "hero" (*vīra*) is to be understood as including everything; for example, just as teaching [of a king] implies the inclusion of his entire retinue. This is how it should be practiced by one who meditates on the stages of generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

It should be understood that, likewise, one should worship by means of non-dual meditative absorption with the heroes during the four periods, while the goddesses such as the ḍākinīs—who are the nature of the four liberations—remain present. Furthermore, according to the stage of complete perfection, since the time for abiding in the pride that is without beginning or end is indefinite, what [need is there for further elaboration]?

Having entered into meditative equipoise together with the mudrā as it was taught, one who possesses the yoga should meditate upon the awakening of the Buddha—the self-nature of all Samantabhadras, who abide throughout the entire expanse of space as the Great Vajradhara pervading everything—beyond expression and belonging to the three realms, until midday.

Just as the sun at dawn does not conceptualize whether it is inferior, intermediate, or supreme, yet illuminates everything, so too the yogi, having thoroughly suppressed all non-Buddhist systems as well as the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas by means of the wisdom that is universally radiant, becomes at some point devoid of [dualistic] appearance; at that time, by the light of the Buddha-sun—

In all the buddha-fields of the ten directions, one causes the dharmadhātu of all the Tathāgatas to appear throughout the three realms; to know this through non-conceptualization and the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*)—this is the meaning of the term "samādhi. "Mi" means unchanging; just as it is understood that the bliss of the human self is gathered into a higher state...

"Bya'o, when one wishes to hear this subtle vajra and other yogas, even sixteen parts [of it] will not be tolerated"—this is merely an illustration; that is to say, it will not be tolerated even in part, it will not be tolerated in calculation, it will not be tolerated by way of example, and it will not be tolerated as a cause. Now, the excellence of the location is described: "In mountain clefts," and so forth. As for the sound...

The meaning is easy to understand. However, in order to indicate the Buddha’s mudrā—the great lotus endowed with qualities, the supreme secret site—by means of symbolic terminology (*saṃketa*), he spoke of "mountain peaks" (*ri sul*). The sense is that it refers to a forest grove, a secluded location; one should understand that those who dwell there are intended here. Since the primary [subject] is thus understood, the retinue should also be understood.

Thus, the mudrā of the woman is agitated by the forest of passion and so forth; its purification through skillful means becomes the path to enlightenment. Its purification leads to the ultimate limit. The object is taught as the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), which is the excellence of the vajra family and so forth, consecrated by all the Tathāgatas.

It is secluded because it has arisen from the maiden of the *parcan* (a class of celestial beings). Alternatively, it is a mountain that is immovable, for its nature is the great bliss of suchness (*tattva*), and it cannot be shaken by the winds of those who have gone forth from among the base heretics. It is pure, for its depths cannot be fathomed by inferior sentient beings. It is a cavern, for it has become a hollow completely filled with the nectar of the Victorious One.

Regarding the phrase "the banks of the great river": because it has become a locus for the waters of wisdom—profound and vast—through the perfect union of method and wisdom, it is called "the banks. "Primordially established" means eternally and completely perfected; having abandoned arising and ceasing, it is perfectly complete, always equal to space. Furthermore, [it is free from] attachment...

It is called a "charnel ground" (*dur khrod*) because it burns away the enlightenment of the śrāvakas and others by means of my blazing [wisdom]. Alternatively, it is called a "charnel ground" because it abides with equanimity within the mental continuums of all sentient beings. "Therein" refers to such a specific distinction. It is a "mandala" (*maṇḍala*) because it takes up and holds that essence. "Should be drawn" means it should be meditated upon mentally.

The meaning of the syllable *bā* is as follows: "External" (*phyi rol*) is easily understood. That very maṇḍala is the sublime; it is the glorious Heruka of great primordial wisdom, arisen from the body of Vajravārāhī. The *bhaga* is the lotus maṇḍala. Within that is the gathering of the maṇḍala; the maṇḍala is the supreme bliss. The maṇḍala is the yoga of the Hero (Vīra) and the Yoginī, the non-dual union. This is my own reality (*tattva*).

Meditative equipoise and likewise the reality of the deity, the reality of mantra and the mudrā—this is the supreme maṇḍala. Transcending the meditation on all its branches, by abandoning the conceptualization of discursive thought, free from the *guhya*, *utpatti*, and *bindu*—this is the supreme maṇḍala. When analyzing what is dharma and what is non-dharma, all phenomena are unobservable, like the utterly pure sky.

That is explained as the "maṇḍala. The radiating of attachment and non-attachment, resembling the blazing of ruby (*padmarāga*), that mind which is intensely attached and the state of attachment—that is the supreme maṇḍala. Abiding within the sixteen elements, formless and stainless, the conceptualizer and the motivating mind—that is what is called the "maṇḍala. It is taught that the body is the maṇḍala.

The mandala of Bhaga itself and the mandala of the Bodhisattvas are designated as the three mandalas. Thus, it is said that all that is below the earth, upon the earth, and above the earth, as well as all that is moving and unmoving, is the mandala of the Omniscient One. This concludes the explanation of the first chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*.

"‘In that place’ means in the location of the literal sound. ‘There’ refers to the ground where [the substance] has not fallen; it should be connected with the phrase ‘one should apply [it] there. The ritual manual for this is to be understood as the procedure for the methods of the maṇḍala. Regarding the statement ‘One should conduct oneself in the charnel ground,’ this refers to the manifest preparation of the five-colored pigments arising from the very nature of the charnel ground."

For the blue pigment (*tsōn*), use the flour of charred bones; for the red pigment, use the bone-ash of a pig from a charnel ground; for the white pigment, use the flour of human bone; for the yellow pigment, prepare it by mixing together *yung ba* (aconite) and the flour of human bone; for the green pigment, use the flour of human bone combined with the flour of green leaves. With these, one should draw the terrifying mandala.

Furthermore, because he is the source from which universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) arise, he is fearless. "The master possesses excellent characteristics" means he is skilled in the ritual procedures for consecration (*pratisthā*). "Knowing the application" means he abides in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Regarding what was said, "having gone beyond," by first washing away all sins through the method of the ocean of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he is stainless like the sky.

Beginning with the five types of great compassion and loving-kindness, one should meditate on oneself as the glorious Heruka, endowed with the enthusiasm of diligence, joy, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "adorned with a skull upon the crown": it means that the head is highly adorned with a variety of locks of hair, which are garlands depicting the forms of the five Tathāgatas. "All limbs smeared" refers to being anointed with the ashes of cremated corpses.

It is by mixing [the remains] with the five nectars and the *pāyasa* (milk-rice) offering. "A single piece" refers to the wheel of the five fingers. "A garland of bones, variously arranged," means a garland made from all fifty heads. If these are not available, one may do so by drawing them or through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). "Khaṭvāṅga" refers to the left hand together with the skull-cup; the right hand is the vajra.

It should be drawn; "oneself" is easy to understand. Having done so, it should be written—thus the connection is made. Regarding "the cord of a corpse": one should take the cord from a corpse that has been carried to the charnel ground together with a human corpse, and consecrate it with the great blood of ten and a half humans. Alternatively, "the cord of a corpse" refers to a marking-cord (*sūtra*) made from the sinews of a human corpse.

Regarding the phrase "one cubit" (*khru gang*) and so forth, it refers to a measurement from one cubit up to twenty; one must not exceed that. The statement, "The mantra practitioner should employ [the cord] in a double [length]," describes the characteristics of the marking-cord for the layout. The phrase, "Offering to the ḍākinīs, the Supreme Bliss," indicates that the offerings should be made. As for what was taught regarding measuring and marking, it is the sequence of the *cha ’phen pa* (the casting of the proportions).

Regarding the passage beginning with "By means of this, one should draw the mandala lines of Blo-bzang," and so forth: the term *cha-'phen-pa* (extension of parts) refers to the extension of the three parts; the sequence of that is the "sequence of the extension of parts. By means of that sequence of the extension of parts, the mandala lines should be drawn. As for the measurement of the mandala, one should take hold from east to west; having laid out the lines by doubling [the distance], below that is the *bya-rog*.

One should proceed from the east to the south, and likewise from the west; having measured toward the northern direction, one should strike the Brahma-line. Having established the four lines starting from the eastern direction and so forth, and having divided each of the outer directions into eight parts, one should measure the large sections there, and then further divide them into four parts.

Having established the boundaries at intervals of twelve and four [units], one should draw the lines. By drawing the lines from each respective boundary, this is the supreme *sūtra* for the assembly. Measuring each external portion by two units, and having measured the proportions of these drawn lines, one should arrange the sense faculties and so forth in pairs. Holding the correctly measured *sūtra*, however many [units] are sought, they should be joined together. That...

The wheel of great bliss, as many as there may be, should be made the measure of the body, speech, and mind; possessing seven spokes each, it is the supreme method for circling the *thig-skud*. From that central wheel, six [others] should be fashioned, beautiful with their spokes. The hub and the lotuses should be made with four and three spokes respectively. On the two faces of Brahmā, they should be made beautiful within the spokes; indeed, all three are thus.

One should always visualize [the deity] as being perfectly complete, with the mind encircled by a garland of vajras, speech by a garland of lotuses, and the body-wheel (kāyacakrāvalī) encircled by a garland; the remainder should be arranged as beautifully as possible. Therein, in the eastern direction, at the abode of Indra, upon a śirīṣa tree, is the white assembly of gods; in the southern direction, upon a tūta tree, is the black Yama; in the western direction, upon an aśoka tree...

In the east is the red king of clouds, Abhrarāja; in the north, on the Bodhi tree, is the yellow general of the yakṣas; in the southeast, on a *karañja* tree, is the red assembly of ṛṣis; in the southwest, on a *latājāti* tree, is the blue assembly of rākṣasas; in the northwest, on the wind-lord *Bhūtisiddha*, is the green [assembly]; in the [north]west...

Regarding the boundary of the enclosure, the mass of *yi-dags* (pretas) dwelling in the *nyagrodha* tree, appearing with the color of smoke, is called "the Great, Extremely Terrifying Charnel Ground. As for the phrase "the hero to be manifested at the navel," this indicates the manifestation of the deity. Regarding the phrase "possessing majesty," it refers to one who causes even the most fierce [beings] to tremble with extreme ferocity; his first face has the color of a rain cloud.

His third eye blazes with light like a mass of great, powerful Indra-fire, intensely flaming like the fire at the end of an eon; his fangs are bared and he is majestic, striking terror even into those who are themselves afraid. He laughs "Ha Ha," filled with joy as he embraces the goddesses, his lotus-like face wide open.

With the light of his heart, which is like a mass of shimmering and radiating jewels, he illuminates both the moving and the unmoving; with his two feet, he treads upon a variegated lotus and a sun mandala at the summit of Mount Meru, the king of supreme flavors, while uttering the syllable *hūṃ* along with the sound "hūṃ. His right face is intensely yellow, like refined gold.

With wide eyes of supreme joy, he illuminates the three worlds. His left face is as brilliant as a marakata jewel, radiating a swirling mass of green light rays, and is set in a joyful expression. The western face is deep red like a bandhūka flower or a dāḍima blossom, with radiant light rays as beautiful as the color of the rising sun’s orb.

Possessing meditative experience (*nyams*) and sporting with grace, he gazes with passion upon the most excellent maidens. One should draw him with twelve arms: the right hands hold a hook (*aṅkuśa*), and the left hands hold a battle-axe (*paraśu*). The others are as previously explained; one [arm] holds a skull-cup (*kapāla*) together with a *khaṭvāṅga*. Regarding the phrase "of that" and so forth, it means "the body color and ornaments of that [deity]," which refers to the human [form].

It is the time when the activity of pleasing [the deities] is primary. At that time, Vajrasattva is red in color and holds a vajra and a skull-cup in his hands. Following that, one should arrange the vajra, lotus, and wheel according to the sequence of the three circles. As for the crow-faced and other [deities], their characteristics are exactly as expressed by the words "ḍākinī" and so forth. Then, the flask...

Regarding the term *pa*: victory (*rgyal*) and auspiciousness (*bkra shis*) are at the eastern gate; accomplishment (*dngos grub*) and miraculous power (*rdzu 'phrul*) are in the north; victory (*rgyal*) and complete victory (*rnam par rgyal ba*) are in the western direction; attainment (*grub pa*) and grinding (*srub pa*) are in the southern direction; and the ninth, "complete victory over all accomplishments" (*dgu pa ni dngos grub thams cad rnam par rgyal ba*), should be placed in front. As for the phrase "oneself" (*bdag nyid*) and so forth, it refers to the ritual activities of painting.

One should diligently perform the accomplishment of the maṇḍala. That which is called "lamp" refers to the offering of fire, flowers, incense, divine food (naivedya), and so forth. Then, at the age of sixteen, together with flowers, having properly abided in the union of the mudrā, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi. Having performed worship endowed with all desires, the maṇḍala arises from bliss.

The mantra practitioner should visualize [the seed syllable] at the navel; within the center of wind and fire is the *ālikāli*. In the center is the line of emptiness, which is the sublime analytical discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) and the accomplishment of reality (*tattva-kriyā*). This is explained as the utterly pure, the Guru of Gurus. One should behold one’s own wheel (*cakra*), which unifies all phenomena into a single taste and gives birth to the three realms of beings without exception. Dream...

First, one should meditate [on the deity] as being like an illusion or a reflection. Regarding the phrase "the abode of various qualities endowed with compassion," it means that one should perform the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the body and so forth exactly as they appear in the abode, just as will be explained below; furthermore, the eyes and other faculties should also be consecrated. In the two eyes, from the transformation of the syllable *Oṃ* resting upon a lotus and moon, a wheel arises. From that, [compassion]...

The three-faced, six-armed Mūrdha-vajra, adorned with a crown of matted locks and all ornaments, is the form common to all. Specifically, his left face is yellow and his right is green; with two hands holding a wheel and a bell, he embraces the Mūrti-vajrī, while with his other hands he holds behind his back the skin of Brahmā, the embodiment of delusion (*moha*).

In the PA [syllable], he holds a small ball (*rde'u chung*) and a skull-cup (*thod pa*) in his mouth; this is applied to all [the deities]. All likewise abide in the bodhisattva posture (*sattvaparyaṅka*) and are adorned with the crown of Vairocana. In the second [case], from the syllable *Hūṃ*—which has completely transformed from a vajra resting upon a lotus and sun—there arises the Vajra of Hatred, whose entire limbs and primary face are blue.

One should visualize [the consort] Pṛthivī: her left hand is yellow and her right hand is green; with both hands she embraces Śabdavajrā while holding a vajra and a bell. She wears the skin of Vyāḍi, the embodiment of hatred, as her garment, and is adorned with the crown ornament of Akṣobhya. One should meditate thus.

Upon lotuses and sun disks at the two nostrils, the syllable TRĀṂ completely transforms into jewels, from which arise yellow-jewel vajras. Their central face is yellow, the right face is blue, and the left face is red; with their two hands holding a jewel and a bell, they embrace the scent-vajra. The others likewise hold the garments of the gods of desire, who have been torn asunder by the nature of the yellow-jewel [deities]. These are the jewels.

One should meditate on [the deity] adorned with the crown of *Abhijit*. At the root of the tongue, upon a lotus and sun disk, the syllable *ĀḤ* completely transforms; from that lotus arises Rāgavajra, whose principal face is red, the left yellow, and the right white. With his two hands holding a lotus and a bell, he is in union with Rūpavajrī. Furthermore, he is the lord of the nature of passion.

One should meditate on [the deity] wearing the skin of a great wealthy man as his lower garment, bearing the crown of Amitābha, and possessing a sword born from the complete transformation of the syllable *Bāṃ* situated upon a lotus and sun disk at the heart. From that sword arises a wrathful vajra; he has three faces and six arms, with matted hair tied in a topknot. All his limbs and his central face are dark blue, while the left face is yellow and the right face is blue. He holds a sword and...

Holding a bell, he embraces the Vajra with both hands; wearing the skin of the Lord of the Assembly who was slain out of envy by others, and adorned with the crown of Amoghasiddhi, one should meditate [on him]. At his heart, upon a lotus and sun disk, the syllable *Hūṃ* completely transforms into a vajra, from which arises Īśvaravajra, whose all limbs and primary...

One should visualize [the consort] with a white face on the left and a yellow-blue face on the right, holding a vajra and bell in her two hands, entering into the meditative absorption of the vajra-dharmadhātu in perfect equanimity; she wears the skin of the Lord who has torn asunder all other sovereigns, possesses the crown-ornament of Akṣobhya, and is embraced by Wisdom (prajñā) just as the mundane [consort] is.

One should visualize Vajrarūpa and the others embracing [their consorts] in their respective order, holding in their right hands a mirror, a lute (*vīṇā*), a conch of fragrance, a vessel of flavors, various garments, and the *dharmodaya* mudrā. Following that, one should contemplate the armor mudrās: beneath the heart-vajra, they abide upon lotuses and moons at the hearts.

From the complete transformation of the syllable *AṂ*, from a vajra arises white Vajrasattva, with a reddish complexion, embracing Vārāhī. At his head, upon a lotus and moon disc atop a body-vajra, from the complete transformation of the syllable *NAMAḤ* arises yellow Cakravartin (Vairocana), with a blue complexion, embracing Yamamathani. At the crown of his head (*mūrdhan*), resting upon a lotus and sun disc...

From the complete transformation of *svāhā hūṃ*, from a lotus arises Padmanarteśvara, red with a white complexion, embracing Mohanī. In his two shoulders, from the complete transformation of the *boṣṭha he* situated upon a lotus and sun, from a vajra arises blue Heruka with a greenish complexion, embracing Kṣobhaṇī. In his two eyes are *hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ* situated upon a lotus and sun.

From the complete transformation of the jewel, there arises a Red Vajra Sun with the color of smoke, embracing Bhīṣaṇā. On all limbs, from the complete transformation of the syllables *Phāṭ* and *Hām* situated upon lotuses and sun disks, there arises a Supreme Horse (Ucchuṣma) from a variegated vajra; his entire body pervades like the wind element, and he is green with the color of smoke, embracing Caṇḍikā. [He likewise embraces] Vajrasattva and the others.

The heroes of the *pā* [mantras] have one face, four arms, and three eyes; their faces are wrathful with bared fangs, and they are adorned with all ornaments. Their hair-tufts are bound with silk, and they stand in a posture with the right leg extended. In their primary hands, they hold respectively a vajra, a wheel, a lotus, and a blue vajra; and [in the others] a jewel and a *viśvavajra*.

The Lord should be visualized as embracing [the consort]; all [his] left hands hold a bell, while his other two hands hold a small drum (*ḍamaru*) and a *khaṭvāṅga*. The goddesses, such as Vārāhī and the others, are similar to him: they have one face, four arms, and three eyes; they are naked with loose hair, adorned with the five mudrās, and hold a bell and a *khaṭvāṅga* in their left [hands].

You, holding a *tvaṃga* and a skull-cup, with a small mace and a copper knife in your right hands, have entered into meditative equipoise in non-dual union; through intense passion, you experience the sublime bliss of gathering. All deities, such as Vajrasattva and the rest, are crowned with Akṣobhya. Likewise, the body, speech, and mind of the Bhagavatī Vajravārāhī are also the Wisdom Being (*jñānasattva*).

One should perform the consecration with *Oṃ Āḥ Bāṃ Hūṃ*. Furthermore, the eyes and so forth are [consecrated] by means of Mohavajrī and the others, as previously taught. At her navel is Vajravārāhī with *Oṃ Bāṃ*; at the heart is Yamamathinī with *Hāṃ Yāṃ*; at the throat is Mānavī with *Hrīṃ Māṃ*; at the head is Cundā with *Hreṃ Hrīṃ*; and at the crown of the head is Uṣṇīṣā with *Hūṃ Hūṃ*.
"O Terrifier! PHAT PHAT to all the limbs—this is Caṇḍī. Following that, light rays radiate from one's own seed-syllable: JAḤ!"

By joining *hūṃ bām hoḥ*, one offers the cleansing torma (*bsang gtor*), the water for the face (*zhal bsil*), the drinking water (*mchod yon*), and so forth, according to the sequence beginning with the vajra hook (*rdo rje lcags kyu*). One should worship perfectly with all offerings according to the ritual procedure. Regarding the phrase "of the sky" (*nam mkha'i*) and so forth: the three realms are successively summoned (*dgug pa*), entered (*gzhug pa*), and bound (*bcing ba*) into the wisdom mandala (*ye shes kyi 'khor lo*) and the commitment mandala (*dam tsig gi 'khor lo*).

To bring [the deities] under one's control: light rays emanate from the seed syllable at one’s own heart, and having exhorted them perfectly, [one prays: "O Bhagavān Tathāgatas, may you bestow upon me today the empowerment of all the Tathāgatas! O Great Buddhas, from the radiation of light rays, please manifest the Yoginīs in the sequence beginning with Vajrarūpā and so forth, throughout the expanse of space."

Holding in his hands vases filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), he confers empowerment by means of this verse: "The great vajra empowerment, Honored by the three realms, Arising from the locus of the three secrets, Bestowed by all the Buddhas— Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasaṃyogaśrīye hūṃ. By means of this empowerment...

The Lord of Mind becomes the crown ornament. The ḍākinīs and so forth are sealed by Vairocana and the others. The mudrās of body, speech, and mind constitute the third wheel. Those with the faces of birds and so forth, as well as those residing in the intermediate directions, are also to be marked with the mudrās of Vairocana and the others. According to the ritual procedure, one emanates the vajra with the syllable HŪṂ.

With the syllable *Āḥ*, generate the third lotus of the goddess; with the syllable *Āḥ* [at the heart] and the syllable *Bāṃ* [at the center], generate it. Then, having summoned [the Tathāgatas] by means of light rays from the vajra hook, visualize that the seminal fluid descends into the center of the lotus, and cultivate passion. Recite: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ*. By being exhorted with the sound of the place of birth, all the Tathāgatas...

Having entered through attachment to the *cāru* [beauty], one should cause it to melt into the heart; from within the vajra, it should be emanated into the interior of the lotus. Emanating in the form of the sixteen offering goddesses (*pūjā-devī*) from the tips and boundaries of the pores, one should offer worship according to the ritual procedure and present the offerings, reciting: *Oṃ śrī heruka arghaṃ pratīccha svāhā*. Thus, with "arhaṃ," the washing of the feet is performed for the feet.

As for the "face-cooling" (zhal bsil), it is offered to the face and subsequently presented as an offering by the ḍākinīs with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. This concludes the explanation of the second chapter from the introduction to the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the commentary on the means of accomplishment (*sādhanopāya*).

Then, "one should satisfy the master," and so forth: having worshipped according to one's capacity for the purpose of entering the maṇḍala and other rites, one should make the formal request (*adhyeṣaṇā*).

Regarding the statement, "First, one should please the master with all things through practice," this means that for the purpose of entering the mandala and so forth, one should perform offerings to the best of one's ability and then make a formal supplication.

One should sound the bell with a beautiful tone, together with the *paṭahikā* and the *ramarukā*. Now, the bell is considered to be sixteen years old; the *paṭahikā* is twelve years old. One should play the *susvarā*, which has a sweet voice, along with a lovely woman who possesses splendor and grace. This means one should arouse passion. "Having covered," and so forth, is easy to understand.

Regarding the passage, "The practitioner beats the drum while the very melodious bell resounds," it is held that first there should be a *caṅ te'u* (small hand-drum). Then, as for the bell, it is said to be a sixteen-year-old maiden, while the five [hand-drums] are twelve-year-old girls. "Very melodious" (*śin tu sgra snyan*) refers to having pleasant speech, a beautiful form, and a lovely complexion. "Dust" (*rdul*) refers to those who are to be cherished.
"That these [syllables] are on the face" is indeed easy to understand;
their characteristic sequence should be known in the context of the ritual procedure of consecration (*sekaprakriyā*). It is not stated here due to the excessive length of the text.
The sequence of the ritual procedure for the *Ḍākārṇava* should be understood from the *Abhiṣekaprakaraṇa*; fearing that it would become too voluminous, I have not written it here.

"By relying on Dakṣiṇāmūrti"—[this refers to] the attainment of kingship and the earth, the sword [siddhi], and the siddhis of the underworld (*pātāla*), as well as health, knowledge, and liberation, at the eastern gate of the mandala. It bestows mercury, elixirs, and health, and grants wealth and grain; it eternally grants fortune, glory, and peace at the southern gate of the mandala. [It also grants] subjugation, attraction, and abundance of wealth, etc.

Regarding the phrase "relying on the southern direction": for the sake of attaining sovereignty over the earth and its realms, the accomplishments of the sword and the subterranean (*pātāla*), as well as health, primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), and liberation, one should [enter] through the eastern gate of the maṇḍala. For the sake of alchemy, elixirs, rejuvenation, and health;

For the purpose of bestowing jewels and grain, and for the sake of glory, auspiciousness, and perpetual peace, [one enters] through the southern gate of the maṇḍala. For the purpose of empowerment, summoning, prosperity, pacification, enrichment, being pleasing to people, and the increase of children, grandchildren, and so forth, [one enters] from the western gate of the maṇḍala. For the purpose of protecting the Teaching, [one enters] through the [northern gate] for those who are malevolent.

In order to sever the *nams tsar* [obstacles] and to repel and defeat all enemies, one should cast flowers from the northern side of the maṇḍala. Regarding the phrase "with its heart," it should be offered in order to increase faith and satisfy the mind; one should stand in the posture with the right leg extended (*ālīḍha*), join the palms at the heart, and [visualize] upon the wind seed-syllable atop the wind maṇḍala.

With both legs pressed together, and the heart center stirred by the wind-seeds of wind, earth, and fire, while maintaining the yoga of Vajravārāhī; with the terrifying syllable *Hūṃ*, one utters "Hūṃ," and: *Āle le le hūṃ āḥ*.

Thus, one should cause the sound of the vajra bell and terrifying sounds to resound; by means of these, one should strike all those who are superior, inferior, and middling. Then, for those of inferior fortune, one possessing secret gnosis should empower their five limbs with the seed-syllables of the five Tathāgatas, and [administer] the seven medicinal substances mixed together with a great amount of clarified butter and large quantities of incense.

Having performed the ritual actions, one should apply the fumigation using a preparation of incense containing *chang-dang* and *gu-gul*, and recite the mantra of Vajravārāhī. By the mere scent of that [incense], one will be empowered at that very moment. Through the descent of speech, one will utter verses never heard before; through the descent of mind, one will know the past and the future; and through the descent of body, one will leap with a stride of a cubit.

"Oṃ siddha samaya paripālite hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho ho ho svāhā. With this mantra, one should hold the vajra at the crown of the head and request the departure [of the deity]. Then, having scattered flowers, they should be given to whichever family [of the disciple] the flowers fall upon, or alternatively, to whomever is desired. "The abodes of Śrī Heruka and so forth should be shown to them" refers to that very maṇḍala.

One should teach [the ritual], but that is not the reality itself. Following that, one should perform the water initiation and so forth. After that is the vase initiation. Then, regarding the phrase "and so forth," for the purpose of bestowing the secret initiation, the master should enter into profound meditative equipoise and perform the worship. "On the following day" means at midnight. "Greatly exerting oneself" refers to body and speech.

Regarding the phrase "recited three times because it arises from the mind of passion (*dang sems chags pa las byung ba'i phyir*)," it is by means of these syllables: *Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ*. As for the statement "therein, one should apply the *bindu*," this refers to [the application] at the heart, the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows), the throat, and the head. Then, regarding the phrase "opening the face and showing the maṇḍala," this refers to everything after having grasped all [the deities], such as the reality (*tattva*) of the maṇḍala and so forth.

Thus it was perfectly taught. Then, regarding the passage beginning with "The Guru and the Consort," the *Ādibuddha* states: "Peace, victory, and the attainment of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—these are the stages of the two-fold union. One enters into four such stages; there is no entering into any others. Furthermore, according to the lower [tradition] of the descending seed, that which abides within the mother’s womb is the seed.

Regarding the manner of abiding, at the time of death, death occurs because the seed emerges from that path. Furthermore, regarding this very [channel], it is said in the *Indrabhūti*: "When all embodied beings die, the nectar of the moon descends. As for the phrase "at the times of birth and death," this refers precisely to what was explained above. "The seed flows from the union" refers to that which is below, from the central channel. Others...

Regarding the ordinary discourse on all embodied beings as being under the influence of the *yang-rlung* (prāṇa-wind), it is said: "Equal to the transition of the sun. Here, "sun" refers to the right [nostril], "transition" (*'pho ba*) refers to the left, and "equal" (*mnyam pa*) refers to both. "The dark one descends above" means that the wind of equal flow descends from above. At the boundary where the *yoga* (auspicious conjunction) arises, by means of the central [channel]...

Regarding the phrase "flowing equally" (*mnyam par 'bab*): furthermore, each of the twelve temporal conjunctions (*dus sbyor*) flows six times from the right and six times from the left. Moreover, that which is called the "sixth," known as *jñānin*, flows equally from both [nostrils]. As for the remaining [conjunctions], they flow five mandalas each from the right and the left; it is intended that this very one called *jñānin* constitutes the boundary (*sīmā*).

"...by the central [channel], they flow equally. This means that with the [two] legs, there are fifty-six and one-quarter [units]. Each of the five mandalas flows and moves into the center by eleven and one-quarter [units] each; thus, from the five mandalas, fifty-five and one-quarter are the flow of the central [channel]. When such [units] are multiplied twelve times, they become twenty-one thousand.

"Six hundred and seventy remain complete throughout day and night; the arising and entering of the breaths is not subject to human control. This refers to the aforementioned very same arising and entering of the central channel. "Not subject to human control" is an address [to the breath]. "By more than seventy-five, six hundred [breaths] are for the day and night. This means that in a complete day, there are twelve shifts (*prahara*), and from each shift, [there are] one and a quarter... [footnote 13B]... [breaths].

The five, ten, and thirty-six *bcas pa* circulate through the central and lower [channels]; by arranging those very same as twelve, they circulate six hundred and seventy-five times in a single day. As for the statement, "Furthermore, twenty-one thousand and six hundred," this refers to exactly twenty-one thousand six hundred; regarding that, according to the method of the Compassionate One (*Brtzi ba'i lugs*), one places three *thig le* beneath the mark (*mtshan ma*) of one [channel], and therein [there are] twenty...

When transformed by a single *ṛ* vowel, it remains as twenty-one thousand; therein, because two drops (*bindu*) reside below the sixty signs, it becomes twenty-one thousand six hundred. Regarding the statement, "In the right and left channels, these flow from the lower side," this means that out of the twenty-one thousand six hundred, seventy-six hundred are subtracted, and the remainder is twenty-nine thousand.

It abides in twenty-five [thousand] branches; it flows through the right and left channels. From the twenty-one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five [channels], some flow as *lalanā* and *rasanā*. Specifically, from each of the right and left, two hundred and forty-two [channels] flow through the two legs. When these are divided, including the three [additional ones], they constitute three years and a half—meaning three years and one and a half months.

If one asks how this transformation occurs, it is said: "In a hundred years, it becomes the Middle [Land]. This refers to a person with a lifespan of one hundred years. In that case, there are thirty-six thousand days in a hundred years; when these thirty-six thousand are multiplied by six hundred and seventy-five, it should be understood that they become two *ayuta*s (two million) plus four *niyuta*s (four hundred thousand) and three *lakṣa*s (three hundred thousand).

Regarding the phrase "On top, right and left, the ram and the goat, and the others, the sun and the moon": because the names "Sun" and "Moon" refer to the other heterodox teachers who have entered [the teaching], they are called the "Ram" and the "Goat. Alternatively, "Sun" and "Moon" are above, while "Ram" and "Goat" are below. "The nature of water and fire" refers to the upper and lower [positions] on the right. "Holding lotuses and jewels" refers to—

This is the manner of establishing [the channels] as belonging to the lineage of the Tathāgata. Regarding the phrase "below, the great scent and the scented water flow," this refers to the left and right [channels] below. Regarding the phrase "of the nature of earth and wind," these are the upper and lower [channels] on the left. Regarding the phrase "the right and the left channels," this is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "holding a wheel and a sword," this is the manner of establishing them as the Tathāgatas; [this applies to] the left...

The upper and lower sequences are extremely excellent; they are the "Flowing Belly" (*lto ba 'bab pa*). Go-tsando-ha is called *kham k'a nyi tsar*, which is the "Great Terrifier" (*mahābhairava*) and the "Horse" (*aśva*) at the heart; this is the "Explanatory Flow" (*bshad pa 'bab pa*). Hi hi ma la ya is called [the deity] at the genitals, namely *durdarī* and *kākāsyā*; this is the "Flow of the Thighs" (*mdoms 'bab pa*). Nyeba-tsando-ha is *preṃ pre ta pu ri*, meaning "Abode of the Yakṣas."

*Mañjuśrī* is Mahābala and Cakravegā; phlegm flows [there]. *Grīhadevatā* is Ratnavajra and Khaṇḍarohā; feces flow [there]. *Āḥ* is [the seat] at the two knees; blood flows [there]. *Sūṃ Sūrāṣṭrā* is Hayagrīva and Gajanāsā; blood flows [there]. *Sum Suvarṇadvīpā* is [the seat] at the two calves.

In *Ninamkha'i snying po* (Nābhikūṭa) and *'Khor lo'i go cha ma* (Cakravarmiṇī), there is the falling of *rajas*; it is the *Upamelaka*. In the place called *Nam na gar* (Narmadā), in the fingers, there is Śrī Heruka and Subhadrā; there is the falling of *cilla*. In the place called *Sim sindhu* (Siṃhasthāna), at the perineum of the feet, there is Padmanarteśvara and Mahābalā; there is the falling of *bindu*. It is the *Śmaśāna*. In the place called *Mam ma ru* (Maru), at the anus...

On the two *bong* [shoulders] are Vairocana and Cakravartinī; these are the excretors of saliva. On the two knees, called *kum ku lu ta*, are Vajrasattva and Mahāvīryā; these are the excretors of nasal mucus and phlegm. These are the near charnel grounds (*upacitipati*). Within the Mind, Speech, and Body [mandalas], there are, respectively, the Sky-farers (*khecarī*), the Earth-farers (*bhūcarī*), and those who dwell beneath the earth (*pātālavāsinī*).

Regarding the statement, "May they dwell here! These were accomplished in the past," twenty-four [deities] are taken as the principal ones; thus, those numbering as many as the atoms of Mount Meru are grasped and condensed. "Countless tens of millions of Buddhas" refers to the logical principle. As for the phrase "the mantra that expresses one's own name," it means that one’s own name is recited together with the clarifying *oṃ* mantra.

"Append *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* at the end; recite the ritual in that sequence. Regarding "one's own name," this refers to the supreme [mantras] of the male and female lords (*īśvarīs*), such as *oṃ dakiniye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, and so forth, as well as *oṃ kara kara khaṇḍa kapālini pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, and so forth. Alternatively, it refers to the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

Recite the root mantra, which is identical to the mantras of the deities of the maṇḍala or the intermingled [deities]. Furthermore, with the subsidiary limbs unimpaired, using a rosary of conch shells: for pacifying, it is the Buddha-yoga; for enriching, the Ratna-ḍākinī; for magnetizing, Padmapāṇi; for expelling, the King of Horses (Hayagrīva); and for subjugating, the Lord Akṣobhya. For the sake of all purposes in every way, there is the wheel of the Wheel-bearer (Cakravartin).

Thus it is said. This concludes the explanation of the fourth chapter from the introductory section of the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the method for the practice of the difficult-to-master [tantra]. Then, regarding the phrase "the source of all phenomena, the manifold": "all phenomena" refers to the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth; because it is the source from which these arise, it is here called the "source of phenomena" (*dharmodaya*). "Manifold" means stable.

"Of a nature that is free from fear and wavering. Regarding the phrase "indestructible virtue," the indestructible virtue is Vajradhara, because he holds all virtues. Therefore, it is connected with the statement "all phenomena should be gathered into one," which means they should be increased. Here, "here" refers to the source of phenomena (dharmadhātu). "Abiding there" refers to the application of the three wheels.

"Endowed with power," "fully expanded"—these refer to the arrangement of the syllables in a garland. Regarding the phrase "the fourth with the fifth," and so forth, the root mantra is extracted together with the eight-verse mantra of the Blessed One and the [syllables] beginning with *karaka ra*. This is from the *Introduction to the Means of Accomplishment*, a commentary on the difficult points of the *Śrī Heruka*.

This concludes the explanation of the five aspects. Furthermore, regarding the statement "the twenty-two syllables, the seven-syllable essence, and the near-essence," these will be explained below. Regarding what is called "the seed-syllable of the eight *ya* [consonants]," it refers to the twelve *ha* syllables. "That which is to be discarded" refers to those residing in the center together with the long vowel signs: *a oṃ ha na maḥ*.

HI SVĀ HĀ | * | HŪṂ BHOḤ ŚĀT HE HŪṂ HŪṂ HOḤ PHAṬ HĀṂ || From the complete transformation of the syllable HA and the vajra at the heart, there arises white Vajrasattva, with one face and four arms. His right hands hold a vajra and a small drum (ḍamaru); his left hands hold a bell, a khaṭvāṅga, and a skull-cup. He embraces the red-colored Vajravārāhī. At the head is the syllable HI.

From the complete transformation of the wheel arises yellow Vairocana; his right hand holds a wheel, while the others are as previously described. He embraces Yamamathani, who is blue in color. At the crown of the head, from the syllable *Hūṃ* and the complete transformation of a lotus, arises red Padmanarteśvara, holding a lotus in his right hand and grasping the neck of Mohani, who is white in color. The rest is as before.

As previously taught: from the complete transformation of the syllable *He* and a vajra within the two shoulders arises Heruka, blue in color, holding a raised vajra in his right hand, and embracing Sparśavajrā, who is greenish-blue in color; the rest is as previously taught. From the complete transformation of the syllable *Ho* and a jewel within the two eyes arises Vajrasūrya, with the color of refined gold.

Holding a jewel in his right hand, he embraces Trāsā, who is sky-blue in color like the atmosphere; the rest is as previously described. From the transformation of the syllable *Hi* at the forehead and a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*), there arises Hayagrīva, holding a crossed vajra in his right hand, who embraces Caṇḍākṣī, who is smoke-colored; the others are as before. All of them...

Adorned with all ornaments, he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture with his right leg extended; his hair is bound with a silk turban. This concludes the explanation of the sixth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-mūla*. Now, regarding what is called "vowels" (*svara*), one should apply the consonants taught in the fifth chapter to the vowels; as for the phrase "thirteen indeed":

Regarding the syllable *ao'o* and the so-called "second syllable," these refer to the letter *ma* according to their respective order.
