The eleven vowels are *ae'o*, and the sixth letter is *ta*; it is said that this same sequence should be applied to all [the others]. This concludes the explanation of the seventh chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*. Then, [concerning] one's own self...

"Thus it is said" means that all phenomena are primordially unborn, devoid of self, completely pure by nature, and free from intrinsic essence; this is the universal contemplation. "Through union with all heroes, one binds the lattice of all ḍākinīs" means that great compassion is the nature of emanation; the syllable of the mantra of one's own essential self is the complete maṇḍala.

The supreme mandala, perfected in an instant of primordial wisdom, is square with four gates, adorned with four archways, and embellished with lattices and half-lattices; it is draped with silk and hanging garlands of flowers. Thus shall the outer mandala be shown. In its center, upon an eight-spoked wheel, one should draw a multicolored lotus; situated in the center of the moon and sun is the perfection of the *hūṃ* of primordial wisdom.

The Great Bliss, the Source of Happiness, with a fierce, pale-blue, terrifying radiance; laughing with great terrors, "Ha Ha," he strikes even those who fear with fear. He has eight faces, each with three eyes, adorned with sixteen arms, and decorated with garlands of heads. His head is marked with a crossed vajra and a crescent moon held within his locks of hair; he is further embellished by the six mudrās.

The *Btāb* deity, together with Bhairava and Kālarātri, stands firmly with his right leg extended. He enters into union with the vajra bell and grasps the breast of the Goddess. He wears the loosened garments of Brahmā as a wet sash around his body. In his right hands he holds a trident, a spear, a battle-axe, a sword, and a copper hook; likewise, his left hands hold a skull-cup.

Her face, mouth, head, and hair, her staff, threatening gesture, and other hands, are blue, white, red, yellow, and green, colored like smoke, dust, and ash. Possessing such qualities, the great body of the Bhagavatī, perfected from wisdom and primordial gnosis, is the pale-green light radiating from Vajravārāhī.

The two hands embrace each other in union; she has three eyes and her hair is loose. She is adorned with a garland of skulls; her face and form are similar to his. She has a dark complexion marked by a third eye, and her lips are slightly parted in a smile. With a gaze that casts longing toward the directions, her lower garment is wide and flowing. The goddess Brahmāṇī is fully endowed with good fortune, holding a bow and arrow.

On the eastern petal with the syllable *Aḥ*, one should arrange the Ḍākinī of the Hand-Symbol (*Cihnadhāraṇī*). On the northern petal with the syllable *Ba*, one should arrange the Ḍākinī of Laughter (*Hasitā*). On the western petal with the syllable *Dzra*, one should arrange the Ḍākinī of Renown (*Yaśasvinī*), who is of fierce conduct. With the syllable *He*, one should arrange the Great Ḍākinī called Suvarṇavatī in the southern direction. [Their colors are] yellow, green, blue, dark blue, white, red, and white.

Blue Jambhala and likewise Red, Blue, and Green [Jambhalas], all with three faces and six arms, possessing three eyes and a most terrifying expression, fully adorned with every ornament, wearing the garments of the quarters and having loose hair, standing with right leg extended upon corpses, utterly subduing the four Māras, bearing fierce garlands of skulls, Padma and Nurgya-ma.

Looking upward with a smile, she possesses the sublime bliss of passionate affection. Holding a bow and arrow, and in another hand a hook for summoning, in her left she holds a skull-cup (*kapāla*) and with her right she brandishes a *caṅte'u* drum. At the four corners of the vase upon the skull-cup, it is completely filled with the milk of enlightenment. On the eastern spoke is the letter *Hi*, the deity known as *Ṛkīṭakarṇī*.

In the east is the ḍākinī called Karmadharī; in the northern direction is the ḍākinī called Kumbhakarṇī by means of the syllable RU; in the west is the ḍākinī called Śaṅkhinī by means of the syllable RU; in the southern direction is the ḍākinī called Kaṅkālī by means of the syllable KAṂ; in the southeast corner is Hūṃkāriṇī by means of the syllable HŪṂ; in the southwest corner is Phatkāriṇī; and in the northwest corner...

The beautiful one is the Mother known as Kilikili in the northeast. Those eight Mothers all have faces the color of the Blessed One’s body; they each have one face and four arms, holding a skull-cup and a bell. All of them also hold a khaṭvāṅga and a copper knife. They wear garments of the directions, stand with their right legs extended, likewise wear garlands of skulls, and are adorned with the five mudrās.

One should meditate on her abiding upon the back of a rooster, fierce, sharp, and terrifying. At the boundary of Īśāna is Pūrvakā; at the boundary of Vāyu is Garuḍottamā; at the boundary of Rākṣasī is Lambodarā; and at the boundary of Agni is Śailaputrī. She is yellow, green, and blue, with the fourth [face] slightly red. She has one face and four arms, holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga.

In her other hand she holds a copper knife (*zangs gri cang te'u*); in the fourth, a vajra-spear. She possesses the bliss that subdues the *ḍākinīs* of the directions; her belly is pendulous and protruding, and her breasts are long and full. Her three eyes have a terrifying expression, and her hair is loose, striking fear into [all beings]. She wears a crown of skull-ornaments and is adorned with every kind of ornament. At the eastern gate: *BĀM*.

The dakini named *Gyis mi bzad drag shul can* (She of Terrible and Unbearable Ferocity) is in the south; the dakini named *Yi ge ras rol rtzed drag can* (She of Fierce Play with the Letters) is in the southwest; the dakini named *Svā yas rang od dra ba mchog* (Supreme One Resembling Self-Radiance) is in the west; and the dakini named *Hā yas rgyal ba'i do shal mchog* (Supreme One with the Victor’s Necklace) is in the north. These [four] have three faces and six arms, and are blue and red...

White in color, with a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga* in his left hands, and a head and a threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*) in his right; he holds a hook, a copper knife, and a rattle-drum in his [other] right hands. His southern face is white, blue, and green; below the skull-cup and *khaṭvāṅga* is a copper knife, while the left hand makes the threatening gesture and the right holds a hook and a rattle-drum. The western direction is red, blue, and green, holding a bell and a rattle-drum.

With a copper knife, a skull-cup, and a bell; with a head and a wrathful threatening gesture; the northern faces are green and white, yellow, and mixed red, joyful in expression; with a gaping mouth, a cang-te’u, a knife, and a wrathful threatening gesture; holding a skull-cup and a severed head—all with loose hair, extremely fierce, three eyes, and distorted faces; with wide-open mouths and bared fangs; the right...

Seated in the posture of royal ease, adorned with a stainless garland of skulls, and clothed in the garments of the directions; abiding upon a corpse and a lotus in the center of the sun, with Akṣobhya as her crown ornament; casting sidelong glances and moving with grace, possessing the bliss of passionate affection—she should be placed at the northern gate in the seat of the essential gnosis. Oṃ śrī vajra he he ru ru kāṃ hūṃ hūṃ.

PHAT D’A KI NI DZA LA SAM PĀRAM SVĀHĀ. Together with the Body, Speech, and Mind, adorned with the six ornaments, the faces are the purity of the eight liberations, and the hands are the sixteen emptinesses. Following that, the great mantra consisting of the seven syllables—the essence and near-essence—of the mandala of the Supreme Vajra shall be recited: from the complete letter *HŪṂ*, the Vajra...

The Great Blissful Dakini, the actual manifestation of Ālikāli, the principal deity with three faces and six arms, possessing three eyes and adorned with all the [major] marks, endowed with the eighty minor signs of beauty, in non-dual bliss with Vārāhī; through the union of emptiness and compassion, she enters into equipoise with the vajra and bell; her other hands hold human skin, a garment, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and the sixth—

She has three central prongs, adorned with a garland of skulls, and is arrayed with all ornaments; she holds a crossed-vajra and a crescent moon in her locks, and stands with her right leg extended. Upon a variegated lotus and sun disk, she tramples upon Bhairava together with his consort, bestowing the fruit of all desires. Outside of that, draw a six-spoked wheel and assign the six Yoginīs there.

One should draw [the deities] within the center of the six-spoked wheel, bestowing swift siddhis. They are to be arranged by circling counter-clockwise starting from the eastern direction and so forth. With the syllable *Phāṭ* is Śrī Lalitā, the first goddess; with the syllable *Hūṃ* is Vajrabhairavī, the second; with the syllable *Ha* is Caṇḍakṣobhī, the third; and with the syllable *Ho* is Vajraprabhā, the fourth.

The syllable *Hrīḥ* is the fifth, Vajracaṇḍī; the syllable *Āḥ* is the sixth, Vajraḍākinī. These goddesses have one face, four arms, three fierce eyes, loose hair, and wear garments of the cardinal directions. They all abide upon sun discs. They are blue, yellow, green, red, and smoke-colored (smoky white), and all hold a *caṅte'u* (small drum).

Holding a *dril-bu* [bell] and wearing two human skins, adorned with a crown of a garland of skulls, she dwells in the posture with her right leg extended. Perfectly arisen from the six syllables, she is the lady who bestows accomplishments (*siddhi*). Just as is the color of the Lord’s body, so too is that of Vārāhī; her form and mudrās are identical to his. Having cast off the human skin, the goddess holds a bow and arrow.

The one who acts as the protector, with all limbs, the central channel, and the face blue; the right and left [sides] yellow and green; completely adorned with all ornaments; embracing the two thighs of the goddess; intoxicated by supreme bliss; visualizing the abode of primordial wisdom at the heart; blessed by body, speech, and mind; beautifully adorned with the two types of armor; through the yoga of emanation and reabsorption—extremely...

One should perform the mantra recitation while in meditative equipoise: *Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. By means of those six syllables, one should meditate on the six supreme branches of enlightenment of the ḍākinīs. As for the seventh, which is situated in the center, it is the syllable *Hūṃ*, the maker [of the seal], Heruka; this is indicated by the words, "Mindfulness is the branch of enlightenment," and so forth. *Oṃ dhi dhi dhīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Then there are the syllables *Pam*, *Yom*, *Mom*, and *Hrīṃ* itself.

Regarding the statement: "Dang, Hūṃ, Dang, Phat—these are known as the six yoginīs; each syllable is correctly situated," the ritual sequence for this shall now be set forth. One should draw a five-petaled lotus with its pericarp and filaments. In its center is Vārāhī, perfectly arisen from the syllable Bāṃ, red in color and blazing with light, with three faces and six arms, peaceful.

Furthermore, she has three eyes and loose hair; her head is adorned with a garland of skulls. She performs a dance while draped in a half-cloth of human skin. Her body is marked by the six mudrās, and she wears a garland of flowers upon her head. Having cast down the signs of the times, she tramples them with her feet. When all those who harbor hatred, the gods, and the māra-enemies are thus subdued, she is the Great Red One, blazing like fire. Her right and left [hands] are dark red.

The skull-cup, the Khaṭvāṅga, the noose, and likewise the hook; holding the head and the bell—these bestow all siddhis. One should visualize the goddesses of the eastern direction and so forth as moving counter-clockwise: with *yom* is Yamamathī, with *mām* is Mohanī, with *hrīṃ* is Saṃcālinī, with *hūṃ* is Trāsany, and with *phaṭ* is...

Furthermore, they are all one-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed, with disheveled hair, clad in the garments of the directions, and supreme in their dance. They are adorned with the five mudrās and wear necklaces of severed heads. Their head ornaments consist of the appearance of self-awareness, and they possess the sublime bliss of the agitation of passion. [They are] blue, white, yellow, green, smoky, and pale grey, and with skull-cups...

Khaṭvāṅga, bell, and curved knife; furthermore, through the union of non-dual meditative absorption, all [deities] such as Vajrasattva and the rest, according to the sequence of embracing and so forth, have blue-colored hands and implements. At the navel, heart, throat, head, crown of the head, and all the limbs are the implements—so it is said. Following that, the syllables of the mantra, which is the essence of the goddess, are complete in their entirety.

The supreme of all mandalas, arising according to their proper sequence, is explained: from the complete perfection of each individual syllable, there arise the ten wrathful deities and the three lords, who bestow all siddhis. Arising from the dharmadhātu is the delightful celestial palace, four-sided and four-doored, adorned with four horse-treasures, embellished with lattices and half-lattices, and [hung with] silks...

In the center of a garland of dangling flowers, there is a red lotus adorned with eight petals. Upon its hub is Vārāhī, and the goddesses are depicted upon the petals. One should meditate on the heart-mantras of the goddesses in the directions of the boundary gates: Namaskārī and Hāsā at the eastern and northern directions, and Jṛmbhaṇī and Caṇḍākṣī at the western and southern directions.

In the eastern direction is the wrathful goddess herself, Khaṇḍarohā, and Kanakaprabhā; these are the goddesses of the cardinal directions, to be arranged starting from the southeast. The goddess who performs *hūṃ* is named Piṅgalā; she who performs *phaṭ* and she who performs *guptā* are the goddesses of the petals in the east, north, west, and south respectively. From the syllable *ha*, the central goddess arises—blue in color, fierce, and of great majesty. Extremely...

The fierce one who subdues all demons, with all her marks completely perfected, known as Vajravārāhī, the bestower of all siddhis—blue, yellow, red, and green, with a white upper face, five faces in total, twelve arms, and three [upper] faces; her form is wrathful and terrifying, standing firmly with her right leg extended and her left drawn back, trampling upon Bhairava.

She is fainting from the fear of the *tsh'a mu* and is adorned with all manner of ornaments, including garlands of skulls. With a protruding belly and loose hair, she wears the garments of the directions and abides perfectly in the blissful means of her own radiance. Agitated and intoxicated by compassion, she enters into union with the vajra and bell; she brandishes a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a spear, a copper sword, and a *caṅ te'u*.

Holding a *pāśa*, a hook, a severed head, a battle-axe, and a threatening gesture, with two hands he raises aloft a human skin garment. The colors of the petal goddesses are yellow, green, red, and blue; residing at the four gates are those who are blue, green, white, and yellow. Red, smoke-colored, blue, and white are those who reside between the southeast and the northeast, starting from the fire [direction].

Those twelve [deities] have one face and four arms, with three eyes, and are adorned with all the ornaments. Upon seats of corpses, they remain in a very stable posture with one leg drawn up. Clad in garments of the directions, their hair is loose; their two breasts are full, and they possess beautiful forms. Their faces are joyful and expressive, looking askance with a sidelong glance. With the right hand, they hold a vajra-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*).

The left hand holds a skull-cup filled with blood, which serves as the vessel and the bell. Nevertheless, upon the seats of the female deities of the gates: in the eastern direction is Indra; in the northern direction is Yakṣa; in the western direction is Varuṇa; and in the south is Yama. They abide in the posture of right leg extended, with three eyes and hair standing erect.

Bha has a garland of skulls and is adorned with various snake ornaments; in his principal hands, he holds, in successive order, a hook, a noose, a chain, and a bell. The others brandish vajras, hold skull-cups, khatvāngas, and severed heads. His faces are contorted, his belly is protruding, and all are adorned with garlands of heads.

PA STE (PHA) means "to cause the lotus to bloom," which generates the splendor of the bodhicitta and brings about exhilaration; it signifies that all maṇḍalas are filled with one's own radiance through skillful means and supreme joy. Having adorned the two types of armor at the locations of the body, speech, mind, and heart—the abodes of primordial wisdom—and having conferred empowerment, made offerings, and offered praise, one should emanate by means of mantra recitation: Oṃ.

*BADZRA BEE RO TSA N'I YE HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ*. "The four precious [jewels] above the earth; this is the sublime mantra of the garland" means that these act like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) to accomplish the desired aims of all wandering beings without exception. This concludes the explanation of the eighth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*.

Regarding the phrase "according to the sequence of the supreme *las*," some achieve accomplishment through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) alone; some achieve it through meditative concentration and mantra; and others achieve it through meditative concentration, mantra, and the activities of ritual diagrams (*yantra*). Thus: "By oneself, as the King Vajradhara, Through the excellent application of the wheel of command, Whatever exists within the three worlds, May pacification and so forth be accomplished as desired."

"By means of the *Dod tsham gyis* [subjugation] ritual, one who knows the procedure for this supreme mantra will accomplish all of that in a single instant. Regarding the 'voices of all the nāgas,' this refers to Varuṇa, Ananta, and the others; having recited the mantra once and exhorted them through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are summoned. Terrified and overcome with fear, those who possess great miraculous powers depart into the sky of the intermediate space by means of their miraculous power."

One should cause a continuous stream of water to flow. Alternatively, one should visualize the Great Majestic Lord, the Vajra Garuda, issuing commands to the nāgas along the banks of rivers, oceans, ponds, wells, and lakes; then, with a noble mind, one should recite the mantra while agitated by wrath. [One should visualize] a delightful eight-petaled lotus with its center and pericarp...

In the center of a mass of swirling garlands, the Great Vajra is terrifying with bared fangs; he has eight arms and four faces. His first face is blue like the color of a cloud, wrathful and fierce. The right face is smoke-colored, and the left is a pale blue; above them is an extremely red face of a Garuda, blazing with the brilliance of twelve suns, sharp-fanged and with bared fangs.

He who causes terror, with his right hand brandishing the supreme vajra and his left hand making the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) while frowning; with his other two hands, he wears a garment of elephant hide; holding a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a hook, and a spear; and with an eighth [hand] desiring a drum; treading with his right leg extended, the Lord of Water is struck down, overcome by fear.

In the *Bar-'gyur*, regarding the one with half-moon-shaped matted locks tied up, adorned with various vajras, his body decorated with the six mudrās, and further embellished with a garland of heads; wearing a lower garment of tiger skin, baring his fangs with his tusks, and gazing with a wrathful look—on the eight petals, the eight nāga kings should be drawn. In the eastern direction is Ananta.

In the northern direction is Vasuputra; in the western direction is Padma; in the Ishāna (northeast) is Mahāpadma; in the Agni (southeast) is Śaṅkhapāla; in the Rākṣasa (southwest) is Balin; and in the Vāyu (northwest) is Aṭavī. They are white, blue, red, green, yellow, and smoke-colored (greyish-green). Possessing jewels, their necks are held high. With palms joined in the supreme gesture, [they pay homage to] the Blessed One...

"Look at the face of *Daśa*; one should assume a terrifying posture and look on with fear. Alternatively, one should meditate on the Great Bliss of the Twelve-Armed [Lord], as previously explained, [visualizing] Varuṇa together with his wife as white in color. On the hearts of the *nāgas* and Varuṇa, write the syllable *Hūṃ*. Focusing on the painted image and facing east, [one should engage in] the channel..."

One should recite the mantra of Vaiśravaṇa; when one hundred thousand have been recited, he will appear before one, and by the mere command of the great lord known as Vajrakrodha Garuḍa, rain will fall. Oṃ āṃ āṃ nandāya hūṃ nā hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ bāṃ bā suki | Oṃ tāṃ takṣaka | Oṃ pāṃ padma | Oṃ māṃ mahāpadma | Oṃ sāṃ sāṃ khaṇḍapāla | Oṃ kāṃ karkoṭaka | Oṃ oṃ ānāvata |

"BATA, AṂ BAṂ BA RU NĀYA NĀGĀDHIPATYE NĀGĀNĀM VARṢĀPAYA HŪṂ NĀṂ HŪṂ SVĀHĀ. This is how it should be viewed. By meditating on the Great Wrathful One, one should offer [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. Remaining silent and in profound meditative equipoise, one should observe celibacy and consume milk and śāli rice; and [one should also offer] the *nāga* bali.

Being thus endowed, one should bathe with milk and perform a milk *homa* offering. One should burn fuel sticks (*samidh*) produced from milky trees, each a span in height, together with the fire; and having filled a vase with milk, one should distribute milk-offering *bali*s in the ten directions. For such a feast offering, one should recite [the mantra] four thousand times during the four periods of the day; within seven days, the entire earth-base will certainly [be purified].

It will descend as rain. Alternatively, pour water and *yungs kar* into a silver vessel and recite [the mantra] twenty-one times. Bathe an image of the Buddha together with its relics using scented water mixed with ghee. Then, taking soil from both riverbanks and making it into a single mass, fashion the form of a nāga; place it there facing west with nine heads. After that, bathe it and offer incense.

One should cast the *de* and *de dang* along with the bathing water into a river. Immediately thereafter, the *nāgas* will be pleased, and they will cause rain to fall continuously throughout the entire world of Jambudvīpa. The earth will become endowed with crops, and all sentient beings will come to dwell in a state of pleasant touch. Then, one should perform the application of the *yantra*; [this is] the *mantra-yantra*.

If even hearing the name of the Lord of the *Khadiraka* Forest, who arose from the *khora*, the most marvelous investigation, causes one to tremble with fear, what need is there to mention all the *khadirakas* when their names are written down? On a piece of white cloth, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus; upon it, the three wheels—vajra, lotus, and rosary—should be arranged in sequence. Poison and...

In the directions of the *tsa-ske-tse* and the three *tsa-ba*, and in the cremation grounds, in the various directions of the left-hand circuit, with the mind in perfect meditative equipoise, one should summon from the eastern direction and so forth, and from the intermediate directions such as the northeast, by means of these mantras beginning with *kāra kāra*. Having summoned them, one should firmly establish Pracaṇḍā and the others, ending with Mahābalā, writing their own names together [with the mantras].

One should append *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. *Oṃ* illuminates everything; it bestows accomplishment and illuminates all desires. One should draw the eight nāgas, such as Ananta, encircling the three wheels at the tips of the spokes and the rim. In the center of the eight petals and the hub, one should write *hūṃ* or *hūṃ sarvanāgabalśapa ya śī ghraṃ phaṭ*. Outside the mandala—

With three necks possessing precious gems, their tails entwined around one another; at the base of those necks, one should arrange the syllables *hūṃ*, *nāṃ*, and *hūṃ*. Using earth from a molehill together with the five products of a cow, one should fashion an image of Vaiśravaṇa about a span in height. One should place a wheel upon its heart, perform the summoning and other rites, and then worship it perfectly.

Having closed the opening of the *karavīra* flower, perform the water ablution without interruption. With a *guḍūcī* stalk recited once, apply incense continuously. If [the water] does not flow forth, then on the seventh day, having cut it into pieces, place them inside a vase and cast them into a great river. By that, all the *nāgas* will be defeated; overcome with fear, they shall fall into exhaustion.

One causes water and so forth to descend. Visualizing a wheel on the left hand with the mind and writing the actual name [of the victim] upon it, by reciting [the mantra] once, one causes a snake that has bitten at the proper time to vomit [its venom]. By merely pointing with the hand, one will be liberated from being seized by all gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and other malevolent spirits. Alternatively, one does not release the mouthful of food.
Having drawn the three maṇḍalas with barley, rice, and so forth, and having drawn the sacred maṇḍala marked by lotuses with spreading petals, one should write the syllable BĀM at the center.

One should bind with the two syllables *Hūṃ*; likewise, upon the eight petals, one should write the binding of the essences of the eight *nāgas*. Then, this mantra should be recited: *Oṃ vajrakrodha mahābala hana hana paca paca vidhvamsaya utsṛja tāya sarvanirmāraya hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, having performed the summoning and so forth, one should offer worship correctly.

If one joins the palms together and places them at the site of the *nāgas*, and fumigates with incense made from a mixture of *gu-gul*, *sardzara*, and white radish while reciting the mantra, rain will fall. Regarding the phrase "it causes [rain] to be averted," this is accomplished by means of the application of the *ājñā-cakra* (wheel of command). Alternatively, if one takes flowers offered upon the crown of the head of a Vajradhara, recites the root mantra seven times over them, and fumigates a scorpion with them, by this means rain in the sky will be averted.

"PAR 'GYUR RO" (It shall become dry), "RGYA MTSHO SKEMS PAR BYED DO" (It dries up the ocean): by means of the ritual as it has been taught and the mantra that pierces the ocean through meditation, it will undoubtedly be dried up here by the great majesty of extreme wrath. "If one strikes [the ground] after reciting [the mantra] over each mouth [of the vessel], the flow of the river will be reversed. "It causes lightning to be averted" means by merely snapping the fingers. Recitation.

Regarding the phrase "by performing the *bum* [the earth] causes to tremble": while dancing with the right leg extended in a posture of joy and enthusiasm, one thoroughly delights the circle (*cakra*) of ḍākinīs. As for the passage beginning with "climbing a tree" and so forth, it means that at the time when the practitioner attains accomplishment, they perform all these deeds. "Many hundreds of thousands of forms" refers to...

As for those such as Bala, what need is there to mention the Buddhas who have attained accomplishment in this world by abiding in the state of Mahāmudrā? Those who have fulfilled the aspiration that enters through great compassion will always assume various forms according to the needs of those to be disciplined. Furthermore, when a practitioner of weak diligence desires accomplishment, at that time—

Accomplished through mantra and tantra; "mantra" is renowned as that which protects the mind. Having obtained the excellent tantra, the great method, for whom would spiritual accomplishment not be achieved? It transforms everything without exception into form. Even those whose nature is of meager merit will find the accumulations; thus, it generates all activities in order to inspire attachment in sentient beings toward various [forms] and so forth.

First, one should become the nature of the deity; thereafter, the substance of the seed-syllable is accomplished. If one asks what kind of seeds and so forth they are, they are explained as the *eranda* (castor oil plant), the *unmādana* (intoxicating plant), and so on—such are the seeds. One should perform the practice according to the ritual for those and others once they have fully ripened, under the sun of non-white [i.e., dark] elemental spirits.

Adorned with flowers from low-caste families and anointed with the five nectars, it should be left to dry day and night. On the eighth or fourteenth day of the waning moon, fill a black dog’s skull with charnel ground soil. Having generated [the deity] in the abode of the *mātṛkā* as taught, take the seed-syllable of the practitioner, perform special offerings to Heruka and the Guru-Mahākāla with mantras, and cast [the offering] into the charnel ground.

Having worshipped that mask and recited the mantra over it, one should visualize it in the form of whichever deity one intends; having bound it at the throat and transformed it into that form, if one releases it, it will once again become its own original form. Furthermore, taking seeds of the golden tree (*campaka*), one should anoint them with the bile of a black snake during the waning moon. On the eighth and fourteenth days of the waning moon, one should remain in meditative equipoise in the place as previously described, within the skull of a black crow.

Without generating the *paśu*, one should take the seeds of the *smiṇma* plant and perform the ritual according to the procedure. Visualizing [the victim] in whatever form [is appropriate], if one binds their neck, they will be struck down instantly. First, one who knows the ritual may take the skull of a Brahmin born of the highest caste, even if it has been struck by a wooden stake or a weapon; having filled it with the earth of a fortress, at the time of midnight—

In cemeteries, at the crossroads of great paths, at the junctions of three roads, and on the banks of rivers, one should plant seeds, scatter water, offer *bali* cakes, and protect each day with the following ritual conduct: assuming the form of glorious Heruka, adorned with all ornaments and mudrās, holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga in the left hand, and holding a small ball in the right hand.

If one intends to protect [the image] by means of the *zhugs* (entry/incantation), those who eat meat and the like will not cause harm; otherwise, it will manifest [as a malevolent spirit]. For the completion of an excellent medicinal [image], one should fashion and take up [the materials] on an auspicious day, lunar mansion, and planet. One should remain in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) with the mantra of whichever form one wishes to produce. With the blood of whichever [being], the fruit [is achieved].

One should scatter [the substances] many times over [the disciples], anoint them with its flesh and so forth, and massage them with those very substances. One should generate that skull as it has been described, and diligently perform the offerings of *bali*, fumigation, and anointment with its marrow, water, flesh, and blood again and again. When it has ripened, one should take it; having loosened the hair-knot at the crown of the head, [one should place] the hand of a young girl [upon it].

Placing the skull-cup in the left hand, one should hold it so that the fruit does not fall to the ground. Having carefully gathered those seeds of accomplishment, divide them into three portions. Offer the first portion to the Guru Vajradhara; offer the second to all the Tathāgatas, heroes (vīra), and yoginīs; and as for the third, take it yourself, [visualizing] the faces of the crow and so forth.

If one dwells in the center of the maṇḍala of the Yoginī Bhūtamātṛ and places [the seed-syllable] upon the tongue, the yogin will appear identical in form to various [manifestations]. By means of the ritual procedure exactly as prescribed, he will certainly see such a form. Through the power of the application, it will be accomplished so as not to appear to any person; even a mere portion of the accomplishment of the seed-syllable samaya is like that of an owl.

If even those born on earth cannot see them, what need is there to mention those born as humans? If one who possesses intelligence remains in meditative equipoise for as long as desired, they will sport together with divine maidens. If they so wish, they can be seen by speaking aloud; if they do not wish it, they will become invisible, attaining mastery over invisibility. [They will also possess] excellent palaces and trees...

Regarding the phrase "one should reduce *rtse-mo* and so forth to ashes and butter": the King of Mantras shall cut [them] as if with a blazing sword. If one arranges this wheel, stainless like the light of the moon, with the left hand, then poisons—whether stationary, mobile, those produced from limbs, or those arising from combinations—will be transformed into nectar merely by the display of the palm of the hand, becoming like the light of the moon.

By the blazing radiance of stainless light, even those exhausted by various poisons are revived. It is said that they take up the essence of nectar, such as by consuming nectar and so forth. "It acts as poison" means that, without effort, simply by being recited in a dark manner, it becomes poison.

Alternatively, take the seeds of the *ku ba khaṅ* plant and anoint them with the bile of a black snake. On an inauspicious day at midnight during the month of Maghā, place four black snake skulls filled with the dust from a crossroads. Having prepared a drop of semen from a man, whatever food, snacks, drinks, and so forth one looks upon while reciting the mantra will turn into poison.

"It will turn into liquid mercury; 'moon' refers to wine, and 'milk' refers to the drink of milk. By means of meditative concentration alone, stainless like the light of the moon—or alternatively, by burning white *arka* wood with fire and offering lotus fibers as fine as a hair, having soaked them many times in milk and performing one hundred and eight mantra-homa offerings—one should [use] its ash."

Mix it with the juice of *tzing ka* and dry it in the shade for as long as seven days. Then, at the time of offering, yogins should fill the hollows of their fingers and cast the ashes into a vessel of liquor; [thereby] milk, *kunda*, and the moon will become stainless. This rite should be performed for the sake of sentient beings who are deluded by conceptual thought. Just as...

If one grinds the powder of *sumāgadhā* flowers that have been dried, repeatedly sprinkles it with the juice of *jambīra* fruit, washes it with goat’s urine, and pours it into a lotus vessel, it will act like milk or wine. If one anoints the neck and other parts with the powder of *karañja* fruit together with its thorns and *nārikela* husks, it will steal away [the scent of] perfumes. Such is the flower.

When all things such as sandalwood and its fruit are perfumed, or when various flowers are mutually incensed or burned, they cause the fragrance to spread wherever one desires. Regarding the statement, "The spirit of Garuḍa causes beings to move," and so forth: that very wheel is adorned with the moon and the daughters of the gods, having cast out the *nāgas*.

One should combine the names of two men and write them with *gorocanā* during the time of the constellation Puṣya. Having performed a great offering and taken hold of it, one should apply oneself to the identity of Śrī Heruka. Abiding in the samādhi of non-dual yoga, having thoroughly visualized one’s own consort as Vajravārāhī, if one recites the King of Knowledge (*vidyārāja*) throughout the night, then oneself—

"Gathering with the *oṅgas* means gathering with women. From the *vidyā*, dust arises spontaneously, and thus the women also come together. That which is called 'moving with the face of Garuḍa' refers to drawing forth [the essence] from the opening of the channel containing blood, which has entered into the center of a fully blossomed lotus by means of the inverted posture. This is the nature of all the Tathāgatas.

Because he belongs to such a lineage, he is the supreme among men; he shall be endowed with glory and possess stainless marks. No one whatsoever shall be able to usurp the glory that resides in the palms of his hands. Since he becomes an object of worship for all beings, he is equal to a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) in his possession of glory; he is distinguished by the excellence of long life and freedom from disease. By his mere remembrance, [he can] slay...

Regarding the phrase "it acts" (*byed do*): one should draw [the victim's name] together with poison, *laṅtsā*, and *ske tse* within the interior of that very wheel placed inside a sun-maṇḍala. Having fashioned an image using charnel ground ashes and charcoal, one inserts it into the heart. While recollecting the person to be accomplished, one summons them and inserts them [into the image]. Having hidden it in a charnel ground, one strikes the heart with a stake of human bone and pours water [upon it]; if one then recites the mantra with wrath, [the result follows].

"Death will occur within seven days. By abiding in the samādhi of the blazing garland of the wrathful *spar ba*, if one fans and blows with the wind from the southern direction, fire will be produced wherever it may be. By brandishing the single-pointed vajra and reciting the mantra, those dwelling beneath the earth are subdued. Having empowered the palms of the hands, one strikes following the path of the wind."

"Wherever one desires, there the lightning will strike; by mere recollection, it causes lightning to arise," and so forth, is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "ashes from a cremation ground" and so on: on the eighth or fourteenth day of many months, one should burn *arka* wood in the fire of a corpse's cremation, extinguish that fire with *datura* juice, and then, using those ashes mixed with poison and *laṅtsva*, [one should write] upon a cloth from a cemetery...

Having drawn a wheel with its hub in the center, fashion an effigy from charnel ground ashes; insert the name [of the victim] together with the syllables into its heart, perform the summoning and so forth, fumigate it with a great amount of *guggulu*, and seize the person by name. If one strikes it once while reciting the mantra, that person will fall down instantly. That very wheel, using a *sarkarā* reed from the land of *Kvataka*, should be placed in the heart of a flesh-eater (*piśāca*).

If one draws [the figure] according to the prescribed method and strikes it while reciting the name of the person to be targeted along with the mantras as spoken, that person will be seized by hunger. Regarding the so-called "charnel ground ash," using the ashes previously described, on a night during the day of a spirit, one should draw a circle in the center of the hand-symbols of the planets upon a slate, a wall, or any secluded place.

If one inserts the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) into the mantra *lo la* and fumigates it with a large incense ball (*gu-gul*), that person will be seized by the seizure-spirit (*gza’*). For the purpose of restoration, one should diligently wash all of those [images] with milk and recite the mantra with a peaceful mind. Regarding the phrase "the branch of the *ātīmukta*" and so forth: one should fashion an image of the person to be accomplished from red sandalwood powder on a cloth from a charnel ground, using [human] flesh...

Having first drawn the wheel described by Sen rtzi and Ro tsa na upon a moon mandala and placed it at the heart, one should perform the cleansing with scented water and carry out the summoning and other rites. Then, having recited seven times the mantra interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished on a *ātimukta* flower, wherever one strikes [the target], they will become intensely joyful, red in color, naked, with disheveled hair, intoxicated, and [intent] upon awakening.

One should imagine that the continuous flow of the mind is struck by a drum and drawn in by the hook of the breath, so that it swirls before one's two feet. When seven days have fully passed, it will come forth through the force of the wind. Having written a wheel inscribed with the name of *laṅgaloṣṭa* (clay from a funeral pyre) and *yūka* (lice-earth), together with the syllables of the mantra, in the center of a solar mandala, [one should place it] in a charnel ground or at a crossroads.

Carve it to the size of a thumb, bury it face down, and strike it with a thorn while reciting the mantra seven times; it will remain bound for as long as one lives. When one wishes to release it, write the name together with the [target's] tears, blood from the nose, and the root of a crow’s feather upon a leaf carried by the wind, and cast it against an upward-moving wind; wherever [it goes],...

"It will go to that state of death. For one suffering from stiffness, one should expel [the obstruction] and perform purgation. Taking the five limbs of a black goat, along with great sesame oil and large pieces of *gu-gul*, one should mix them together, moisten them with liquor, and at the time of worship, apply them as an incense by reciting [the mantra] once; merely by wearing it, [the affliction] will fall away. Furthermore, on a cloth from a charnel ground, using the sap of the *aśoka* tree...

Draw that very wheel which abandons the *gus* and *klu* [spirits] and write the name "Rakṣa" in the center of the letter *ai*. Having made perfect offerings and placed it in one part of the house, all decaying bodies will be bound. On that same wheel, having written the name of the person to be accomplished on a cloth from a charnel ground and [mixed it with] the ashes of a burnt female corpse...

Having fashioned an effigy of the object to be accomplished by mixing it with the red powder of *dang tshandan dmar po*, and having performed the summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) and other rites, one should insert it into the heart. Having made perfect offerings, one should cast a twig of *kāravīra* the size of the object’s hand into a blazing fire of a woman’s corpse. While it is not yet charred, one should quickly take it, recite the King of Vidyās once, and whoever remembers [the name]— [...he shall be brought under one's power.]

By circling it, one summons; by striking it with the thumb, the embryo is transferred. Furthermore, I shall explain the supreme ritual activity of the eight-line mantra. In the center of the expanse of space, one should visualize a moon mandala. In the center of the wheels of body, speech, and mind, one should draw the wheel of great bliss. It is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp, encircled by garlands of vajras, lotuses, and wheels.

In the center of the triple-circle, encircled by a garland of various vajras, one should project a mass of light rays. Furthermore, adorned with light rays of activity in white, red, and blue, one should write in the center the heart-mantra of the Hero (*vīra*) and the name of the one to be accomplished, according to the ritual instructions as they have been taught. This is the great protection; it is the most excellent of all protections against infectious diseases and abdominal ailments.

If even poisons, diseases, the harassment of ḍākinīs, the harm of planets, māras, obstructors, and those with rotting bodies cannot cross over its shadow, what need is there to mention its physical body? One should visualize the syllable resembling the moon’s reflection; it disperses [obstacles] in the ten directions. By means of white [light], pacification occurs; by black, death occurs in an instant; by red—

One will gain mastery; by that very means, one will certainly summon. With yellow [mantra], one paralyzes; together with the host of armies and so forth, one suppresses. This supreme heart-essence of the Yoginī, more secret than the secret, the well-concealed reality (*tattva*) of mantra—the glorious Heruka, the Great Vajra—those who do not know this tantra and lack devotion for the great guru will not obtain the fruit of the siddhi of mantra.

"OḌḌIYĀNA! The yogin desires yoga; by completely abandoning this secret mantra, one will not attain the fruit. It is like someone who, desiring grain, threshes chaff; that is a meaningless labor, and the fruit will not be attained. Therefore, whoever desires the supreme [attainment] should strive to rely upon a Vajra Master; this is the desire for the secret mantra."

"By the blessing of conduct, the fruit is bestowed. This concludes the explanation of the ninth chapter from the *Herukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-mūla*, titled "The Glorious Heruka. Next, regarding the statement "the three bodies (kāyas) shall be explained," the term "three bodies" refers to the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, and the Emanation-body. Among these, there is the "secret of body and speech."

The characteristic of the concordant result of merit is the characteristic of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* of the Tathāgata; it is the characteristic of the conventional and the ultimate. That which enters into and realizes dependent origination is neither annihilated nor eternal; through the cultivation and mastery of meditative concentration that enters the path of mental consciousness, one does not...

That which is without conceptualization (*dharmas*), free from all afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), without purification (*vyavadāna*), not empty, not an object of the body, transcending the sphere of activity [of the senses], and not an object of the nature of the mind—that is the *dharmakāya*, which enters into equality with the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) of all Tathāgatas. Thus, one should view the three bodies of the Tathāgatas through the lens of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Now, the practice for those [deities] shall be explained. What is it? It is "the glorious Heruka, the non-dual union. This means that in the center of the celestial mansion (*vimāna*), from the complete transformation of the syllable *Bhrūṃ*, there arises an eight-spoked wheel. In its center, upon an eight-petaled multicolored lotus, is a moon mandala. In the center of that [moon], from the complete transformation of the *Ālikāli* [vowels and consonants], there appears the body of Vajrasattva.

The white deity has one face and four arms; his right hands hold a vajra and a small drum, and his left hands hold a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a bell. He embraces the red-colored Vārāhī, abiding in the posture with the right leg extended. One should visualize that through the yoga of rubbing the object to be rubbed, he is melted by the blazing fire of passion. From the light rays [emanating] from him, the yogin emerges.

Visualizing that one is being perfectly exhorted by the vajra songs of the Mothers, recite: *Oṃ hūṃ ā ma hā su kha ā la la la ho | Ma hā su kha ra tsa ta stvām | Su ra ta su kha bi yoga su ra to ā ho ma hā su khām su kha ma nu siddhi ho | Su ra ta sa mā ya so khyaba yām | Oṃ hūṃ ā ho ā ho bhaga vān ma hā su khām | Auttra sarbo tha mo so khyama ya hūṃ ā la la ||* (Contemplate that you are being perfectly exhorted by the vajra songs of the Mothers.)

LA HO, STAM BA RA MA SU KHA MA LEN DU PO PO TIM MA DZA LA SU KHĀM Ā LA LA LA HO, BITI SVABHYA MAYA. Immediately after the sound of the voice, which is like an echo, has been uttered, one assumes that very form and remains there; the Lord of the Families, whose nature is the Dharmakāya, is luminous, the glorious Dakini of the Heart-Space, Great Bliss, blue in color and of great majesty, radiant like ten million suns.

On the ground, he has the appearance of a wrathful deity and that of a sixteen-year-old; he is fully complete with all the major marks and perfectly adorned with all the minor signs. He has four faces and twelve arms, and dwells in a posture with his right leg extended. He has three eyes, a frowning face, and is slightly distorted; his left and right faces are white and yellow, while the western face is red.

Red in color, his first two hands are properly joined holding a vajra and a bell; with another pair of hands, he seizes the head of Viṣṇu and wears Viṣṇu’s garment. In his remaining right hands, he holds a battle-axe, a trident, a sword, and a *caṅte'u* (small drum). In his left hands, he holds a noose, a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and makes the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*). [The skull...]

The hero is bound by a garland of skulls, his topknot tied with a crescent moon at the crown of his head; he wears ornaments marked with various vajras, is girt with a tiger-skin loincloth, and is adorned with all the [ornaments]. He embraces the Vajraḍākinī; he has one face, two arms, three eyes, is naked, and is blue in color. He holds a skull-bowl marked with a *duṃ* syllable and possesses all the ornaments.

Her right hand is completely extended and her left embraces [the consort] while holding a skull-cup; her right [other hand] brandishes a vajra and makes the threatening mudrā (*tarjanī*). On the petals are the ḍākinīs and so forth. On the eight spokes of the wheel are Pracaṇḍā and the others, and from Khavāmukhī up to Yamamathinī—these are the twenty yoginīs.

Regarding the one-faced, four-armed [deities], the white, yellow, red, and green ones are the ḍākinīs and so forth; they are marked at the boundaries by severed skull-cups. Furthermore, the white, yellow, red, and green ones occupy the cardinal directions in counter-clockwise order. The light-blue, yellow, green, and yellow ones reside in the intermediate directions in clockwise order. [Skull-]Cup.

The heroes (vīras), such as Pa'i dum bu can and Rab tu gtum mo, have four arms; the yoginīs (yoginīs) have two arms. For the heroes, [the hand implements] are the vajra, the bell, the khaṭvāṅga, and the ḍamaru; for the goddesses, they are the skull-cup, the vajra, and the threatening gesture (tarjanī). At the time of the empowerment of the heart and so forth, there are only the four vajras. [This concerns] the body...

The meditation on the *samādhi* of Speech and Mind (*vākcittasamādhi*) and the *sattva* is as before. As for the Vajra of Speech, it is also red in color; its distinction is that he wears the head of Mahādeva and holds a lotus and a bell. White, red, blue, and green are the colors of the left-turning direction. Yellow, white, green, and sky-blue are...

This is the boundary of the right circumambulation. As for the Wheel Power-Maiden (*cakravega*) and the others of the Body Vajrī family, they are as before; however, the distinction is that they hold a wheel, a bell, and a Brahma-head, and wear the skin of Brahmā. They embrace the Buddha-Ḍākinī, who is white in color, holds a skull-cup and a wheel, and makes the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*) at those who are hostile. She is blue.

The green, red, yellow, and blue [colors] are those of the ḍākinīs and so forth, arranged counter-clockwise. The black, yellow, red, green, moon-white, smoke-colored, pale, and white [colors] are those of the cardinal and intermediate directions. *Oṃ śrī vajra he he ru ru kāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | ḍākini jvalasambara svāhā*. This is the mantra of the Mind-Ḍākinī.

Oṃ hāṃ bha ga dha ka āḥ arolika dākini dzala sambhara hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the heart mantra of Padma Khachöma (Padma Ḍākinī). Oṃ āḥ arolika dziṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the near-heart mantra. Oṃ padma ḍākini hrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ sarva padma ḍākiniye āḥ.

HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. This is the heart mantra and near-heart mantra of the Goddess (Lhamo). OṂ ŚRĪ DĀKINĪ JVALA SAMBARA RULU RULU BHRŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. OṂ BHRŪṂ ĀṂ BHRŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ. These are the heart mantra and near-heart mantra of the Buddha-Ḍākinī. OṂ BUDDHA DĀKINĪYE VAIROCANĪYE BHRŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. OṂ HŪṂ SARVA-BUDDHA-DĀKINĪYE.

*Hūṃ Bhūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā*. This is the heart mantra and the near-heart mantra of the Goddess. One should understand the ritual application for inferior yogins: having repeatedly smeared many *yung kar* seeds with the blood of a victim’s flesh, one should plant them in a secret field on the eighth day under the constellation Puṣya (*skar rgyal*) at the time when the sun is rising.

Having summoned that [spirit] into its skull-cup which is smeared with marrow and blood, one should generate it and take whatever seeds of ripening are appropriate. Then, with a focused mind, one should press the wick of the lamp so that it does not touch the oil, and place the lamp so that it does not touch the ground, protecting it through mantra and yoga. Thereafter, on a particularly auspicious day, having prepared a maṇḍala before oneself, one should recite the mantra.

Having made offerings according to the ritual procedure, one should present a *bali* offering consisting of meat and blood to the deities who are non-dual with glorious Heruka. Then, resting in the conduct of Heruka, the great yogin should perform the recitation and bestow blessings; he should cause the essence-mantra of the syllable *HŪṂ* to resound with a terrifying sound. Thereafter, upon a wind mandala stirred by the wind, [he should visualize...]

Visualize a victory banner (*dhvaja*) with the syllable *HŪṂ* arranged upon its feet, and smear it with the previously mentioned marrow. Then, starting from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head, continuously fumigate it with the incense of great *guggulu*. With the flower of the maṇḍala, strike the hearts and heads of all the yogins; while reciting the mantra with pride, ring the bell forcefully.

Having performed the ritual, I shall now explain how to place the mudrā of the birth-place upon one’s own forehead. At that time, various obstructing spirits (*bgegs*) will arise within the body of the corpse and create hindrances. To repel those obstructors by means of substances that accomplish the great mantra, one should not be afraid; rather, one should appropriately display the heroic commitment (*samaya*) through fierce forms, [using] the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) together with liquor.

One should say, "Bestow the *torma* upon this skull-cup and grant me the accomplishment of the yogic power of moving through space (*khecarī-siddhi*). Then, taking the marrow dripping from his body and pouring it into any suitable vessel such as a skull-cup, if one anoints the soles of the feet with it, the accomplishment of moving through space will be achieved. Furthermore, if one takes the seed-syllable of *sbur ter* (a type of resin) together with the semen of a fish-eater and a *byi dang ka*...

Repeatedly soak the seeds with blood and yogurt, place them inside a skull filled with soil from a charnel ground, and perform the *torma* offerings and other rites as previously described to an appropriate extent. Then, take the fully ripened seeds and place them on a donkey; they will become [the desired substance]. Likewise, repeatedly soak those seeds with blood and yogurt, and fumigate them with incense made of meat and bone powder.

Having generated it within its skull, if one takes the fruit that has ripened at that time and places it in the mouth, one will see it as having such a form; it will grant longevity, freedom from illness, and all excellent prosperity. Likewise, one may create the forms of owls, crows, hawks, peacocks, domestic fowl, and so forth. If it is expelled from the mouth, it is as before. On the day of the *Pūrṇamā* constellation during the waning moon, under the influence of the sun planet, [one should perform this with] *lita*.

Having taken the seeds of the *la'i sa bon* (the "la" seed), on a Sunday during the waning moon, one should take the seeds of *ma du lung ga* while naked; place the best of whatever limbs [are available] at the top, generate it from flesh, and adorn the consort’s hands with the essence of bone, marrow, fat, and bone. Having smeared oneself with ashes, if one sprinkles them upon that, [it will subdue] the *'bu srin* and so forth.

One will not be oppressed by the New Year’s festival. With the ritual of the yantra accompanied by mantras, the wise should always wash [the image] with warm water. Having performed the ritual of recitation with the mantras of Yamāntaka and Vighnāntaka, one should offer a *bali* cake to the meat-eater. Otherwise, it will be carried away and taken off. With the mantra of Buddhalocanā, one should [wash] the form...

One should wash it with the heart-mantra of Māmakī; one should generate it with Tārā, and likewise, one should protect it with Pāṇḍaravāsinī. In that way, being free from defects and having been generated, it will undoubtedly become a substance for accomplishment (*siddhi-dravya*). Therefore, one should take its seed-syllable as previously taught and wrap it three times. Three *māṣas* and seven and a half *ratis* is the measure of the sun; four *māṣas*—

Three *dang ra* and one half-*rati* is the measure of the moon; three *ma sha* and four and a half *rati* is the measure of the fire-maker (*sreg byed*). Thus, when pills of the sun, moon, and fire-maker are prepared in that successive order and placed in the mouth by one possessed of intelligence, they cause [the tongue] to fall out. The three worlds will not be seen by the sun or moon, yet if [the pill] is taken from the mouth, they will be seen once again. Furthermore, [as for] the iron...

If one places it in the mouth without wrapping it with the three [wrappings], it will immediately transform into the form of Madulunga; if it is removed, one will be liberated. Regarding the statements such as "the words will be stolen," these refer to the accomplishment of mantra, and not otherwise. Then, the wheel of mantra is the supreme ritual action.

In the center of the expanse of space, one should visualize a moon mandala with the color of refined gold as recited by the mantra. In its center is a blossomed lotus adorned with sixteen petals; in the center of that is an eight-petaled [lotus] with a pericarp. On the eastern side of the sixteen petals: *oṃ śrī he he ru ru kaṃ vajradākinī jvalasambhara*. In the center: *ra* and *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. As for the directions...

The left side is clockwise, and the cardinal and intermediate directions are adorned with skull-cups. At the navel, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) interspersed with the syllable *svāhā*. The center is encircled by a garland of crossed vajras (*viśvavajra*), and the exterior is surrounded by a rim of vajras. Adorned with blazing red light, it is further embellished with the smoke of human fat and vermilion sandalwood; its limbs are decorated with bone ornaments, and it is naked.

Having become one with them, write it yourself; go to the equal abode of the Mamos. Seated upon a very soft cushion and visualizing the yoga of the deity, bind that mudrā of the birth-place. Facing toward the object of accomplishment, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. From red sandalwood powder, fashion the image of the one to be accomplished, and place a wheel at its navel. Birth...

Having positioned it, one should draw out the thread, either from the nostril or by moving the little finger while holding the mudrā. Grasping the thread, one should rotate the wheel abiding in the mind throughout the three times. Even if killing a brahmin, there is no doubt that accomplishment will be attained within seven days; alternatively, one may anoint it with the three pungent substances.

Even by means of *spratsil* (mercury), one should thoroughly smear [the site]; with a bed of copper, one should clear away the birthplace. Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over countless *seng ldeng* leaves, a person of intelligence will, within seven days, certainly summon the object of accomplishment. Then, having written down the names of the daughter of the lord of men (*mānavendra*) and so forth, together with their retinue, and at the footprint of the one to be accomplished, [using] red sandalwood and... from the charnel ground...

Having gathered the remnants of the wrathful feast offerings into one through mantra, one should take two handfuls of dust with both hands and perform a fire offering (*homa*) in a smokeless fire of acacia wood while reciting the mantra. With those ashes, one should fashion an image of the person to be accomplished and place it in the center of a mandala wheel. Anointed with *piṣṭa* (ground flour), it should be heated; as long as the *piṣṭa* has not melted, if one performs the practice for seven days, [the deity]... of the gods.

If even the Lord of the World were to come, what need is there to mention ordinary people? Intoxicated, deluded, and exhausted, he will arrive driven by the force of the wind. By means of this, one shall also perform a binding: having written a wheel with the names mixed with *laṅgā* and *yūka* powders on a dry skull-cup, if it is hidden in a charnel ground or at a crossroads, one will be bound for as long as one lives. Śrī He...

This concludes the explanation of the tenth chapter from the *Herukābhidhāna-tantra*, the Commentary on Difficult Points (*Pañjikā*) concerning the introductory section on the methods of accomplishment. Now, with the words "Furthermore, [it] shall be explained," and so forth, [the text] describes the seizing of those who are wealthy for seven births and so on—that is, those whose births are uninterrupted by others. Since its characteristics are taught in the forty-ninth chapter, they are not discussed here. The glorious *Heruka*...

This is the explanation of the eleventh chapter from the *Bai dka’ ’grel* (Commentary on Difficult Points), concerning the introductory section on the methods of accomplishment. Then, regarding the statement "Next, the *upahr̥daya* (near-essence) will be explained," it is: *Oṃ hrīḥ*.

HA HA HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ; this is the essence that summarizes the activities for summoning and so forth. Upon a six-petaled lotus marked with a seed-syllable and a *kośa*, beautified by the moon and adorned with an excellent vajra garland, one should draw an outer wheel resembling the stainless light of the moon. On the six petals of the lotus, the great vidyā-syllables should be drawn, circling from the left. [The syllable] of the Māras...

This is the *Cakravartin* (Wheel-King) known as the "All-Repelling. Regarding the arrangement of that wheel: the six yoginīs are the heart-mantras; in the center is the seventh, Heruka. In the charnel ground at the corner of the tongue, one should draw [the syllables] together with one's own semen. Then, reciting the King of Secret Mantras from the mouth, and extending the hand toward the direction of devotion, one should visualize the object of accomplishment before oneself and remain in meditative equipoise.

If one performs the rite with devotion and longing, one will come to the world of the gods; what need is there to mention ordinary beings? Alternatively, take red sandalwood, long pepper, and asafoetida, and mix them together with earth from the footprint of the person to be accomplished. Having fashioned an image of that person out of this [mixture], draw a wheel and place it in the heart. Then, while reciting the name of the person, perform the visualization.

One will certainly be summoned; by this application of practice, one gains mastery over the lords of the earth, as well as wealth and people. "Emaciated" means possessing power. "Completely casting this into water" means by visualizing a wheel upon the hand. "Human blood" refers to the blood of that very hero. "In a vessel" refers to a skull-cup (*kapāla*).

Regarding "Par ro, nyan mig" (Blood-Ear, Hearing-Eye): "Nyan" means the ear. By the mere touch of it, the eyes become sharp; this is obtained from the edge of the continent. "Khrag dang" (and blood) refers to the blood of the hero’s heart, which has been soaked again and again and dried in the shade. "Lcags gsum" (the three metals) is as previously explained. "Lhag par gnas par byas la" (having performed the consecration) means having bestowed [the blessing].

This is the sequence of the ritual for consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Regarding the phrase "having entered the mouth of glorious Heruka": on top of a corpse, in a secluded place such as a charnel ground or a cemetery, one should draw a maṇḍala with the five types of pigments; in its center, the object of accomplishment should be placed, and it should be fumigated with incense sticks (*guḍūcī*). The passage beginning with "by means of this near-essence mantra" and so forth is clear. Alternatively, at midday, [one should enter] into the wrathful...

With a mind overcome by the pride of the five elements, one should draw the wheel as previously described using fierce substances such as human bone powder, poisons, and so forth, upon a cloth from a charnel ground or on the leaf of an *arka* tree. Having fashioned an effigy (*pratimā*) of the victim with charnel ground ashes and inserted it into the heart, one should smear it with hair and marrow and repeatedly heat it; [by doing so], the body—

Having applied *tsa ba* (black salt) and scattered it upon the ground, one should bury it in ground scorched by fire. Then, having driven a human-bone kīla into the heart, fill all the joints with *tsher ma* (thorns), and pour water mixed with *tsi tshe* (vermilion) into the heart; [the victim] will experience great suffering and die. Alternatively, having taken the fruit of *yungs kar* (white mustard) grown on a human corpse, [recite the name of the person] and [apply it] to the image.

If one recites [the mantra] while striking that person with it, they will die instantly or be afflicted by a fever; however, if they are washed with milk, they will be liberated once again. On a cloth from a charnel ground, one should draw a wheel with *yung ba* or *ldong ros*. Then, mixing together red sandalwood powder, *ske tse*, salt, dust from the footprint of the person to be accomplished, and iron filings, one should wrap it in cloth.

Carve a kīla about eight finger-widths long with four edges; recite [the mantra] seven times over it while including the name of the enemy. If it is buried, the enemy will be bound for as long as they live. If it is extracted and washed with milk, they will return to their natural state. Make an image of the person to be accomplished using the ashes of a corpse that has smallpox scars; write the name of the individual along with a *cakra* and insert it into the heart. Then, of that very...

It is said: "If one recites the *thal bas* seven times and strikes [the victim], one will seize their form. Regarding those to be afflicted by disease, if one writes a wheel with the name of the person mixed into the heart of the syllable *yi dags*, they will be afflicted by it. For those to be caused to suffer abdominal pain, it should be done at the navel of the syllable *yi dags*. For those to be made to stammer, one should use a wheel of wind and clouds. For those to be pierced with sharp pain, it is at the knot.

Regarding the third [application]: for poison and leprosy, one should draw [the figure] within the sign of whichever planet it may be; by doing so, [the planet] will seize [the affliction]. Regarding "the ashes of the fire of the burnt offering": having fashioned an image with the ashes from the medicinal burnt offering previously explained, one should insert a wheel into its heart and strike it while reciting the name of the person; then even that deity itself will not see [the practitioner].

If one recites the *chu la lan brgya rtsa brgyad* (one hundred and eight times) and casts [the effigy] into water, it will appear once again. Regarding the phrase "with the mudrā of the joined skulls," one should place [the effigy] inside two mad dog skulls joined together. Having inserted a wheel endowed with the five "maddening" [syllables] along with the victim's name, one should recite [the mantra] seven times without exhaling the breath, bind it, and having sprinkled it with consecrated water, [cast it] into a charnel ground.

If one hides it while reciting its name, that person will go mad; by that same [mantra], even a thousand people will go mad. If one takes it out and washes it with milk, they will be liberated once again. Having prepared excellent medicine, one goes to an empty house, recites the mantra one hundred times, and binds it to one's own crown of the head; this and so forth are taught according to the literal meaning of the words and are easy to understand. [Regarding] the enemy forces of others...

Regarding the phrase "facing toward" (*abhimukha*): one should draw this wheel on the palm of the left hand with red ochre or mustard seed, recite the mantra one thousand times, and then, having tucked it into the armpit, enter the city when facing an enemy army. Alternatively, one may write the *sattvaka* mantra—*śrāvakasārva-āyudhi-vara-nāma*—on a copper plate using red ochre and combine it [with the ritual].

Having made offerings according to the ritual procedure for Bris-la, smear it with *spra-tsil* (dung-smear), recite the mantra one thousand times, hold it in the left hand, and form the *khutsur* mudrā.

Reciting the King of Secret Mantra and adorned with all ornaments, as long as the thumb has not been released, all weapons shall be bound. Even if an enemy brandishes a weapon in his hand, as long as the thumb has not been released, he will be unable to discharge that weapon. Thereafter, the supreme medicine shall be explained in order to repel the five types of weapons.

1) Propelled by a mechanical device, 2) likewise propelled by the hand, 3) grasped after being shot, 4) and the five types of weapons wielded with the hand: throughout the three worlds without exception, these are the weapons. Propulsion by the hand is called the "wheel"; propulsion by a mechanical device refers to arrows and the like; grasping after being shot refers to javelins and so forth; and the hand-wielded weapon is the display of strength.

The sword and so forth are held by Pāñcika; the wheel and the medicinal herbs by Sudarśana; the arrows and so forth by Ākarṣaṇī and Vidhākinī; the nooses and so forth by the Aupatas; the hand-weapon by Aparājita, who is white; the sword and so forth by Unmādinī; and those excellent medicines, having been gathered on an auspicious day and consecrated with the five nectars, are applied to the wound.

A girl from Śāṇa, having anointed herself with blue flowers, was made to fill a brahmin’s skull-cup with the soil from eight or fourteen cremation grounds of Maṅro. After she had performed the pouring of water and the offering of *bali* cakes exactly as instructed, [the master] took a fine leaf of the *smin-pa* plant under the constellation Puṣya and the planet Sun. While remaining in meditative equipoise, the King of Mantras caused the earth to descend.

Having thoroughly protected the *poṣadha* (vow), one should wrap all those [implements] together in a counter-clockwise direction, spin them into thread, and bind it around the neck or the head. Then, even if weapons are turned back and cannot strike, and even if one is struck by all the weapons, no sensation of harm will arise; one will not be cut by weapons, and the body will become a vajra-body. Alternatively, with a single great hero alone, the weapons—

Once the great medicine known as *piṇḍakāra*, which causes all [poisons] to be averted, has been obtained, the practitioner, on an auspicious day, should place its fully ripened fruit within a brahmin’s skull using the previously explained sequence of preparation. Then, when the tree has ripened, at the time of sunrise on a Sunday, one should take its fine roots, pointing them toward the north, and plant them in the earth.

If one holds the *lama* in the mouth and, according to the sequence of instruction, holds it at the throat and the crown of the head, all that is moving and unmoving will be rendered stupefied. Furthermore, one should eat it together with butter; one should consume it with courage until it has dissolved in the throat. As long as it has not been digested, the body becomes like that of a Vajradhara, such that even if struck by weapons, [one remains unharmed].

It will not cause harm, like a drop of dew. Alternatively, one should take the root of an *aśvattha* tree that has been placed inside a brahmin’s skull according to the sequence of the armor-mantras of the past, and fashion it into a pill according to the ritual procedure. One should place into the mouth a pill encircled by the three syllables (*om āḥ hūṃ*) which abide in their respective parts—the sun, the moon, and the fire-giver. Then, with all weapons, the Great Hero...

Cancer shall be averted, and by the mere scent of this [substance], epidemics, abdominal ailments, poisons, the harms of ḍākinīs, and the planets will flee far away, just as an elephant flees at the scent of a lion. Furthermore, one should place a peṭā seed within the skull of a brahmin according to the ritual procedure and extract excellent medicine; then, on the constellation Puṣya and under the planets the Sun and the Moon, one should perform offerings and bali rituals.

Having performed the practice with the mudrās and the deity yoga of the practitioner, while reciting the mantra as before, one becomes naked with loose hair. Remaining in meditative equipoise, one gathers [the earth] entirely and places it in a skull-cup in the hand of the Yoginī so that it falls upon the ground. Then, having divided it into seven portions and bound them with white thread, if one holds them upon the crown of one's head, whatever weapons exist upon the surface of the earth—

The *cha du ma* [mudrās] will be destroyed, just as darkness is by the sun. Then, the ritual for the *paṅka* [mudrā] is explained: having sought the Great Black One (*Mahākāla*) and the Great Medicine (*Mahauṣadhi*) from the King and the Sun, and being provided with offerings and *bali* cakes, one should listen at the time of midnight. At dawn, with the nature of a deity, naked and with hair loose, one should take [it] while remaining in profound meditative equipoise. Like a preeminent bull...

Having taken the shoulder-blade of a goat, one should later mix it together; having had it bound by a young maiden, one should anoint the body with it. As long as it remains on the body, for that long the weapon will not take its toll; even poison will not affect the body, for the Great Self shall consume the medicine. Furthermore, having taken the *kumārī* plant and combined it with earth from the footprint of a young maiden, along with the parts of a sheep’s shoulder-blade...

If one makes a cord of equal measure and applies it as a binding, it will not be severed even by thirty [blows]. Furthermore, if one takes a *cāṇakī* stalk and anoints the body with a preparation made from earth containing a single mark and a single tree, that body will not be destroyed even by thirty [blows]. One should perform those [rites] for a period of one year; thereafter, others may be performed. Then, the great hero Vajrapāṇi shall worship all heroes.

Having performed [the rite], the first emergence from the womb is as follows: having found the corpse of one who died while still nursing at the mother’s breast, one should perform the non-dual worship of glorious Heruka. By placing the *bali* offering in meditative equipoise, one provides protection. Having slit it open from the nape of the neck, one should take its tongue. [The mantras] are *Bhringga*, *Ra*, *Dza*, *Du*, *Du-ra*, *Kām*, *Kām*, *Dza*, and *Ga*; it is invincible by others. Having taken [it] from the King and the Sun, it is endowed with the five [substances].

Having bound it together and made it into a pill, one should dry it in the shade and then roll it between three iron bars. One with seven and a half *rati* [of mercury] is for three parts of meat; one with two and a half *rati* is for four parts of meat; one with five *rati* is for three parts of meat. They should be rolled in this sequence. Having rolled them and performed the perfect worship, if one recites the mantra one thousand times and places them in the mouth, as long as they remain in the mouth, the earth-dwellers will be struck down.

Even those who are merely looked upon will be destroyed, just as dry grass is consumed by a blazing fire. It repels epidemics, abdominal ailments, poisons, the harms of ḍākinīs, and all the grahas, according to the command of Vajrasattva. Furthermore, that which is to be explained next shall be taught:

All sentient beings, being utterly deluded, diligently during the day take forest bark and weave it with the thread of a young maiden. Having wound it to the left side, they should weave it in three folds. After reciting the root mantra ten thousand times and having tied it, they should form a knot; there, with the left hand, they should examine the *mātr̥kā* [letters]. Twenty.

Abiding in the non-dual *rtza bzhi* and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), one should perform the offering of speech and bind the right hand. One must turn back all weapons; it is not otherwise for swords, arrows, and the like. With a focused mind, one should take the wool of the *śālmali* tree grown in the forest from the King. The hands of young maidens should be rubbed with earth and then weighed. [This is done] with the auspicious constellation *Skar ma*.

For those with powerful intellects, one should perform the knots while in profound meditative equipoise through the previously explained ritual actions. By holding this in mind, one will not be bound even by the thirty [knots]; rather, since all weapons become binding, the ritual procedure for the *karma* should be observed. Thus, from the Secret View, the great secret should be concealed by secrecy; the wise person should [protect] the minds of the unworthy at all times.

This concludes the explanation of the twelfth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-mūla*, titled "Can la mi sbyin" (Not to be Given to Others). Now, regarding the phrase "Then" (*atha*), it refers to what follows immediately. As for the statement, "The ritual activities are to be explained in their proper sequence," it begins with: *Oṃ hana māḥ*.

HI SVĀ HĀ HU BŪ ŚĀṬ HE HŪM HŪM HO PHAṬ HĀM STE RE RE ZHING NGAM. These are the syllables of the words of union; they should be applied appropriately with the forms of the six syllables and the various classes of heroic deities. Regarding that, as for the phrase "if one enters the path of the terrifying" and so forth, it means that by reciting [the mantra], one accomplishes everything desired in the mind according to the ritual procedure. Then, in the center is the mantra of the Hero (Vīra), which is that very same [mantra].

By means of the meditative concentration of intrinsic awareness (*vidyā-dhyāna*), through the thorough application of the hero’s wheel, all activities are to be performed.
