This should be drawn according to the following sequence: in the center of the moon is a vajra with three prongs and likewise six faces; in its center is a lotus well-situated upon six petals, which should be inscribed with the syllables of the mantra. The name of the one to be accomplished, as prescribed, [is written] along with Vajrasattva and the other Buddhas.

As explained in the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*, one should first draw the mantra in the center; the others likewise upon the lotus petals. Having completely abandoned the six long vowels, they should be placed in the hub of the vajra. With saffron, yellow orpiment, one’s own blood, and human fat, the practitioner should draw it according to the ritual procedure at the time of the moon or the sun. Having performed the recitation during the three periods of the day, one should make offerings.

Having performed this, one should take hold [of it]; having empowered it seven times with the mantra, it should be tied to the hem of one’s garment. When setting out on a journey, one will not be threatened by thieves or robbers.

One will be protected in all respects; there is no doubt that accomplishment itself will be attained. Furthermore, having drawn a circle around the center of that very wheel with a line made like a *bindu* ornament, one should tie a knot in the hem of one's garment with the syllable *mohana* interspersed with the name of the one to be accomplished along with their retinue. If one then departs while reciting this while meditating on the *dharmadhātu*, one will not be seen by gods or humans.

RO, [one should] place the *sambhāra* seed-syllable of Yang bi sha da ta ka ri'i (*yabhiṣadantakari*) in a brahmin’s skull according to the ritual procedure and generate it. Then, at the time when the moon is eclipsed, one should take a root growing toward the north, wrap it three times with iron, and recite the mantra one thousand times; it will become a rain-cloud. Alternatively, having taken the fruit of the *nyagrodha* tree that has been eaten by a black crow—the excrement of the fruit—one should, on an auspicious day, [place it] in a brahmin’s skull...

Having filled [a vessel] with earth scorched by lightning and offered it with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should pluck two leaves from a newly sprouted plant, wrap them three times with iron wire, worship them with offerings, recite the mantra, and place them on the shoulder. Then, gods and humans will not see [the person]. Regarding the phrase "whomever is touched by the hand that has recited the armor-mantra": [one should take] the smoke of *vārṣika* on a cloth from a charnel ground.

Having drawn a *āśvakarṇa* leaf with chalk and yellow *yung ba* (barley) flour, marked with a wheel and lines, and having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) along with their retinue and mount outside [the diagram], one recites the mantra one thousand times. Furthermore, having fashioned an image of the person to be accomplished from the dust of their footprints and charnel ground ashes, one places it within the center of the wheel, scatters yellow flowers over it, and [tramples] it with the feet.

Pressing with the left hand, one should recite eight hundred times and hide it; then, having constructed a house [of mantra] residing at the heart above that, whomever one seizes by name will become rigid like a spear, such that even those of the Thirty-three Heavens cannot move them. To liberate others from enemy armies, if they are washed with milk, they will return to their natural state. Regarding "with one's own blood," and so forth, it is clear.

Visualizing oneself in the form of the Wrathful King (*krodharāja*), all the subtle atoms of water are generated as the deities of the maṇḍala; by means of the form of their crown ornaments, they will travel upon the surface of the water. When the circle of yoginīs and heroes enters into union, if one pleases them with both the left and right hands, the yoginīs of the six families will be brought under control. *Skar ma rgyal* (Victory over the Stars).

Regarding the phrase "having made it into cloth": having obtained a king of snakes, one should cut all its white and black stripes into separate pieces. Having distinguished between the black and white, one should take seeds of cotton and, on a Sunday during the white lunar fortnight, soak the white pieces in milk and ashes for a day and a night, bury them in the ground, and plant them. As for the black pieces, [soak them] in milk and ashes...

Having consecrated the *kyang sa bon* (the seed-syllable of the *kyang*), on the day of the *rgyal* (the eighth lunar day) of the waning moon, one should also perform the *spag* (the ritual of weaving) upon that very day and portion of the earth. Having taken the wool that has been produced according to the division of the white and black parts, on another *rgyal* day, for the wool that has produced the white qualities, it should be spun by a yellow-clad yoginī; during that day, the thread should be woven by a yellow-clad person. Thus, [for] the black...

For the cloth used to move the *po'i* [the ritual implement], one should offer it to the Yoginī on the day of the *nakṣatra* Maghā during the dark fortnight; then, while the sun is still in that same sign, one should fasten it with a blue cord in such a way that it wraps around the body. One should perform the accomplishment under another sun of the *nakṣatra* Maghā during the blue and white phases; having recited the mantra thirty-nine thousand times over the cloth, one should then recite it eight hundred times.

One should perform fumigation: on cloth produced during the waning moon, one should fumigate with the flesh and bones of a black *ākāru* and a black *dumbu*. Likewise, on cloth produced during the waning moon, one should fumigate with the flesh and bones of a white *dumbu*, together with *saṅkhapuspa*. Then, having venerated the Guru, the heroes (*vīra*), and the yoginīs (*yoginī*) with devotion, one should visualize the deity yoga and [proceed with] the King...

One should issue the command to the yoginī upon the cotton cloth used for the practice (*la bsgrub pa'i ras*). By reciting ten thousand times with the body on the left side, success will be achieved; one's shadow will become invisible, and one will travel and return through the sky over a distance of a thousand *yojanas*. Even that very deity will not see [the practitioner], and one will travel upward as far as the limit of Akaniṣṭha. Furthermore, as for the emanation...

If one places [the substance] inside the belly of a *gyi-rgyal-po* (serpent-king) and burns it so that the smoke does not escape, and then adorns it with spontaneously arisen *thalaba* flowers, reciting the mantra thirty thousand times over it, and uses it as an eye salve, one will become invisible. Alternatively, one may place a *gyi-rgyal-po* inside a human skull; once it has rotted and the bones have fallen away, one should take them and cast them into a river flowing toward the ocean.

Having recited the mantra ten thousand times over a piece of its bone and ground it, if one makes a *tilaka* mark on the forehead, one’s shadow will become invisible. Alternatively, having consecrated its skull and made a *tilaka* mark with that powder, one’s shadow will likewise become invisible. Regarding the statement, "Whatever sense faculty [is affected], one proceeds with the nature of that very [faculty]," this refers to the sense faculties such as the eye and so forth.

Because the [faculties] (*rnams*) focus on their respective objects, such as forms and sounds, they are the "masters" (*bdag po*); the meaning is that those very faculties experience the taste of the nature of whatever is encountered throughout all modes of conduct. The term "supremely" (*mchog tu*) refers to having previously focused on the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). The phrase "of the application of meditative equipoise" (*mnyam gzhag sbyor ba'i*) refers to the vajra [recitation] of the sequence of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).

Having cultivated the pride of the *sattva* and abiding firmly in the great yoga (*mahāyoga*) of oneself, one who has attained the source of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*) through mental familiarity with the manifest awakening of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), that preeminent great yogin—“all things become the nature of the Buddha,” it is said—is like the essence of the *piṇḍīta* tree.

If one recites the essence of the juice of the *aśvattha* tree—which has been produced by the ritual procedure as previously taught—one thousand times, and then forms a *bindu* (drop) from it and meditates upon it, by the power of that meditation, whatever is emanated will turn into wood. By that same ritual procedure, having taken the seeds of white mustard (*yavaka*) produced within a Brahmin’s skull and placed them inside an elephant’s skull, [one should mix them] with the flour of the fruit that has grown there.

If one recites [the mantra] one thousand times over the dust from the footprint of an elephant and strikes someone with it, that person will become an elephant; and riding upon that elephant, one will be victorious over a thousand elephants. This concludes the explanation of the thirteenth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-mūla*. Now, regarding the statement "Next, the method of accomplishment (*sādhanopāya*) shall be explained," by this it is established:

"Because it acts as a protector, it is the great *sādhana*. For the sake of reversing [the state] through the power of the mind, by means of the yoga in the form of a donkey," refers to the power of the mind—that is, the mental force—and being endowed with its ritual procedure, one is turned away from all evil views and obscurations. Thus, by swiftly and completely exchanging the purified body for one like a dream, one becomes free from agitation and indestructible.

The one who holds all yogas without exception, the supreme yogin of the *khara-yoga*, through union equal to all Buddhas, binds the net of the ḍākinīs. In the groves of Padmaśrī, the barbarian seal of all Buddhas, amidst the flavors in the center of the forest through the bliss of all joys, are the ḍākinīs, the lāmās, the khaṇḍarohās, and the rūpiṇīs.

Sporting in various forms with [diverse] retinues, radiant and adorned with every ornament, they should be arranged as previously described. Furthermore, the ḍākinīs—whose faces have the form of donkeys, whose eyes are blood-red, and who hold tridents whirling upward in their hands—possess four arms, carrying khaṭvāṅgas and skull-cups, and they stand upon seats of human corpses.

[He is] one who blazes like a fire of *śiṃśapā* wood, has three eyes, loose hair, and is naked. As for the marks, ornaments, garments, and so forth of all [deities], including the Lord [Vajradhara] and the others, they are to be viewed as previously explained. However, all the heroes (*vīra*) of the mind wheel (*cittamaṇḍala*) have the faces of Garuḍas; the faces of the heroes of the speech wheel (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) are peacock-faced; [and those of] the body wheel (*kāyamaṇḍala*)—

Dpa’ bo (Vīra) has the face of a lion; Khva’i gdong pa (Kākāsyā) and the others have faces corresponding to their own names. Gshin rje’i gdong pa (Yamāsyā) and the others at the intermediate directions have the faces of a *mahiṣa*, a leopard, and a tiger, and likewise the faces of a wolf. All the maṇḍalas also have three eyes, with red eyes, completely embraced by great compassion, and arisen from the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). This...

O supreme yogin, you who bring all suffering to an end! From the root at the navel, by means of both the right and left [channels], the moon and sun are explained. Like the flower of the plantain tree, standing upright from the root at the navel, the lotus resembling a cow's hoofprint should be known as being the size of a thumb. As for the lotus directed downward, it is like the light of the moon.

That which is eternally empty in the center is the syllable *Hūṃ*, whose very nature is wind. Blazing like a lamp, it moves upward from the heart due to the complete filling of the lower wind; it is explained as passing through the crown of the head. The yogi who is equal to the three worlds has a mind that abides in the hearts of all sentient beings; his mind has become equanimous, and he has attained mastery over all minds.

Having attained the supreme *pāramitā*, in a single moment of intense radiance, he destroys all masses of darkness. Just like the sun’s light or a jewel, he illuminates the three worlds—both moving and unmoving—without exception. Blazing with majesty like the fire at the end of an eon, he is unwavering and unerring; he transcends causes and analogies, is immutable and unstained. As for the five obscurations:

Rnam par spangs, the glorious Heruka himself, is by nature devoid of self-cognition; therefore, in that very instant, one perceives the omniscient mind itself—past, future, and present—all at once. This yogin of the "donkey" beholds it as clearly as if it were resting in the palm of his hand. For the sake of this realization, having abandoned all distractions, he remains for about six months in a state of profound darkness.

Through the accomplishment of the *pas* (seed-syllable) of the joyful ḍākinī, one who possesses this accomplishment will attain all yogas. Though devoid of ascetic discipline, one becomes possessed of it; though stained with impurity, one becomes pure. Though poor, one becomes wealthy; though ill, one becomes free from disease. Having attained freedom from aging and death, one teaches the Dharma without having heard it, [liberating beings] from manifold sufferings.

In the *Tshogs la* [Tantra], it is said: "The liberator of sentient beings, the unsurpassed teacher of the doctrine, shall behold in a single instant everything that exists within the three worlds—attainments such as invisibility and the others, the divine eye, and the five superknowledges; likewise, the exhaustion of life, the prolongation of life, and the transformation of species, whether into a donkey or an elephant, wherever it may be."

Even across many thousands of births, the yogin will here perceive them in their various forms. Having recognized those born here seven times, one should offer *bali* and perform fire offerings. Abiding in the secret at night with a non-conceptual nature, and having applied oneself excellently, there is no doubt that one will become a divine body and attain accomplishment. *Jalpa*.

"Bya ba" (the action) refers to a garland of conch shells; "gsang ba" (the secret) refers to the characteristics of the mantras of one who has been born seven times [as a brahmin]. This concludes the explanation of the fourteenth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-mūla*. Then, as for "brda" (the signs), these are the signs established by the yoginīs; they should be understood by those who desire the accomplishments (*siddhi*). First...

The phrase "thus it is said" is easy to understand; it means that because of the single-mindedness of intention, one will experience joy. This concludes the explanation of the fifteenth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*. Then, as for the word "then," it refers to the successive order. "Secret" means that it is not to be revealed to sentient beings who lack the fortune [to receive it]. "Great siddhi" means...

The practitioner himself is the agent of the non-dual Mahāmudrā. Who is he? He is explained as the Brahmin Vairocana; he is known as Ratnacandra, the Lord of Infinite Dance, the Painter Amoghasiddhi, and the *ḍombī* of Akṣobhya. He should be understood as belonging to the royal caste (*kṣatriya*) of the sixth, Vajrasattva. The seventh is that of Heruka.

The various classes of *sna* (nose) and so forth are the common people (*dmangs rigs*). Regarding the passage beginning with "Any woman who moves from the left," and so on, this is easy to understand; because it accords with the methods of the practitioner, it should be understood through diligent application. This concludes the explanation of the sixteenth chapter from the *Pañjikā* titled *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, concerning the introduction to the methods of accomplishment. Then, regarding the passage beginning with "Difficult to obtain," and so forth...

The very nature of great passion is difficult to find through means such as detachment from desire. What is that? It is the samaya mandala, the supreme pledge. Regarding the phrase "the five nectars," the five are earth and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the reality of the entity" (*dngos bden pa*) and so forth, it is because all phenomena are subsumed therein. Then, the nectar of the five [deities] has emptiness as its essence; through authentic union, they are condensed into one. That which is the essence is bliss; the bodhicitta called "wind" is this, the sovereign of all the sense faculties. One should generate it correctly in the center of that, beginning with the syllables.

Rūpa, Rūpiṇī, and Yoginī, Lāmā, and Khaṇḍarohā—these are explained as the four faces. Possessing the four unions, the fifth is the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), joined at the heart and the navel. Perfectly marked by the four petals, in its center is the Great Hero, adorned with eight arms. The first [pair] is completely filled with flesh. That...

With the blood of the second [deity] of the same nature, she holds the lattice mudrā that bestows empowerment with her remaining two hands. The fifth and sixth embrace the goddesses; the others kiss her mouth. Her body is white in color, radiating light like the stainless autumn sky. It is said that she has four faces—white, red, blue, and green—that blaze with splendor. She is Yamamathani and Bhīmā.

Nairṛtī, Bhīmā, Kuntī, Cakravegā, Surābhakṣī, and Aṣṭamī are correctly described as Vārāhī. The four-cornered [maṇḍala] has gates and intermediate directions; it is transformed into eight terrifying forms. They consume flesh and blood; first is the mudrā of spreading, second is the mudrā of rending the heart, third is the mudrā of causing bewilderment, and likewise, fourth is the mudrā of begging.

The fifth is the mudrā of dance; likewise, the sixth is the mudrā of slaying. The seventh is that which performs the placement, and the eighth is determined to be the mudrā of arising. Thus are the eight mudrās explained. Perfectly endowed with weapons in his hands, from many garlands of light rays, clouds of Buddha-multitudes stream forth. This beginningless and endless Being is Vajrasattva, the Great Bliss.

Alternatively, as previously explained, the three wheels pervade the sky with light. One should describe the supreme maṇḍala: in the center, the wheel should be correctly drawn, complete with spokes and a hub, described as having four petals, blazing with various colors. In its center is the Hero; pure like crystal and stainless, his first face is smiling.

He gazes with a passionate look, his brow furrowed in a blazing frown; terrifying with bared fangs, his right face is distorted, while the left is exceedingly wondrous. His broad face is most fearsome, and all his faces are ablaze. He has faces that are white, red, and likewise blue and green; he should be correctly depicted as having eight arms.

Possessing the glory of all ornaments, with a coiled tongue that is terrifying, fierce like the time of universal destruction, and fearsome and awe-inspiring in the charnel grounds; laughing loudly with the sound "Ha Ha" and uttering the syllable "Phem"—these four deities are explained as having one face and two arms: Vajrasattva in the east, and Vairocana is said to be in the south.

In the southwest is the meaningful King Amoghasiddhi, and in the north is Padmanarteśvara. Holding a skull-cup in his hand, he partakes of blood and semen. At the center of the wheel is Heruka, abiding while holding the implements previously described. Second is the great eight-spoked wheel, ash-colored with blazing red light rays. Through its clockwise and counter-clockwise arrangement, it is renowned as the "Manifestation" (Vighnāntaka). Its form...

Caṇḍā and Oḍḍiyānī, Lāmā Viśvavajrī with the child, Acalā, Devī, and Dīpā—the eighth is called Vajranarttī. These eight inner goddesses have white complexions and are radiant; they have one face and two arms, holding skull-cups filled with blood and khaṭvāṅgas in their hands. They possess three eyes, are adorned with all ornaments, and are full of grace.

The body of the deity of passion (*rāga*) is endowed with the beauty of compassion and joy. Then, the emanation of the deities of the wheels of mind, speech, and body is explained. According to their natural order and its reverse, starting from the eastern direction and so forth: Śaṅkhinī, Pukkasī, Māraṇī, Pītā, Bhedinī, likewise Caṇḍikā, Parvatī, and Tārā. That...

These are the deities of the Mind Wheel: Bhṛkuṭī, Trailokyavijayā, Daṃṣṭriṇī, Tathāgatī, Mahānāsā, Gajavaktrā, Mārjārī, and Hastijihvā. These are the deities of the Speech Wheel: Gavākṣī, Sunetrā, Caṇḍākṣī, Śyāmādevī, Mahābalā, Vanadharī, Gandhālī, Citrā, and Vāmanā. These are the deities of the Body Wheel...

Khorlo’o, those [goddesses] have beautiful faces and are accompanied by smiles; they are filled with compassion, longing, and intoxication. By joining the mantras that utter their own names with *oṃ*, *hūṃ hūṃ*, and *phaṭ*, through the differentiation of mind, speech, and body, the goddesses are blue in color and hold a copper knife and a skull-cup. Furthermore, the goddess whose body is red holds a lotus and a skull-cup, and the goddess whose body is white—

Daṅga, Khaṭvāṅga, and Khaṭvāṅgī, Durgā, Revatī, Tvaritā, Umā, Brahmāṇī, and Vaiśravaṇī are correctly explained as guarding the gates; they are to be applied at the four gates. She who holds a Khaṭvāṅga and drinks blood and semen—each of them is fully adorned with all ornaments, with hair loose and naked, [possessing] compassion and joy.

This king of all mandalas, which has never arisen and will never arise, is that which is logically fit to be consumed by all. Having blended things together as equal in their essential nature, one should not view them as pure or impure, nor as appropriate or inappropriate. Through the knowledge of the ten suchnesses, one should consume and enjoy everything.

"Having recognized the characteristics of the woman, one should worship her with the knowledge of reality. Regarding the phrase "with intense attachment" and so forth, it is literal and clear. However: "She who has form is called Citriṇī; she who has a conch is said to be Śabdā; Lāmā herself is Hasticarī; Parāvṛttā is Padminī; she who is irreversible is known as Airāvatī; Dīpikā and Kīlikā are each..."

Regarding the two types of *re-yaṅ-ni*, each has its own specific characteristic: one is like the fragrance of a lotus and the strength of a rutting elephant; the other possesses a melodious voice, speaks pleasantly, is gentle, and has a body radiant with youth. Her limbs are slender, her eyes resemble lotus petals, her hair is curled, her nose and teeth are well-proportioned, her fingers are short, her limbs are supple, and her nails are smooth.

Her complexion is the color of refined gold, her face is perfectly serene, and she who desires glory is like a lotus. She should be employed for rites of pacification (*śāntika*). She has the scent of an elephant, protruding lips, and thick thighs; she walks with the gait of a rutting elephant. Her fingers are long and her body is tall; her breasts are prominent and her hair is coarse. Her navel is deep and her breasts are firm; her eyes are subtle and [dark] as honey.

She is thin-waisted, speaks pleasantly, and has a melodious voice; she is lustful, with a receding lower lip and thick lips. Her feet are level and well-set. Always delighting in liquor and desiring wealth, she is the "Elephant-like Woman" (*gajinī*); one should diligently apply the practice for her expansion. The "Conch-like Woman" (*śaṅkhinī*) has the complexion of a conch, a slender face, and long forearms; she has the cry of a crow and the scent of a donkey, with thick teeth and long fingers.

With coarse hair and soft limbs, her body tall and her eyes small; with a thin neck and crooked teeth, a prominent nose and sunken cheeks; with a thin lower lip and the appearance of a venomous serpent—such is the Śaṅkhinī, who kills her husband; she should be employed for rites of subjugation (*vaśya*). As for the Citrā, she always delights in patterns, has various complexions, diverse forms, drooping breasts, and short nails.

Regarding the minor characteristics (*skad chung*): she has a small body and small features; her voice is harsh, like that of a crow by nature; she delights in the sound of crows; she possesses the power of coarse speech and desire; she should be employed for dark activities (*kṛṣṇa-karman*). The *Padmāvatī* belongs to the divine lineage (*deva-gotra*); the *Hastinī* belongs to the *yakṣa* lineage; the *Śaṅkhinī* is known as human; the *Citriṇī* belongs to the *gandharva* lineage; the *Vātāyā* belongs to the divine lineage; [the one of] the *graha*...

With long arms and a long neck, teeth that appear bright and lips that are thick, eyes as red as lotuses, a broad and expansive birth-place (vulva), large buttocks, thick and yellowish-white hair, a body that is firm and tall, a high and sharp nose, soft limbs and long hands, the gait of a swan and the voice of a swan, craving for fragrance, flowers, and milk, and being relaxed in giving— [This is the description of the female organ.]

Devoted to the gods, chief among powerful women, eating little yet possessing wealth—such a woman should be employed for rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*). She is called *Pilapiṇī*, the "Full-Breasted One. Tall of stature with thick calves, she has a broad face and narrow eyes; her ears hang down and her hair is coarse. Her voice is like a bee and her lips protrude; her body is full and she eats much, yet she has few desires and is always strong.

Delighting in assemblies, with slender waists, limbs that are robust, and long hair; with soft teeth and nails, feet that are even, and long noses; with bellies as full as vases, and faces as beautiful as the flanks of a vase—these should be applied for the rites of Pacifying and Increasing. As for the Kīlamātṛkās: their eyes are tremulous, they have downward-glancing eyes and narrow faces; their teeth are prominent, their bodies are emaciated, and their hair is wet.

Falling with great force, walking like one with white hair, limping and small of stature, with short arms, high breasts, thick calves, a small forehead, and thick eyebrows—when touched by such a person, one does not die; rather, one's kinsmen will weep for them. This is applied to black karma. The eighth is the mountain-dweller, Ri-dags-ma, Skal-bzang; she has a small belly and small feet, and her neck is like that of a mountain-dweller.

Her hair is fine and glossy, and her teeth are like the tips of a crow’s beak; beautiful in form, she has breasts like drops of nectar, and her touch is soft—she is said to be full of passion. Her voice is like the cry of a crow, and she is always naked and poor; her mind is harsh, she delights in sin, and she is of a lineage that reviles others. She should be employed for rites of power (*vaśya*); these eight are well known as the skull-bowl and the enemy-slayer.

The eight symbols of the attendants are the primary hand-symbols of Rūpiṇī and the others, according to the sequence of their respective families as taught. Furthermore, they consume the blood and semen from the mouths and skulls of others. This concludes the explanation of the seventeenth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, the pure state to be explained is the supreme station of the ḍākinīs": "supreme" (*parama*) refers to a multitude, meaning the various classes that become manifold. As it is said: "The noble classes are of one hundred types. Because they are perfectly established, they are called "stations" (*pada*); their very definition, as it has been taught, is that which is completely pure. "Samaya" refers to the yogins.

The suffix *kyi* follows [the preceding term], meaning "by that" it abides. This concludes the explanation of the eighteenth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-mūla*. Then, regarding the phrase "that which is to be correctly explained," it refers to the sequence of colors and marks (*liṅga*). The term *lāma* (l'a ma) means possessing the characteristics of qualities such as being desirable to the touch and so forth; it is a limb.

"All are completely perfected. The passage beginning with "of whomsoever" and so forth is easy to understand. "Rākṣasī" refers to the Single Application. Regarding the "lotus mudrā": one should offer the two hands encircling a lotus. Alternatively, the "lotus mudrā" is indeed the lotus mudrā; having placed the fortunate one before oneself, whether they have risen or are seated upon a cushion, in whatever manner appropriate.

One should cause the lotus to fully blossom; by swiftly joining the two together, the wise one should perform the vajra-consecration. The tortoise mudrā consists of joining the two palms together. In the Bhagavan’s tortoise mudrā, one touches while striking the palms together. Through the application of the mudrā and mantra, one causes the earth to quiver. It is the invincible mountain-scaling [mudrā]; or else, it is gentle.

One should know that the "Good Characteristics" (Mtsan Nyid Bzang) are the invincible *stanu*; it is called the "General Oblation Skull" (*spyi blugs thod pa*), or alternatively, it is called the "Oblation Body. Having bound the two hands in an embrace at the neck, one embraces while assuming the cross-legged posture; however the mudrā is understood, it is expressed as the "Response to the Mudrā. The passage beginning with "the fourteenth day" and so forth is easy to understand. Alternatively, it refers to the occasion of the fourteenth day.

Just as it is obtained, it is the fully blossomed and blazing lotus. That glorious one whose mind is equanimous possesses the characteristic of the Lotus-Bearer (*Padmavān*). The phrase "smiling with two lips" and so forth is easy to understand. Regarding the term "spear," one should grant the mudrā that displays a single yellow [object]. Then, by means of the vajra-paryaṅka, one abides in one's own vajra. This is the dance itself.

Regarding the phrase "the horse shall be taught": having embraced firmly and uttered the sound "oṃ," one performs the mudrās bound by the actions [of the deities]. Having performed the circumambulation, there are the Elephantess (Hastinī) and the Bliss-Attaineress (Sukhasādhinī). The fourteen [deities] are easy to understand. "One should worship according to one's ability" means [to offer as much as possible]. This concludes the nineteenth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-mūla*.

This is the explanation of the *pā* [syllable]. Furthermore, that which is to be explained next concerns the signs of the left hand; that is to say, the natures of both types of signs become one, and having become like a husband and wife in a state of intense passion, they perform all meditations. This is from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*.

This is the explanation of the twentieth chapter. Then, regarding the statement: "Next, I shall explain the great secret by means of five characteristics," the phrase "by means of five" refers to Vajradhara. By the power of great compassion, whatever method brings accomplishment to yogins—that very thing is the characteristic of the great secret; it is not within the sphere of experience of the Śrāvakas and others.

Because it is so; as for the passage beginning with "Whichever person touches the crown of the head," and so forth, this is literal and easy to understand. This concludes the explanation of the twenty-first chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*. Then, furthermore, the excellent explanation begins: "The distinction of the limb-mudrās" refers here to the Great Secret.

Regarding the term *lakṣaṇa*, "other" (*anya*) refers to that which is excellent (*dam pa*), by which the yoginīs are pleased. Regarding the term "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), the distinction from the palm of the hand is the fingers. As for the phrase "by which [one] knows," and so forth, it is to be taken according to the literal meaning of the words. This concludes the twenty-second chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*.

This was the explanation of the *pāda*. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then," it is literal and easy to understand. "Having made the ground the basis" means rising from one's seat. "Worship" refers to embracing and kissing [the consort] excellently. "Without moving the eyebrows" is for the sake of maintaining some degree of modesty. "Circumambulating in yoga" means accomplishing extraordinary bliss.

That which is surrounded by the meaning of *pa* is that which is completely surrounded by the bodhicitta; it blazes within the mandala of the navel of the perfectly transcendent great bliss through the wheel of the restraint of life-force and effort, and by means of the mantra that enters the center of emptiness, it becomes one with the three worlds—earth, water, wind itself, fire, and space itself.

"Now, at that very moment, neither self nor other can be perceived; immediately thereafter, one turns back [from conceptualization], thinking: 'I am experiencing bliss. The passage beginning with "In the house" and so forth is easy to understand. Alternatively: "The vajra in the center of the bhaga is meditated upon as utterly empty; all is equal to space. The faults of conceptualization—the flickering of the mind such as ignorance and so forth—"

Arising from the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-satya-alaṃkāra*: The mind, naturally luminous and utterly pure, Should be viewed as being like a mirror. All phenomena are like reflections; Luminous, pure, and equal to space. The sword that cuts through the afflictions, Sharp in accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, Like a victory banner raised by merit, And like a short spear that pierces the afflictions— The mind is one-pointedness itself. That very [mind] is fire...

"By the yogin, the bliss of joining the mouth is attained; this is called the clear manifestation of the characteristics of the hand implements. This means that the vajra, wheel, jewel, lotus, sword, and double-vajras (viśvavajra) are, respectively, the victory banners (*dhvaja*) and short spears (*kunta*); thus, according to the distinctions of the families (*gotra*) of the Tathāgatas, there are the vajra, the victory banner, the sword, and the spear.

The *thung ni* [seed-syllable] is the size of a grain of barley; the wheels, jewels, lotuses, and various vajras are the size of a *srāñcana* bean. Within the five-colored respective insignia (*cihna*) of Akṣobhya and the others, in their proper order, the mandala-circles are contained. Through the meditation on the yoga of the subtle stabilization of mind, the yogin [visualizes] the mudrā—

The excellent nature of the mind will be accomplished as the *siddhi*. This concludes the explanation of the twenty-third chapter from the introductory section on the methods of accomplishment in the *Pañjikā* (Detailed Commentary) called the *Śrī Heruka*. Then, furthermore, regarding the phrase "the language of signs" (*saṃketabhāṣā*): the language of the distinctions of various regions is called "sign" (*saṃketa*), which refers to the unintelligible [vernacular]; it is the secret hand-gesture (*samayamudrā*) of the yoginīs.

Regarding the phrase "Rgya'o, pro tam gi" and so forth, which means "speaking in secret" and the like, these are easy to understand according to their literal meaning. One who understands these symbolic languages is undoubtedly a yogin here. This concludes the explanation of the twenty-fourth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*.

[38 recto 2] Now, regarding the phrase "of Sarvārthakāma, joined with the eight ends": the "eight end" is the letter *ha*. It is joined with the letter *u* and the bindu (*m*). *Oṃ namo bhagavate vīreśāya* is clear. This concludes the commentary on the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Pañjikā*, a treasury of sādhanas within the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

Regarding the phrase, “Having joined the eight secret syllables desired by all the gods,” the “end of the eight” refers to the letter *ha*, together with the vowel *au* and the bindu (*oṃ namo bhagavati vīreśāya*, etc.). The [meaning of] these is easy to understand. This concludes the explanation of the twenty-fifth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-nidāna*.
CHAPTER 36

"Beyond this" means: the majesty of Śrī Heruka. "By way of direct and reverse order" means without transgressing the training in yoga. "Bestowing the accomplishments of the lower and the upper": "lower" refers to whatever exists in the subterranean realms (*pātāla*) and so forth; "upper" refers to the great mudrā of the upper accomplishment. Like a messenger (*dūtī*), they become messengers; they are all constant achievers of enlightenment, eternally established everywhere, and bestowers of non-dual bliss. "One's own messenger" refers to the foremost practitioner of the co-emergent conduct (*sahacaryā*).

Furthermore, the phrase "and then again" refers to the great identity of Śrī Heruka. The expression "by way of the natural order and its reverse" means not deviating from the stages of training in yoga. Regarding the phrase "the accomplishments (siddhi) of below and above": "below" refers to whatever exists in the subterranean realms and so forth; "above" refers to the accomplishments of the upper regions, namely Mahāmudrā. PHO.

Because she is like a messenger (*dūta*), she is a "messenger" (*dūtī*); she is the messenger who dwells well through the nature of non-dual joy in all the perfections of enlightenment, being certain in every respect. As for the phrase "my own messenger," it refers to the supreme conduct, the consort (*sahacarī*).

"Omnipresent" (*sarvagām*) means that [acts] such as kissing and embracing for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings who are capable [of liberation] should be performed at all times. "Specifically on the seat of yoga" (*yogapīṭhaviśeṣataḥ*): "The seat" (*pīṭha*) is said to be the earth; the seat is called the excellent lotus. Wherein the King, who is equal to non-dual bliss, abides in great happiness—that excellent seat is especially strewn with blood and semen; there, one should perform kissing with the tongue in a graceful manner, while being delighted by the drinking of wine.

Then one should take delight in the union of the vajra and the lotus, as long as the yoga is perfected—this is what is intended by the *Ratiśāstra* (Treatise on Passion). The gestures and postures (*karaṇābhinaya*) are said to be those of Vajrasattva; such is the accomplishment of awakening. Having understood the distinctions between the characteristics of the natural state (*prakṛtilakṣaṇa*), one should offer all that is truly existent; never otherwise.

"Kun 'gro" (All-pervading) means that it accomplishes the welfare of fortunate sentient beings by bestowing everything, such as the act of "o" and embracing. Regarding the phrase "the excellence of the yogic abode," the *Abhidharmakośa* explains that "abode" (*sthāna*) refers to the earth; it is spoken of as the abode of the lotus mandala. O Victorious One, whose nature is non-dual bliss, because Great Bliss abides therein, it is—

Thereafter, having especially made the supreme lotus-seat filled with the mixture of semen and blood, one should take it up by rolling it thoroughly with the tongue. Then, with the great joy of drinking wine, one should join the vajra and the lotus in union. As for the phrase "all the hosts of yogins," Vajrasattva has taught that all those methods explained in the treatises on joy [are to be performed]; thus, awakening—

Therefore, one should understand the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate characteristics through this very [realization]. For that reason, it is said: "It should be given to all who possess the truth; otherwise, never at any time."

"Mother, sister," and so forth, are according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*). "To whomsoever one should constantly speak the mantra"—by that very application of the mudrā, there is the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*). "Now I shall explain the commitments (*samaya*)," and so forth, is clear. "There is no other yoga superior to Śrī Heruka"—the meaning is that nothing whatsoever should be performed except through the yoga of Śrī Heruka, and not otherwise.

The passages beginning with "Mā and Sringī" and so forth are to be taken according to their literal meaning. As for the phrase "whoever always bestows mantras," it refers to the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) attained through union with that very mudrā. The passage beginning with "I shall explain the five samayas that are difficult to find" is easy to understand. Regarding the statement "there is no other union than Heruka," it means that everything which has been taught belongs to Heruka.
The meaning is that it is to be accomplished through application, and not by anything else.

The teacher Abjayavā is a practitioner of yoga (*yogavān*); he is the mother of yogas, thus [he is called] *Yogamātara*. Therefore, it is said: "nor even to be drawn away," and so forth. "Due to union with another deity" means that having abandoned the supreme yoga of means (*upāya*) characterized by great compassion and joy, one might resort to another yoga for the sake of attaining the siddhi of some other divinity. But he who is deluded by the desire for worldly accomplishment is like those blind from birth; he will surely suffer, just as kings are inevitably ruined when their kingdom falls.

For this very reason, it says, "of the master who is a yoginī herself. A yoginī is the mother of yogins; therefore, it is said, "one should not show contempt," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by uniting with another yoginī," [it means]: having abandoned the supreme method of yoga which is intensely delighted by great compassion, for the sake of accomplishing the siddhi of a desire-god, one should practice yoga...

Those who, relying on others for their livelihood, desire spiritual accomplishments, are utterly deluded like the blind; they will surely fall from their sovereignty like a king, and be bewildered by suffering.

**"The conduct of the pledge (*samayācāra*) is indeed gnosis."** The threefold entwinement is proclaimed to be performed with a non-conceptual mind: the practice of equality toward all castes; the application of the two organs; and the pervasion of the ear and all the sense faculties by bliss, wherever the Lord may move. Through the yoga of mindfulness, celibacy (*brahmacarya*) becomes the void. The foundation, the attainment, the bliss, and the purity of the path to awakening—this is the immutable reality (*tattva*) revealed as the conduct of the pledge.

"It should be known constantly by practitioners as being established for the sake of achieving awakening in all common tantras"—that is, in the *Kriyā*, *Caryā*, *Yoga*, *Yogottara*, and so forth. By means of the "equal application" (*tulyayogena*) in the ritual activity that generates the *Mahāyoginī* tantra, one should not "slay"—that is, one should not view [them] with equal contempt—because there is no [valid] reason to do so in those various tantras. The conduct of the *samaya* is well-guarded; one should not give this teaching to anyone who is an unsuitable vessel.

Regarding the statement, "One should engage in the conduct of the samaya," and so forth, various [teachings] have been spoken: "With a non-conceptual mind, one should unify all families; by joining the two organs in union, all the senses, such as hearing and the rest, are to be blended and gathered into bliss. Wherever the primary conduct is practiced, the pure conduct becomes emptiness. This is the mindfulness free from expression."

The basis for realizing bliss through conduct, the supreme reality that purifies the path to perfect enlightenment—this is taught as the practice of the samaya. It is said to be "constant" for the practitioner who abides in the accomplishment of enlightenment; this applies commonly to all tantras, including those of Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, Yoginī, and Yogottara.

It is not equivalent to the practice of acting according to the nature of the great tantra. Regarding "unassailable," one should not view it as having the nature of equality, because the tantra and those [practices] are not the cause. One should not employ the samaya and keep it strictly secret; it is not to be given to anyone, but is to be explained to fortunate sentient beings.

The eight [deities], such as Kākāsyā and the rest, increase devotion and faith; they are certain effectors of desired aims, all-pervading, and established upon the path to awakening. "By mere faith" means that one partakes [of the practice] through faith, or through wisdom, according to reality. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Dvikalparāja*: "The wise do not know [the consumption] with the hand, nor with a small, crooked [finger]; it increases longevity and health, and is the cause for the arising of knowledge. "The little finger" (*kaniṣṭhā*) refers to the joint of the little finger, the eleventh... [and so forth].

Regarding the phrase, "By expanding these one hundred [syllables] beginning with *kha* through devotion and faith," it means that the excellence of the objects of desire is certain, and because they pervade all aspects of the path to enlightenment, they are well-established. As for the phrase, "By means of faith itself," it is said: "The phenomena are to be grasped through faith; those possessing wisdom realize suchness. For this very reason, it is the second *Viniścaya-rāja*.

It is said: "Not with the hands, nor with the teeth; the wise should take it with the tongue. Since it increases longevity and freedom from disease, it is the cause for the arising of authentic primordial wisdom. Regarding the term *mthe'u chung*, *mthe'u chung* refers to that which possesses joints; having grasped the entity of the eleven-year-old [plant], one takes it with the tongue. To strive for the siddhi of Rasāyana is the cause for the arising of great bliss. [The practice].

Regarding the phrase "the *pāpa* resides in three ways," this refers to the distinctions of small, medium, and great. This concludes the explanation of the twenty-sixth chapter from the *Sādhanopāyamaṇḍalapatala*, the commentary on the difficult points of the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

Regarding the phrase "The hero who has undertaken ascetic practice" (*vīravratadhara*): it is called "practice" (*caryā*) because he practices toward all [objects]; "ascetic practice" (*vrata*) refers to the ornaments of power and so forth; "hero" (*vīra*) refers to the yogin. If one asks who that is, it is "the one who thoroughly accomplishes the yoginīs. Regarding the phrase "having understood the distinctions of their characteristics": having condensed the aggregates, elements, and so forth, [one understands them] as being like an illusion.

Having fully understood the eight worldly dharmas, and having prostrated to the glorious Vajra-holding Master, the protector of all, the Master who has completed his tasks should engage in the secret conduct. Without abandoning the staff, the alms bowl, the mendicant’s robes, and the ascetic virtues such as living by water, one should follow the instructions of the oral lineage. A yogin who has not realized the oral lineage... [Buddha]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

He becomes the expansive one with the garland of skulls; his focus is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). He is the sole supreme deity, from whom the gnosis of emptiness perfectly arises. Terrifying all malevolent beings, he possesses the glorious manifestation of fierce conduct as before. He strikes even those who inspire fear; his fangs are most formidable. With a half-moon upon his brow, he is adorned with a variegated vajra-sword. The Liberating One...

Adorned with a garland of skulls, complete with all ornaments, and girdled with a tiger-skin, he stands firmly in the half-lotus posture. He subdues all who are hateful and transforms desire, delusion, and envy. With Kālarātri pressed beneath his feet, he has three eyes, four faces, and four necks; blue, white, yellow, and red like the sky, with an upper face that is greenish-black.

Entering into union with the vajra bell, he rejoices non-dually with the Noble Lady (Phag mo). His hands hold a dharma wheel, a skull-cup, a spear, a noose, and a hook; likewise, a head and a small drum. His two [other] hands hold the dharma robe. He is draped with two human-skin cloaks. The Noble Lady is red in color and naked, with three eyes and loose hair, blazing brilliantly with all her ornaments.

The left hand holds a skull-cup filled with blood, while the right hand holds a small drum that proclaims the *dharmadhātu*. Her two hands are held in the gesture of embracing equality (*samāliṅgana*). She possesses great bliss through compassion and joy. Upon the petals in the east and the other directions are: the Hunteress and the Outcaste, the Leather-worker and the Pukkasi, the Butcheress and the Mountain-dweller, as well as the Fisherman’s daughter and the Sha-vārī; they are yellow, green, red, smoke-colored, and white.

Red and green, and likewise the eighth white; in natural order and in reverse order; laughter, peace, compassion, eroticism, ferocity, and ugliness—endowed with the moods of the wrathful and the fierce; holding a staff, a skull-bowl, a small drum, and a copper knife in hand; one should arrange the wrathful goddesses at the four gates. The self-manifestation of Heruka is Vajracaṇḍī.

O Vajra! O Vajrabhairavī, the fierce and wrathful subduer of all who are difficult to tame! You who have the color of ashes, green, red, and blue—terrible and fearsome! In your left hands you hold a skull-bowl and a staff; in your right, a dharma-wheel and a small ball. Upon your shoulders you brandish the dharma-robe. All of you have one face and four arms, adorned with every ornament, standing upon corpses.

The twelve ascetic qualities (*dhūtaguṇa*) are: wearing a single robe; having matted hair and being naked; being a mendicant; possessing three religious robes; not accepting [robes] later; being a rag-robe wearer; eating at a single sitting; being without a roof; dwelling at the foot of a tree; dwelling in a forest; dwelling in a charnel ground; and wearing dust from a cemetery. These twelve ascetic qualities belong to the pure yogi of the sublime word.

With the ethical discipline of the twelve branches of the Dharma-vinaya, he is thoroughly delighted and possesses great compassion; he is most beautiful with joy. Together with those who practice and follow him, his mind is gladdened. Having performed the vajra-consecration, one should recite with the bliss of the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā): *Oṃ śrī mahāsukha vajra he he ru ru kāṃ hūṃ*.

HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. One should enjoy the samaya food, and practice according to this sequence of the conduct of the Buddhas and the *bhūṣuku* conduct of ascetic discipline. As for that sequence: *bhu* means "eating"; thus, one should merely recollect that, completely abandon all socializing and distractions, and engage in austerities, fasting, and so forth.

"One should not think even for a moment" means that these, which are characterized by the ignorance of one who is asleep, are to be directly realized as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) and then cultivated as virtuous. Why is that? Because they must be entered once again by realizing them as being luminous by nature, since they are naturally stainless. "All" refers to what is to be explained.

"Having grown weary, one should cast off even a portion of the explanation. Having reflected upon that alone, one should completely abandon social distractions and not contemplate the nature of the body, sensations, objects, or sense faculties. Regarding the phrase 'from object to object' and so forth, when one becomes fatigued, one should go outside, examine the characteristics of a messenger, and then engage in the conduct of a Buddha."

Through the harmonious union of male and female messengers, one will attain the state of Mahāmudrā; thus, the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment will be attained without effort. Regarding the phrase "very swiftly," it means that the primordial wisdom of luminosity will become purified. One should always be designated as a yogin; by means of this accomplishment of meditative concentration, if the jewel of the mind remains constant, it will grant its blessing.

One should dwell upon the awakening of the Buddha for sixteen years, adorned with every kind of ornament. Having found a maiden of beautiful countenance and wide eyes, one should practice the ascetic discipline of knowledge (*vidyācaryā*). During the four periods of the day, the great ascetic should constantly perform secret offerings. Within six months, all these will undoubtedly be accomplished; one should always consume food [as prescribed].

Regarding this, it is said: "Entering into the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is the gathering of all foods; it is the universal practice for all families (kulas). One should contemplate them as being of a single family. Just as gold is purified by fire, so too are foods prepared by mantras. *Oṃ sarvavajrakāmini sarvabhakṣyaśodhani guhyavajriṇi hūṃ svāhā.* With the five ambrosias (*amṛta*) and honey, and with beeswax...

"Having joined them together, if one drinks, it is the supreme medicine; it wards off old age and death for a long time, and one possesses the glory of youth and freedom from disease. With a beautiful form, one becomes a lord of the desire-realm gods. By means of that very non-duality, for the sake of accomplishing the two female messengers (*dūtī*), one should perfectly arrange the two mudrās, complete with all ornaments, for the purpose of conferring empowerment."

One [seal] is for the purpose of bestowing the secret; the second is for the purpose of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*). Thus, having granted permission for the exhalation of the breath of the Tathāgata and the exhalation of the breath of the second, the Great Vajradhara, one subsequently bestows the single *poṇya*. The great master himself accomplishes the meaning of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) through the yoga of the physical form.

One should perform [this]. Thus, this newly revealed initiation through the stages of the guru’s oral instructions, which arises from the secret locus of the Great Secret, the Supreme True Bestowal of all Tathāgatas, is that which has been perfectly spoken by the Yoginīs; it is the perfection of primordial wisdom, and it is that which is venerated by as many Buddhas as there are.

Regarding "BAR 'OS PA'O ZHES BYA'O" (it is called *bar 'os pa'o*): "Rising early in the morning" refers to arising from the state of clear light (*prabhāsvara*). As for the line "With his own hand, he should practice all the treatises residing in the body": "Heart-hand" (*nyid lag*) refers to the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), such as the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and so forth, because they are extremely subtle. This is for the purpose of clearing away all obstacles. [This concludes] the conduct and the merit.

It is for the purpose of increasing primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Treatises possess the characteristics of yogic treatises, while ritual practices constitute the conduct (*caryā*). Regarding the phrase "having performed the purifiers, the body and... this refers to meditating on the yoga of the deity. Furthermore, one should contemplate oneself through this sequence: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

By means of *Bhrūṃ Āṃ Hrīḥ Hoḥ Hūṃ*, one becomes Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Akṣobhya. The state of being all the Tathāgatas is the glorious Heruka, by means of *Hi*. The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are [purified] by *Oṃ Hūṃ Trāṃ Āṃ Khāṃ Hāṃ*; [the first syllable] *Oṃ* [is for] delusion (*moha*).

*Dang*, *zhe sdang* (hatred), *ser sna* (avarice), *'dod chags* (desire), *phrag dog* (jealousy); *iśvaravajra*. *Jāḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ khāṃ rāṃ*—these are for Vajrarūpī and the others. *Lāṃ māṃ pāṃ tāṃ khāṃ*—these are for Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Space, [who are] Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, Tārā, and Vajravārāhī. *Oṃ āḥ*.

HŪṂ HŪṂ GIS: These are the Body, Speech, Mind, and Wisdom Sattvas. On the eight-petaled Dharma wheel: BHRŪṂ ĀṂ HRĀṂ KHAṂ HŪṂ ĀḤ ĀĪ ĀŪ ĀE ĀO. On the sixteen-petaled Enjoyment wheel: OṂ ĀḤ ĀĪ ĀŪ ĀE—these are the five vowel syllables. On the thirty-two-petaled Great Bliss wheel: HAṂ NGO. The sixty-petaled Emanation wheel...

Regarding the fourth *rtza* (channel-wheel), it is adorned by the eight classes [of consonants]: *a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa*. The letters *ka* and so forth should be joined in the center with those on the left and right. *Pu dza ao ā go rā de ma kha ao tri ko ka la ka hi, bre gri soo su na si ma ku dang khām prām māṃ tsām kāṃ prām bīm māṃ sūm bīm, āṃ khāṃ bāṃ lāṃ bāṃ drūṃ āṃ aiṃ bāṃ māṃ māṃ bāṃ bāṃ, sūm sūm.*

SHĀM, BĀM, SŪM, MĀM, HĀM; BĪM, KHĀM, MĀM, TZĀM, RĀM, KHĀM, HĀM; SĀM, ĀM, TZĀM, SHRĪM, SŪM, PĀM, MĀM; NOM, TZĀM, BĀM, MĀM. [These syllables are located] at the forehead, the crown of the head, the right ear, the back, the left ear, the center of the eyebrows, the two eyes, the two shoulders, the two armpits, the two breasts, the navel, the tip of the nose, the mouth, and the throat.

The shoulders, the heart, the navel, the secret place, the path of explanation, the two thighs, the two calves, the fingers, the insteps of the feet, and the two big toes are *Rūpīṇī*. The nails and teeth are *Pracaṇḍā*. The voice and the hair are *Caṇḍākṣī*. Wisdom and the impurities are *Prabhāvatī*. The flesh is *Mahānāsā*. The sinews are *Śauṇḍinī*.

On the liver is Ma'o; on the bones is Mi'u-thung-ma; on the spleen is Lang-ka'i-dbang-phyug-ma; on the heart is Ljon-'khril-ma; on the two eyes is Sa-srung-ma; on the bile is 'Jigs-byed-chen-mo; on the lungs is Klung-gi-shugs-ma; on the intestines is Chang-'thung-ma; on the kidneys is Lha-mo-sngon-bsangs-ma; on the stomach is Shin-tu-bzang-me.

Chu so (*mūtra*) is Rtārnama; Mo dams (*śukra*) is Bya’i gdong pa can (*Kapotamukhī*); Bad kan (*pitta*) is ’Khor lo’i shugs can ma (*Cakravegā*); Rnag (*rakta*) is Dum skyes ma (*Khaṇḍarohā*); Khrag (*asṛj*) is Glad sna ma (*Ghaṇṭākarṇī*); Rdul (*rajas*) is ’Khor lo’i go cha ma (*Cakravarmanī*); Tsil (*vasā*) is Rab tu dpa’ mo (*Suvīrā*); Mchi ma (*aśru*) is Stobs chen ma (*Mahābalā*); Mchil ma (*kheṭa*) is ’Khor los sgyur ba ma (*Cakravartinī*); Snabs (*siṅghāṇaka*) is Brtson ’grus chen mo (*Mahāvīryā*).

Thus, the *Subhāṣitasamuccaya* proclaims that the nature of all ḍākinīs is the *dharmadhātu*. Regarding the statement, "One should not discard whatever is taught in the treatises," it says: "The nectars are the supreme medicines; by relying on Akṣobhya, the yogin shall overcome all diseases. Through Amitābha, one possesses great stability; through Amitābha, one gains great power; and through Vajrasūrya, one becomes ageless. Whoever... [is protected].

Therefore, O Great King Amoghasiddhi, you who have arisen from the bodies of all sentient beings, endowed with glory and the accomplishment of all aims—by that yoga, there shall be equality. The yogin who drinks Akṣobhya will live for fifteen thousand years; by Ratnasambhava, he is said to live for one hundred thousand; by Amitābha, for an infinite duration; and by Vajrasūrya, he is free from aging throughout saṃsāra.

The Two Roots of Accomplishment: "By this, the yogin who acts as the support shall become equal to Samantabhadra. With a body thus purified, one should always recite the mantra. This refers to: *Oṃ ānānā samaya śuddhaḥ sarvadharmā ānā samaya śuddho hāṃ | Oṃ svabhāva śuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ*.

*Svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*, *Oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. This refers to the Vajra-holder who has been empowered by himself. Regarding the phrase "definitively teaching the abodes of yoga," it means that one should not visualize external implements; rather, this is the complete observance of the samaya, which is itself the great worship of the Tathāgatas. Samaya...

"One should not be angry with those who possess speech" refers to those who are well-established on the path of purity. "One should not neglect diligent effort" means that one must not show contempt for either the master or the disciple who have received the empowerment of the *cakrasaṃvara*; for it is by receiving the command of the female messenger (*dūtī*) that, having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one accumulates the collection of merit over many eons.

At that very moment, he will also be overcome. "Its meaning" refers to the meaning of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). "At night" means performing the worship of the mudrā. "Black" refers to the form of Heruka; "red" refers to Vajravārāhī. "Clearly" means manifestly. "One who desires bliss should enjoy bliss" means [enjoying] bliss exactly as it was heard.

Regarding the illumination of the ten directions by the very nature of that very [wisdom] of the STTS (*Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*): "The yogin who possesses the joy of intense passion, through the light of such a lamp of the nature of wisdom, should practice the coemergent great compassion. As for the phrases "family" and "non-family," the rituals and trainings of the maṇḍala and so forth pertain to those who are beginners.

Sentient beings should be sustained by the cause of compassion; through meditation, those who possess obstacles and are bound by the fetters of existence—those who have reached the height of delusion—are [liberated]. Therefore, once the bonds are abandoned, one will achieve accomplishment in this very life. For that very reason, it is said: "One should act according to one's desire. Regarding that:

That which is spoken of as "four faces" is said to be the nature of the four joys. Because the single enlightenment in which all joys are perfected is the very nature of emptiness, it is renowned as having "one face. The three eyes arise within the three realms of existence.

The phenomena that are without beginning or end, Reversed from the nature of insentient matter, Were spoken for the sake of the one with matted locks. Because he acts for the benefit of diverse sentient beings, He is marked by various vajras. The moon is the transformed bodhicitta; Its nature is great bliss and luminosity. For the sake of the twelve links of existence, He is endowed with twelve manifest hands. The objects and the sense faculties...

By means of the sphere of activity of non-dual aspects, the hands are marked with the [thirty-two] marks; the bodhicitta becomes the vajra, and wisdom is declared to be the bell. Because of the purity of the three bodies, there are the three loops; the elephant is the dispelling of delusion, while the sword is that which cuts through hatred. Arising perfectly from body, speech, and mind, the noose binds down faults; for embodied beings, there is nothing discordant.

Because it performs the benefit of sentient beings in all directions, the copper blade is extremely sharp. By its nature as a pure head, it has the form of an empty mouth; the *caṅ te'u* is the purity of the various methods. By its nature of constant joy, it utters the melodic sound of the Dharma. The skull is the mandala of space, completely filled with the flavor of compassion. This offering is the cause of spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).

It is so! The four fangs are manifest, subduing the four māras. With rays of light swirling together, his face is illuminated by a radiant, wide smile, filled with the flavor of compassion. Because he is the very nature of the four māras of the afflictions, he is adorned with a skull-garland on his head. His threatening mudrā is the purity of emptiness; he is a messenger of pure speech.

"Is the first" means that it is the source of the jewel of bliss for all the Victors. "Peaceful" refers to nectar and wine. "The single food is eating itself" means that because the many families are but a single family, no differentiation arises; thus it should be done. "This purity is to be practiced correctly" is easy to understand. "The wisdom of the pure self..."

"...the stages will also be attained," refers to the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. Furthermore, even if some do not attain it due to an inferior level of diligence, by completely casting off this body like a snake, they will be liberated from bondage in places such as the Pure Abodes, becoming like Tathāgatas. Alternatively, having been born in the human world...

"NI" means "he shall become a righteous king. Because he has arisen from the nature of the accumulations of merit and wisdom, he is like the vajra of bodhicitta; through making aspirations with a mind that cherishes all sentient beings and protects them, he is born into the lineage of the Sugatas in birth after birth. Thus it was spoken by the glorious Lord of the Śākyas.

It will become just so. Therefore, it is said: "Endowed with the drinking of *bca'* and so forth, one should worship oneself as all the Buddhas and the rest. Regarding the phrase "for one's own desired activities," this refers to the rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and so on. The expression "in great numbers" and so forth is literal. [As for the mudrā: "Forming a fist with the index fingers, firmly joining the middle fingers, and the thumbs..."

Firmly binding oneself with the vajra, place this [seal] at the center of the forehead; by circling and revolving it, one should encircle [the body] completely. Recite this mantra: *Oṃ ārali hoḥ, jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ, vajradākini samaya stvoṃ dṛśya hoḥ.*

Thus it is recited three or four times. Since the naked one (Nagna) will be liberated from the crown of the head, the practitioner, having placed [the deity] facing south at a high location, should offer the *bali* at midnight. Regarding the phrase "high location," this refers to offering the *bali* for all spirits through the application of the great divine mandala atop Mount Meru, the king of mountains; it is square with four doors.

Adorned with the four seals of the *mudrās*, in the center of the five stages, upon a variegated lotus and a sun disk, one should meditate on oneself as Heruka, having completely transformed from Vajrasattva. With the conceptualizations of permanence and nihilism subdued beneath the terrifying *kālacakra*, he utterly crushes all māras through the posture of the right leg extended; his body is blue in color and intensely fierce.

Fierce and wrathful like the fire at the end of an eon, with three terrifying and formidable eyes, adorned with a crown of garlands of skulls and empowered by the five Buddhas; his hair is bound by a variegated vajra, graced by the moon of awakening, and his body is embellished with the six mudrās. Marked with all the [major] marks, he has six faces and sixteen arms—heroic, repulsive, and playful.

Fierce, laughing, and with a wrathful gaze, blue, yellow, and likewise red, green, and white; the upper face is extremely fierce, enjoying the expanse of space. Laughing "Ha Ha" and making the sounds "Hūṃ Hūṃ," causing terror with the cry of "Hi Hi," and making the sounds "Hūṃ Hūṃ" and "Phaṭ," while uttering the syllables "Oṃ Oṃ," he embraces [his consort] with the vajra and bell.

Chewing, she performs the dance of the goddess’s breasts; wearing the terrifying, fierce raiment of the end of time, she holds [it] fast. She carries a skull-cup with its mouth wide open, a trident, a copper knife, an enemy-slaying sword, a hook, a severed head, a lute, and likewise a short noose. With two hands forming the lattice-gesture (*dra ba'i phyag rgya*), she is well-established above the forehead; such are the color and the hands of Vārāhī.

The *la sogs pa* (and so forth) is also similar to that; however, having cast off the garments of a sage, the goddess holds a bow and arrow. Her hair is loose and she is naked; with her lower garment marked by a *dum bu*, her two hands are joined in the gesture of embracing. Possessing the bliss of affectionate compassion, she perfectly purifies the existence of the six classes of beings and strives for the benefit of sentient beings. As for the four *pho nya* (messengers) with spreading petals:

Having the nature of *sa*, *la*, and so forth, they are the ḍākinīs and the rest; white, yellow, red, and green, with one face and four arms, three wide eyes, and loose hair. Their breasts are full and swelling, their faces are playful and smiling, and they are adorned with the five mudrās. With the left hands, they hold a hook, a noose, and a bell.

[She performs] summoning, entering, binding, and supreme satisfaction. Holding a sword, a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a *caṅte'u* in [her] hands, she stands firmly with her right leg extended. Even those intoxicated by passion for the heart [of the deity] have completely abandoned all delusion. Above [the vessel], it is surrounded by vases and skull-cups, entirely filled with all kinds of food. At the top...

The skull-cup is completely filled with the milk of awakening. Having empowered the three—body, speech, and mind—and donned the two armors of the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*), one correctly applies the *puṣpa* and so forth; then, having conferred initiation, one should perform the worship.

Having offered praise according to the *bka'* [command], one should invoke the Protectors of the Realm (*kṣetrapāla*) and others, who are surrounded by all worldly and supramundane hosts of deities, following the mantras as they have been taught in places such as solitary trees and charnel grounds. The sequence for this is as follows: Vārāhī and Śubhā, Kumārī and...
Tz'amund'i, Tsangs pa, and Sogs bdag ma, along with Khyab 'jug, Dbang po, and Rgyas pa, are explained [in] the second stage. As for the third stage, there are Dbang po, Gshin rje, and Chu lha.

The yakṣas, primarily the class of piśācas, the burning rākṣasas, and the deity Vāyu; in the fourth row are the Sun, the Moon, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Sanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu. In the fifth row are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, and Śoṣaka at the four gates. In the eastern direction of the second row...

From the syllable *hrīḥ* arises the goddess known as Vārāhī with four arms; she holds a bow and arrow, as well as a victory banner and a skull-cup. She is blue in color, a great fierce one, with the face of a sow and a terrifying appearance. To the north, from the syllable *phem*, is Śvānāsyā, red in color and a great fierce one; she holds a skull-cup, a hook, and likewise a khaṭvāṅga and a mongoose. To the west, from the syllable *hi*...

The Youthful Lady is yellow in color and has four arms; she holds a three-pointed spear and a banner, as well as a bow and arrow. To the south is Tāmarī, marked by the syllable *Hi*; she is blue in color and has four arms, holding a skull-cup (*khaṭvāṅga*), a skull-bowl, and likewise a sword and a *caṅte'u*. In the southeast is Brahmā, marked by the syllable *Bam*; he is white in body and has four arms, holding the body of Brahmā and a water-pot, as well as a bow.

Dang-ma is likewise; she is the mother of the Gaṃ-group of rākṣasīs. She is green in color and has four arms; her hands hold a trident and a skull-cup, as well as a rosary and a lute. In the northwest, Bām gives rise to Khyab-’jug-ma (Viṣṇu); she is blue in color and has four arms. Her hands hold a skull-cup filled with liquor and water, and likewise another hand holds a severed head. In the northeast, Ai gives rise to Dbang-mo (Indrāṇī); she is yellow in color.

In his four hands, he holds a vajra, a short spear, a skull-cup, and a threatening gesture with a noose. All the goddesses have their hair tied upward in a flame; they are adorned with various ornaments, possess three eyes, sit upon human corpses, and have their waists bound with tiger skins. In the third tier, the yakṣa Yamadaṇḍi sits upon a bull; he is white in color and has four hands.

With the *thod pa* (skull-cup) and the three knots, the palms are joined and turned downward. To the east, Aiṣya Śakra sits upon an elephant throne; he is yellow in color with four arms, holding a vajra and a skull-cup, with his hands joined in the gesture of prayer (*añjali*). In the southeast, the Ṛṣi Baṃ is red in color, riding a goat with four arms, holding a fire-pot, a skull-cup, and [a third hand] in a gesture of terror.

In the southeast, Yamī, the Son of the Sun, blue in color and with four arms, riding a buffalo, holding a staff and a skull-cup, bows with palms joined in fear. In the southwest, Rāmā, the Mistress of Rākṣasas, green in color and with four arms, riding a human corpse, holding a sword and a bell, bows with palms joined in fear. In the west, Vārūṇī, the Mistress of Water, white in color and with four arms, riding a water-bull...

In the northwest is Yamī, the Mistress of Wind; she is blue in color, wears a tiger-skin skirt and a skull-topped headdress, and with palms joined in fear, she leans forward. She has four arms and rides upon a mountain. She holds a banner and a skull, and likewise remains intent with palms joined. In the north is Kubera; he is yellow in color, has four arms, and rests upon a vase. He holds a jewel and a skull, and leans forward with palms joined.

Regarding the fourth stage of the ritual procedure (*kriyā-krama*): in the east is the Sun, red in color, holding a lotus with both hands and joining them in prayerful gesture (*añjali*). He rides a chariot drawn by seven horses. In the southeast is Saṃkara, white in color and blazing; he holds a jewel upon a lotus in his left hand and likewise a skull-cup in his right. Joining his palms, he rides a goat. In the south is Ām, red-eyed.

Seated upon a red lotus throne, holding a sword and a noose, he joins his palms in reverence. Holding a roaring *ram* syllable within a skull-cup, his right hand is the sun and his left the moon. With a dark-blue complexion, he joins his palms and rests half his body upon his own seat. To the west, from the syllable *sām*, arises blue Vaiśravaṇa; with two hands he holds a skull-cup, and his joined palms form the shape of a fire-hearth.

Above, she dwells blazing like fire. To the north, Śamī is white like the moon; to her left is a lotus, a moon, and a jewel; to her right, upon a lotus, is a moon. With palms joined, she rides a swan. To the north, Bām is golden-yellow; she holds a kīla in her left hand and likewise a skull-cup in her right. With palms joined, she stands upon a jeweled seat. In the northeast, Kumbhī is white; in her right hand...

In his left hand, RIN CHEN MDA’ holds a skull-cup. With palms joined, he rests upon a vase-seat. KAm GI is a red emanation-form of a victory banner; his two hands hold a sword with palms joined. Likewise, the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) have the forms of women: THA SKAR is white; BRA NYE is greenish-blue; SMIN DRUG is bluish-white; SNAR MA is pinkish-red; MGO is blue; LAG is yellow; NAB...

So ni is yellow; Rgyal ni is blue-black; Skag is white; Mchu is yellow; Bre is greenish-yellow; dbo is green; Me bzhi is white; Nag pa is green; Sa ri is yellow; Sa ga is blue; Lha mtshams is blue-black; Snron is yellow; Snubs is green; Chu stod is blue; Chu smad is white; Gro zhu ni...

Skyebo’o is blue-white; Byi bzhin is blue-grey; Mon gru is blue; Mon gre is yellow; Khrums stod is greenish-blue; Khrums smad is yellow; Nam gru is pale yellow. Visualize them all with golden upper garments and palms joined together. In the fifth stage: from *bāṃ* at the eastern gate, Brahmā is white in color, with four faces and four arms, holding a skull-cup and...

Bhṛṅgī and Śveta, as well as Padma himself; in the northern direction, from the syllable *bim*, arises the four-armed one called Vyāpin, holding a spear, a wheel, a skull-cup, and a staff. In the west, from the syllable *sām*, arises Raudra, smoke-colored and four-armed, holding a trident, a skull-cup, a noose, and a rosary. In the south, from the syllable *kam*, arises Kṣemaka.

As for Ni, Mdog Ser (Yellow Body), who has four arms, he holds a short spear, a staff, a skull-cup, and likewise a rosary. All of them are accompanied by retinues consisting of sons, daughters, and so forth, and they possess the expressions of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) and the rest. Furthermore, in the center of the ground of the reality of that great maṇḍala: in the east is black Rudra; in the north is Mahārudra; and in the west is Devadatta.

In the south is the Black One (Kṛṣṇa); in the northeast is the Terrifying One (Caṇḍa); in the southeast is the Ugly One (Virūpa); in the southwest is the Joy-Passing-Beyond (Ratnatīta); and in the northwest is the Deceiver (Vighna). All of them have one face and three eyes, four arms holding a sword, a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a trident. They are black, yellow, red, and green; those residing at the intermediate points are captivating to the mind.

This is the second section on the forms. In front of Rudra Kṛṣṇa is Tsa-muṇḍī; to the left is Dragmo; behind is Mi-sdug-ma (Aśubhā); and to the right is the goddess Dka’-bzlog (Durgavāriṇī). These are the faces of the ḍākinīs, each with two hands holding a skull-cup filled with the five offerings. In front of Mahārudra are Jayā, Vijayā, Aparājitā, and Anantaparājitā.

In the southeast are the Yoginīs who hold food and drink, and are the color of their mothers; in the west are the consorts of Rāhu—Kṛṣṇāśobhanā, Mahākṛṣṇā, Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā, and the Yoginīs—who are the color of Khaṇḍaroha and hold the five offerings in their hands. In the south are the consorts of Ketu—Indrāṇī, Candrā, Caṇḍikā, and Yuktā—[who are] Rūpiṇī.

In the east are Āryā, Mālinī, Cakrī, and Vajradhātrī, who are the color of tsa-muṇḍī and hold food and drink in their hands. In the northeast are Bhīmā, the consort of Īśāna; Devendriṇī; Śaṅkhinī; and Dīpā, who are the color of tsa-muṇḍī and hold food and drink in their hands. In the southeast are Virūpākṣī, the Yoginī dwelling in the city; Caṇḍarūpā; and Mahārūpā.

In the northeast, as previously described for the one with the color of a peacock’s plumage, she holds a sword in her hand; in the southwest, she has the form of the grieving consort of Nandīpāla, is adorned with a garland of skulls, and bares the fangs of Yama; in the northwest, she is black with a beautiful complexion and holds food and drink in her hands; and in the north, she is the consort of Vāyu, holding a sword in her hand.

The Śaktīs, Vajrahastā, and Padmahastā—those who possess the colors of the Queens (Rājñī) and so forth, and hold food, drink, and other offerings in their hands. Furthermore, in the charnel ground in front of the eastern horse-stable, there are Bhairava with the Garland of Skulls, the Lord of the Piśācas, Gaṇeśvara, and Ghaṇṭā; these four, together with their consorts, are ḍākinīs.

In the cemetery to the north is Caṇḍeśvara, together with his consort, who is dark blue in color; they have the letter *ja*, a fierce skull-staff, and a club.
