In the cemetery to the west are Damara, Adamaka, Phetka, and Bhīṣaṇa, together with their consorts, who are yellow in color like *khaṇḍaroha*. In the cemetery to the south...

Niṣkalaṅka, Mahāghoṣa, Vikaṭotkaṭa, and Śarabha—these, together with their consorts, have the color of Rūpiṇī. All of them have one face and four arms; they hold a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, and a trident, and embrace their respective goddesses. They should be visualized as residing upon the eight trees that mark the boundaries of the cremation ground. All of these...

One should visualize with the mind that [the deity] is established throughout the three worlds of the Cāturdvīpa, surrounded on all sides by vidyādharas, celestial maidens, humans, and so forth, who clear the way before him; that he is attended by hosts of hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, and the like, who utter the sound *kili kili*; and that he is oriented toward the practitioner, bestowing the supreme siddhi. One should place the syllable of one’s own name at the heart, while [maintaining] body, speech, and mind.

With "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ," they arise from the three families. Then, having offered the cleansing torma (*bsang gtor*) and water for the feet according to the ritual procedure, through the yoga of equality with the samaya, one should present the food to one's own mandala. One pays homage; in the center is the syllable *Ā*. By means of the blazing of the syllable *Hūṃ*, the syllable *Hrīḥ*—

In the *Lamp for the Path*, until the activity is completed: With vajra palms joined upward, one should recite this secret mantra. One should offer flowers, incense, unguents, and so forth with mantras such as *khakha khāhi* and others. Then, with a perfectly joyful mind, the supreme [attainment] will be granted. One should visualize [the deity] as primarily abiding within the body, speech, and mind of the Blessed One.

This concludes the explanation of the twenty-seventh chapter from the *Introduction to the Means of Accomplishment*, the commentary on the difficult points of the *Śrī Heruka*. Now, regarding the phrase "I, the pure offering," "pure" refers to the non-differentiation from all phenomena—that is, the luminous nature of non-dual great bliss. This very [nature] is the Dharma of the Buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "The Vīra emerges from that," it refers to the Saṃbhogakāya because it does not abide in either cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) or peace (*śānti*). Furthermore, it is followed by Bodhisattvas because it emerges from the complete accumulation of all the collections. The characteristic of performing the welfare of sentient beings by emanating the Buddha-assembly is the Nirmāṇakāya.

Regarding the term *skū* (body): as for the worship of oneself through the very nature of that essence, it is performed by means of the yoga of one's own deity (*svadevatā-yoga*) according to its application. Furthermore, regarding the statement "one's companions and beloved ones should also be worshipped," this refers to those who are equal [in status], pure in intention, engaged in the same practice, and unified. By the word "also" (*api*), the yoginīs are specifically included; whoever...

Therefore, without those [elements], its perfection would not come to be; for that very reason, it is said to be "firmly established" through the union with the goddess. "Peaceful" refers to liquor, or else to the bliss of peace. "Always arising, luminous," resting firmly within the lotus of the heart—such an emptiness is not to be meditated upon as the mind itself.

Regarding the phrase "together with his wife and children," one must understand that, apart from generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) for the sake of enlightenment through diligent application, there are those who—having heard the teachings on mantras, mudrās, offerings, maṇḍalas, and the *gaṇacakra*, as well as the vajra songs—despise the commitments (*samaya*), revile the master, and bring harm to all sentient beings; it is for this reason that he is called a "Vajra Disciple."

The commander’s son will go to hell, and other sentient beings gathered there will also have their bodhicitta become defiled. Therefore, it is applied that one should partake of food in order to fully sustain them. This is the common [explanation]. What is the specific [distinction]? It is because, by the power of compassion, just as he has generated the mind of awakening, so too—

It should not be taught even to them, for through the power of faith, their generation of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) would become something else. "One should not give the secret mantra to anyone" refers to those sentient beings who have not yet been fully ripened. "It should be given" refers here to those who have received empowerment. Regarding the term "messenger" (*dūta*) and so forth, it is called a "path" (*mārga*) because it is similar to a path; [it is] the Bodhi-...

This is the path of enlightenment. Furthermore, it consists in abandoning limitless afflictions and rebirths; because the afflictions are merely adventitious, by simply clearing away what are like clouds, mist, smoke, and confusion in the sky, one becomes a Vajradhara in this very life. Therefore, to abandon that [path] and rely on other yogas is the conduct of the Śrāvakas and the Kriyā [tantras].

Those who desire all the accomplishments (siddhi) as they have been explained in the *Caryātantra* and other such texts will, through their delusion, come to possess neither accomplishment nor happiness.

"Like a person who has lost his kingdom, he is separated from the wealth of faith"—this is viewed with the perspective of attachment. "Liberation is release"; one is released by being attached to the messenger. Therefore, it is said, "one should enjoy even with bliss," because all bliss is certain to be the very nectar arising from the *bhaga*. One should not merely perform service.

Regarding the phrase "thus it is said," service is not for the sake of worldly gain; rather, it is the joy of gathering through passion. Therefore, one should perform the embrace. Because it is attained by one possessed of subsequent passion, otherwise bliss will not arise. Regarding the phrase "those of inferior birth" and so forth, these refer to the Vajra family and the like. By the word "also," the Brahmin caste and others are included. These too [include] the mother, the sister-in-law, and so on.

Thus, by the power of intense longing, even one who constantly performs worship with great austerity will, through a mind of resentment and inferiority, certainly exhaust that austerity. Regarding the phrase "the wheel is likewise accomplished": this yoga should be bestowed upon those whose commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*) have been impaired, so that they may take them up again. *Ḍākinī*...

The ḍākinī yoginī, within the center of the expanse of space, abides in the unsurpassed samaya vow. Therein is the unsurpassed samaya maṇḍala; in its center is a great wheel adorned with five maṇḍalas. In the center, upon a sun seat, is the syllable ĀLIKĀLI perfectly joined. Holding the thirty-two marks [of a great man] and adorned with the eighty minor signs, she is empowered.

Having formed the syllable *BṚ*, it emerged perfectly from the letter *HA*; terrifying like the light-rays at the end of an eon, with three eyes and bared fangs; his neck coiled, laughing with wrath, he devours all the great gods; agitated like the fire at the end of an aeon, adorned with a crown of matted locks, his loins bound by the skin of Bhairava; standing firmly with his right leg extended.

Bearing the terrifying signs at all times, with a vajra garland upon his forehead, adorned with a crossed-vajra and a crescent moon, his body is arrayed with the six ornaments. He has five faces and six arms, endowed with various moods and supreme flavors; blue, yellow, and likewise red, green, and white above—peaceful. He is the supreme one who restores even the dead, and he utterly destroys all hatred.

The one who abides [as the consort] holds a vajra and bell in union; she perfectly embraces the body of Vārāhī. She wears the garments of a scholar and the attire of a *sa-srung-ma* (earth-protector). Above, she holds a white *dugs* (turban) and grasps a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga*. The sixth [hand] holds a hand-drum (*caṅ te'u*). Like her, Vārāhī has loosened hair and is naked, adorned with ornaments of human bone; nevertheless, she is clothed in the garments of a scholar.

One should arrange the heads of the *su-gri* and Brahmā. To the east is the Buddha-ḍākinī; likewise, to the north is the Karma-ḍākinī; to the west is the Dharma-ḍākinī; and to the south is the Ratna-ḍākinī herself. They are white, blue, red, green, and above, reddish-yellow. They enter into union with their respective consorts by means of the wheel and the bell, and with their two hands they hold the garments of Brahmā.

Furthermore, he holds a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a *caṅte'u'o* (small drum); with his right leg extended, he tramples upon Brahmā and his consort. Moreover, [he has faces] that are green, yellow, red, blue, and likewise a fifth, white upper face; he enters into union with his consort by means of a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) and a bell, wears the skin of the Lord of the Assembly (*Gaṇapati*), and [holds] a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga*.

He wears the *daṅ cang te'u* head-ornament; standing with his right leg extended, he suppresses the lords of the *gaṇas*, husbands and wives, who are terrified and intoxicated. Furthermore, he is red, blue, yellow, green, and white on top; he embraces [his consort] with a lotus and a bell, wearing the torn garments of a celestial being of desire, as well as a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a *damaru*. His right leg is extended.

By standing in the *paryaṅka* posture, he suppresses the lord of desire (*kāmeśvara*). Furthermore, yellow, blue, red, green, and likewise white on top—[these] enter into union with jewels and bells, wearing the skin of an elephant whose senses are pierced, and holding a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*). By standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, he suppresses the lord of the senses.

In the southeast (STE), southwest (KUN), northwest (KYANG), and northeast (SPYAN) directions, there are the Buddha-ḍākinīs, Vajra-ḍākinīs, Padma-ḍākinīs, and Karma-ḍākinīs—white, blue, red, and again blue and white—who possess three eyes and six arms, with their hair bound by silk ribbons. In the intermediate directions of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna, there are likewise [the ḍākinīs].

White, yellow, and again red, blue, and yellow; and green, blue, and yellow—all with three faces and six arms, their three eyes wide and staring with disheveled hair, adorned with the five mudrās. Possessing pride and performing the dance, endowed with compassion, attachment, and joy, [holding] a wheel-arrow, a vajra-arrow, a lotus-arrow, and a jewel...

Chen-mda’ holds an arrow marked with his own characteristic sign; all his left hands hold bows. He holds a skull-cup with its mouth open and a *dāmaru*. He also holds a goad and a lasso cast by others. He is perfectly round with nine eyes. On the outside, it has four corners and four doors. At the eastern door is Bahu-rūpa; at the north is Su-rūpa; at the west is Vajrāṅkuśī; at the south is Vajra...

The Lord, the Manifest One, is three-faced and six-armed, adorned with all ornaments; he bears the same marks as the Buddhas, dakinis, and others previously taught, in their respective order. Outside of that, in the space [of the mandala], is a square enclosure with four doors, adorned with four horse-treadings and draped with garlands of excellent flowers. Within it, at the corners of the divine cloth, is a square fire-limit.

The enumeration by way of the leftward circumambulation of the La-sogs-pa [group] consists of the faces of Vajravaktrā, Caṇḍavaktrā, Vajraśuṇḍinī, Yaśasvinī, Vajradūtī, Vajranakhī, Vajrakumārikā, Vajraśaṅkhinī, Vajramalā, Vajrasuptā, Gandhinī, and Bhīmavaktrā.
Candālī, Bhṛkuṭī, Viśvarūpā, Vajradehī, Vajravāṇī, Māyādevī, Śabdakarī, and Khambhā—thus there are twenty goddesses. At the eastern gate is Vajrajvālā;

In the north is Vajravarttā; in the west is Vajrabhairavī; and in the south is Vajrasiddhā. These constitute the accomplishment of the maṇḍala of the ḍākinīs. All the gatekeepers have three eyes, distorted faces, and protruding bellies. The others have various forms; all the dancing goddesses hold the five mudrās and are adorned with garlands of skulls.

The three-faced hero, filled with the nectar of heroism, grace, and compassion, possesses full breasts and is a fortunate woman with loose hair. Seated upon a supreme seat of the flavor of passionate joy through great compassion, she is the supreme dancer, embodying the skull-cup, the *khaṭvāṅga*, and the small drum; holding a hook and a goad, she brandishes a vajra and rings a bell.

BA'O. Then, having blessed the body, speech, and mind and adorned them with the two types of armor, one should summon that wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*). Having performed the initiation and made perfect offerings, one should offer praise and recite the mantra: *Oṃ śrī vajradāka āḥ hūṃ dākini jvalasambhara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. One should always recite this with a mind of devotion. Vajra...

The Great Silent One should perform the emanation and withdrawal of his activities: Oṃ śrī buddha dāka āḥ bhrūṃ hūṃ dākini jvala sambhara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā; Oṃ śrī karma dāka āḥ khaṃ hūṃ dākini jvala sambhara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā; Oṃ śrī padma dāka āḥ dhṛi hūṃ dākini jvala sambhara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā; Oṃ śrī ratna...

d’a ka ām hūṃ | d’a ki ni dz’a la samba ra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ śrī vajravārāhī bāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Thus, the recitation mantras of all the ḍākinīs have been thoroughly explained. If one maintains this visualization with certainty, the excellent siddhi equal to the Vajra will undoubtedly be attained. Regarding the passage beginning with "the supreme and the inferior," etc.:

Furthermore, one should recall the state of being blessed by the Samayin who was previously established. "Supreme" refers to the co-emergent (*sahaja*); "intermediate" refers to those born from the field; and "inferior" refers to those born from mantra. It is said that the substance of that co-emergent is definitively determined: whatever substance arises from all the faculties that have entered the center.

In a skull-cup containing the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, which are perpetually produced by the conditions of the [five] families, one should fashion a triangular maṇḍala using blood and liquor. Then, in the upper, middle, and lower sections—according to the directions and intermediate points as they have been taught—one should consume the food. Having consecrated those three very [substances], one should drink and offer the supreme samaya; [this is for] the Guru Vajra.

"May the Lord of Adherents, the assembly of Yoginīs, and all others, remain alive! Having taken hold of every practitioner without exception, I shall always provide them with protection. Thus it is said. Regarding the phrase "always purifying by holding the left side of the world," since the conduct of the left side is a source of bliss, one engages in it for the sake of accomplishment. This very Great Yoga is Sukhāvatī and the Palace of Space.

The Lord of beings in the three worlds, with his left hand, bestows all the supreme objects born from the left; because he expands them and grants bliss, he is honored by the left, for the yogi is skilled in all methods, since all the certainties of the principal Heruka are produced from the left.

"Whoever worships the Tathāgata without the offering of Mahāmudrā, their toil is in vain and they shall not attain the fruit. Regarding the phrase "the asceticism that is unimpaired": "asceticism" refers to those who, through the certainty of time and the twelve qualities of purification, have attained Buddhahood over many eons; [Mahāmudrā] outshines all such and abandons that asceticism.

"Indeed" (pa ste) means for the sake of attaining buddhahood in this very life. Because the practitioner who exerts himself in the activity is liberated from worldly conduct, he is a "perfected ascetic" (brtul zhugs rdzogs pa). Regarding the phrase "the commitments" (*samaya*) and so forth, it is logical that they are enumerated by number, as they are spoken of as being six, five, and so on. "Simultaneously" (*lhan cig*) refers to what was previously explained.

Regarding the phrase "Thus, one should practice the conduct of the five families": since the Ratna family is subsumed within Akṣobhya, it is included within the four families. Ultimately, they are also unified within the single family of the Lord of Mind. Those in the maṇḍala are equal therein. One should practice non-conceptual conduct, without grasping at gathering or possessing, and [partake of] foods that are not [ordinary] enjoyments, as well as the objects of desire.

The five qualities: one should rely on that which is free from fault; like fire, one’s conduct toward objects should be equal; like the light of the sun, it is shown to be equal; and like the wind, it gathers all odors equally. Having abandoned the ocean of the delusion of conceptual thought, one should practice all samayas without exception. Regarding the so-called "three-cornered mandala," it refers to a location that is rugged and lacks a central essence.

On a piece of black wood, one should fashion a hearth-pit twenty finger-widths wide and ten finger-widths deep, with its opening facing north. For the rite of execution, the symbols of the Karma-vajra, the three-pointed spear, and the vajra-hammer should have their tips pointing upward; however, for the execution rite, the tip of the spear should be pointed downward. These hand-symbols should be drawn here at a size of four finger-widths. Of that...

Having moved three finger-widths upward, one should encircle the hearth with a rim three fingers wide and high. Then, having smeared it with black earth, donkey dung, mule dung, human bone, rice husks, and charcoal, one should worship it with foul-smelling flowers and incense. [One should use] wood that is foul-smelling, coarse, and thorny, or wood from a charnel ground.

One should perform the fumigation using the dry dung of a camel, a buffalo, or a cow; or with wood such as *nimba*, *śrīparṇī*, thorny trees, or *bāluka* and other thorny species, cut into pieces about ten finger-widths long from the root portion—or even pieces of charred wood split from a funeral pyre—burning them as incense with poison, blood, and melted butter. Furthermore,

The marrow, blood, bile, and marrow-fat of a young goat; the ash of *māpa* leaves; earth from a footprint; the dung of a donkey, a drum, and so forth; hair, nails, the feathers of a crow and an owl; feces and urine; powdered human bone, body hair, flesh, and so forth—each of these substances, as well as whatever poisons can be obtained.

Sprinkle [the image] with the juice of blood and the leaves of the *unmādana* plant; fashion an effigy of the enemy using ashes, charcoal, rice husks, and so forth. Piercing it from the head with a sharp weapon, cut the body into pieces and offer them as a burnt oblation (*homa*) in a rite of wrathful activity. In an iron vessel, [place] blood, water, human urine, and donkey urine, together with the syllable *Phaṭ* at the end.

Recite the Seven-Syllable Mantra of Vajrapāṇi seven times; perform the purification and offering (*saṅsgator*) for the burnt substances; and one should summon those who cause harm to the Three Jewels and those who transgress their commitments. Then, adorned in black garments and equipped with iron ornaments, with a wrathful mind and facing the direction of Yama, one should sit upon a firm seat in the wrathful cross-legged posture while reciting the mantra.

Having established the site at midnight or midday, one should visualize the object of accomplishment within the maṇḍala generated by oneself. Reciting the mantra like the sound of thunder, with the syllables *Hūṃ* and *Phaṭ* at its end, one should perform the fire offering for those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities. Here, the fire for wrathful rites is that from a charnel ground, or produced from bone, or born from stone, or taken from the house of an outcaste.

In the lower left corner of the hearth, fan the firewood that has been arranged according to the instructions with a bellows, and while reciting *hūṃ dzva la dzva la hūṃ*, ignite the fire in the proper manner. Then, placing the ring finger of the left hand, together with kuśa grass, upon the root of the ring finger of the right hand, one should invite the Fire God (*Agnideva*) with: *oṃ āgaccha mahābhūtadevaputra śuddhe svāgatam agne ihāgaccha*.

With the mantra *ĀḤ HŪṂ TI ĀḤ HA RĀM ĀḤ SMIN SAṂNI HI TO BHAVA*, he is invited from the direction of fire. Having arrived, in the center of the blazing heart, he is the wrathful one called "Unbearable" (*Mi bzad pa*), possessing the excellence described in the recitation: with a tawny beard, a complexion like smoke, flickering eyes gazing upward, large ears, four fangs, and great strength, he stands within a mandala of wind.

Abiding within the maṇḍala, by uttering the terrifying syllable *Hūṃ*, he possesses three eyes and four arms; he is intensely radiant with vajra light-rays and is well-established in the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). With seven faces that are wide open and set upon a seat of lions, he is turbulent and fearsome with garlands of smoke, adorned with excellent iron ornaments, and has a face fashioned from iron.

He is adorned with a garland of flames, and with his unequal, reddish-yellow eyes he gazes terrifyingly. Clad in blue garments, he illuminates the three worlds with a fierce radiance like the fire of destruction. With his two [primary] hands he holds a spear and a vajra; furthermore, with others he holds a sword and a copper axe. To his right side is the one called Kṛṣṇa-khaṃsera, who holds a vajra in his two right hands.

The one holding the staff and the curved knife has black limbs and eyes like smoke; he bites his lip with his fangs and presses it. His two left hands hold a skull-cup filled with blood and a flaying knife; he abides with red light rays blazing forth equally. To the left is Yamāntaka, fierce and equal in radiance to a rain cloud; he possesses six faces and six arms, and each of his six faces has three eyes.

One should visualize [the deity] emerging from the heart of Mañjuśrī, possessing a transformed and wrathful countenance with a gaping mouth, adorned with blazing iron ornaments, and mounted upon a majestic buffalo as fierce as the fire of a charnel ground. On the two sides of the hearth, one should contemplate Antaka and Kṛṣṇa, who possess their respective natures; they have four or six arms and are intent on devouring and consuming. Yi...

Just as it is with the King of the Dakas, so too does the fierce and active *bīja* syllable contemplate the fierce activity alone. Thus, everything arises from the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The practitioner who accomplishes all aims should correctly unite with the application of mantras and mudrās that accord with the activity, and thereby consecrate the body, speech, and mind.

Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should perform worship with the water for offerings (*argha*) and so forth according to the ritual procedure: the water for offerings is for the head; the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) is for the two feet. *Oṃ arghaṃ pratīccha svāhā.* Taking the water by closing the thumb and middle finger of the right hand and moving the hand, one should offer it. *Oṃ pādyaṃ pratīccha svāhā.* Then, [one offers] the water for refreshing the face (*ācamana*) and the incense (*gandha*).

One should perform offerings to the deity: flowers upon the head, incense before [the face], perfume at the heart, and likewise a lamp before [the face]. The divine food (naivedya) should also be offered in that same manner before [the face]. Having thus made these perfect offerings, and especially having applied oneself with mental concentration, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth and tooth-cleansing wood. Regarding that, the handle of the tooth-stick should be sixteen finger-widths long, and its length...

It is four finger-widths high and two finger-widths deep; in its center is another triangle, completely encircled by a garland of three-pointed vajras. In the center of this as well, a mark should be made—using the face of a tiger, a snake, or a lion, whichever one desires—and there should be a channel for the downward flow of oil measuring one finger-width. The lip is the size of a finger, consecrated by the brandishing of a vajra.

Similarly, the sacrificial pit for the *bhūta* spirits has a handle fourteen finger-widths long, three finger-widths wide, and one finger-width deep, triangular in shape, and consecrated with the *mudrā*. At the end of the handle, it should be filled with a sacrificial ladle for wrathful rites (*abhicāruka*), which is consecrated by brandishing a three-pronged vajra; it should be made from wood struck by lightning, iron, or wood possessing sharp thorns.

"This means that even the Buddhas will certainly perish. Having thus explained the external fire offering (*bāhyahomavidhi*), in order to further teach the internal [offering], it is said: "Possessing the mantras and mudrās, the heroes likewise consume the food. This should be performed by means of the substances previously taught, while remaining in the yoga of one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

In order to pacify all afflictions and to expand meditative concentration, one should thoroughly accomplish all activities within the hearth of the essence of the three realms. At the navel, which arises by its very nature, the fire of Caṇḍālī is beautifully adorned; the Heruka, whose nature is the channels, should fill all yogins. With a mind devoid of intrinsic nature, one performs the burnt offerings of all the elements.

"O Bya, this unsurpassed fire offering was proclaimed by all the Buddhas. One should understand external entities as being of the nature of one's own self. Thus it is also said: 'Intensely blazing with garlands of light rays, the mandala of light is brilliantly aflame; the hearth at the navel is everywhere proclaimed, the navel itself being the hearth of fire. All the fuel is by the fire of primordial wisdom, and..."

It acts as a means for causing delight; thoroughly stirred by the winds of karma, it blazes intensely within the center of the navel. The mind arising from all the sense faculties becomes fuel for bliss. To pacify the afflictions born of karma and birth, one should perform the fire offering. Through this, the stages of perfect enlightenment will gradually and swiftly flourish, equal to the fires at the end of an eon.

Abiding excellently through the light of radiance, the fruit of the eight channels is joy within the center of the heart. In the very middle of a lotus possessing sixty-four petals, there is fire; in the center of that, one should visualize the deity of fire, the size of a thumb-joint. With two hands the color of fire, holding a blazing solar mandala of coemergent supreme joy, she emits rays of light.

The supreme basis is luminous clarity; it causes all basic spaces (*dhātu*) to blaze forth. One should view it as the root of everything. It is taught that the fuel for all views is found at the limit of the petals. One should offer mental flowers and perform mental incense offerings. Possessing the fragrance of the mind, with the blazing lamp of the mind, one should perform offerings with the mind itself, consisting of a gathered *bali* offering.

It is taught that the *rkyang ma* (the central channel) is the pure speech. The *blugs gzar* (the side channels) are the essence-flavors; their opening is the lotus-petal of the mouth, fully expanded to a measure of two finger-widths. The staff has a vajra and jewel at its end, as far as one’s own vajra blazes. The skull-cup is the vessel for the burnt offerings; all substances are made into burnt offerings (*homa*). Thus the sequence is thoroughly explained. It rests perfectly upon the five channels—five.

One should correctly join the syllables: earth, water, and likewise fire, wind, and space are equal. Like a plantain tree and its flower, they are correctly situated at the center of the navel. Always pervasive and abiding, the wise should encircle them all. The eight petals always face upward; it is taught that they are endowed with filaments. At their center is the very firm [syllable], the coemergent consciousness.

The deity, the intensely blazing Sky-Palace of Wind—its subtle particles should be thoroughly understood by their characteristics. Abiding with an uninterrupted stream of light rays, in the portion of a hundred-strand hair, there is the *bindu* of the intensely blazing *argha*-bestower, a formless syllable. Possessing the characteristics as before, and being equal to five finger-widths, it is taught as the full *homa* offering; [this is] the burnt offering.

Through the preparation of the three-finger-width burnt offering (*homa*), the nectar (*amṛta*) is correctly endowed with syllables. In the center of the nectar maṇḍala are the three syllables of supreme reality. By means of summoning the nectar of great bliss, it is taught that all objects of focus are delighted. Through the sequence of the burnt offering, [the nectar] flows and continues to flow constantly; thus, the Tathāgata [describes] the stream of smoke day and night.

Having condensed [the ritual], that which is described as the peaceful fire offering (*śānti-homa*) is the supreme body (*kāya*) abiding therein. For the sake of increase (*puṣṭi*), one should summon a bodhisattva and form a mental image (*pratibimba*) of him. For the sake of utterly exhausting the afflictions (*kleśa*), one should especially contemplate the form of a wrathful deity (*krodha*). Through various types of attachment, one should contemplate the form of a woman; because she is devoted to body, speech, and mind, she is the female consort (*mudrā*).

It was well-spoken: within the fire mandala of the three boats, the self-arisen *adhidaiva*, the burnt offerings (*havis*) are especially for the vessel; through mantra, all activities are accomplished. The Hero enters into non-dual union; *Oṃ Āḥ Bāṃ Hūṃ*. Recite perfectly the two-syllable mantra, *Ha Ha Siḍ*. Just as the emission occurs, the innate joy (*sahajānanda*) blazes intensely in the fire.

The mandala of luminous clarity is equal in power to the fire at the end of an aeon; through the complete incineration of all things without exception, the five aggregates do not circulate externally thereafter, nor does even their ash remain. By generating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—which is unceasing—together with great compassion and the power of aspiration prayers, one becomes equal to all Buddhas. Through this, the mandala of blissful awakening [is attained].

It becomes perfectly extensive; for the sake of the complete pacification of the afflictions and because it is utterly empty and without support, like a cloudless sky, one masters the perfection of wisdom and the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā). That which is called "the emanation of Śrī Heruka" is the maṇḍala that is the very nature of the three realms. As for "enjoyment," it means that the mind is just as the Buddha is.

All these are the symbols of non-duality. As for the statement "all treatises are expressed," this summarizes the reality (*tattva*) of the Buddha: through this excellent commitment (*samaya*) of the application of the Hero’s Mudrā and the proper consumption of food, supreme siddhi is brought about. It is without self, without grasping, faultless, spontaneously accomplished, and manifold.

Accompanied by the lamp arising from the *las* [substances], one should worship all the Tathāgatas with a mind of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). "Constantly" means without interruption. For that very reason, it is said: "One should worship perpetually through application. "Free from obstacles" means by practicing the commitments (*samaya*). Since that is accomplished exactly as it is in the siddhi of Mahāmudrā, it is said: "That is not otherwise. Thus it is heard.

One will not proceed toward the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and so forth. Regarding the phrase "his other messenger is excellent," "his" refers to the yogin. "Endowed with diligence" means being accompanied by that [diligence] simultaneously. As for the expression "endowed with diligence," it refers to the longing for spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*); it is one who possesses primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and is full of joy.

Having performed that many [actions], the yogin of the glorious Heruka’s union should enjoy the wealth of intensely passionate joy. Regarding the phrase "it is the differentiation of the substance of yoga," "substance" refers to the nectar of omniscient wisdom, which is like an elixir (*rasāyana*). For example, just as the celestial tree grants the fruit of one's desires, so too here does it grant the fruit of awakening.

The tree of the mind bestows the fruit of buddhahood. It is taught as two distinct types of differentiation: conduct and liberation. Having obtained the guru’s oral instructions, one should zealously engage in authentic meditation. By always possessing capability, one accomplishes supreme enlightenment; in this very life, one becomes a Buddha, a Great Vajradhara. This is its meaning.

"Action" refers to the fact that when those whose diligence has become lax have not attained unsurpassed primordial wisdom (*anuttara-jñāna*), they will instead attain the enjoyments of their desired objects and become equal to the donors (*dānapati*). This concludes the explanation of the twenty-eighth chapter from the *Paddhati* (Commentary on Difficult Points) titled *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, concerning the introduction to the methods of accomplishment. Then, as for the word "Then":

Immediately after [the words] "it was said," the phrase "furthermore" (*gzhan yang*) serves as a characteristic of distinction (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). "The teaching" (*deśanā*) refers to what precedes. It is to be construed as: "Then, furthermore, it should be known. "By what" (*yena*) means by way of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). "One who will come to know" (*jñāsyati*) refers to the yogin. "The ḍākinī who abides in the commitment" (*samayasthā ḍākinī*) means one who does not transgress the commitment (*samaya*).

For the benefit of practitioners, regarding the phrase "mother and father," it refers to whichever mother and father one has found. The word "and" (*dang*) follows as a conjunction for those who practice together. "As the lord" means the attainment of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). "Seen in an instant" refers to that very self; its complete perfection by them extends up to what is called "individually cognized" (*pratyātma-vedya*). Furthermore, thus...

It is said: "Whatever bliss is obtained from one's father, that bliss should be enjoyed by oneself. That bliss by which one dies here is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Regarding the term "thick-lipped": she has a broad face and full breasts; her face is short and her hair is short; she smells of elephant musk and is free of impurities. To summarize, it is explained thus: her body is tall and her face...

With long arms and long legs, smelling of fish and emitting semen; with a long birth-place and resembling the moon, being symmetrical, dark-blue, and having firm breasts; with small limbs and fine hair, a small birth-place and coarse hair; speaking calmly, with a high nose and a neck that is not too long; beautiful in form like a white lotus, and constantly emitting dust from the body.

"Extremely fragrant and captivating to the mind, with eyes and a gaze like those of a peacock; with a neck like a peacock, a belly like a peacock, and thighs like a king of peacocks; possessing the scent of a fortunate lotus, her eyes are reddish-yellow"—regarding this, "reddish-yellow" means slightly red; likewise, her hands and feet are also red. She emits the fragrance of mālikā flowers and delights in the assembly of the Sugatas.

She bestows the siddhis upon women; her body is full and her breasts are well-developed. Her hair is curled, and she walks with the gait of a swan and speaks slowly. Though not very tall, she is well-proportioned; at the center of her navel are three folds. One should know that it slopes inward from the center. She is slender, with delicate limbs, and like Devadatta, she disparages others. Her hair is curled and remains in plaits.

With limbs as crooked as a camel’s, she abandons women like a man; she smells like a *śāla* tree, yet is anointed with the radiant scent of *śāla*; she always delights in wine, her conduct of the samaya is perfect, and she contemplates intentions while applying herself to practice. She possesses an extraordinary, neutral fragrance that follows after wine; through the various qualities of wine, and by means of wine itself— (To be continued)

"Intoxication," "likewise copious semen," and "common to all siddhis" mean that, having attained excellence through a virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one follows after everything for the sake of liberation. "Mindfulness" refers to its various characteristics.

“Those called *Sambhāryā* are the yoginīs; ‘along with the positions of the messengers and so forth’—the term ‘position’ (*pada*) means ‘well-established,’ which is to say, the locus of qualities—and it is together with that. If one asks, ‘Whose [qualities]? it is the twenty-four supreme ḍākinīs; by these, all [beings] are gathered without exception. For this reason, by them, throughout the three worlds...”

This is called "Pervasive" (*Khyab pa*); by obtaining these and performing worship, they will bestow upon the practitioner the fruits of wealth and liberation. Regarding the phrase "The root mantra is to be recited constantly": it is called "mantra" (*sngags*) because it protects the mind from all evil paths; it is non-dual primordial wisdom (*advayajñāna*), and one recites the mantra that is its purification. It accomplishes all desired aims.

Regarding the term "action" (*kṛtya*), it is called "desire" (*kāma*) because it is that which is desired; it refers to the forms of Vajradhara and others who act for the benefit of all sentient beings. It is the practitioner of that [attainment], for the sake of achieving buddhahood in this very life. For that very reason, the phrase "arisen from this mantra" means that one will attain complete mastery. If one asks what that is:

Regarding the phrase "the three worlds, moving and non-moving": the three worlds refer to the utterly pure buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*). "Moving" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), and "non-moving" refers to the container world (*bhājanaloka*). At that time, these are said to be of one flavor within the state of Vajradhara. Alternatively, the "three worlds" refer to the Vajra Body and so forth. Their "moving" refers to—

The "vajra of bodhicitta" is the cause, because it is generated by those who desire bliss. "Non-movement" refers to its attainment; these two should be understood as functioning simultaneously. To the question "Whose [is this]?", it says "the practitioner," for he is one who is perfectly endowed with mantras and mudrās and is devoted to the siddhis.

For this very reason, it is said: "Without the mudrā, there is no consecration. This refers to sealing the body, speech, and mind. Wisdom is designated as the mudrā. One who is devoid of that—like a śrāvaka who lacks the wealth of faith—will not be consecrated by mantra. As for what is called "mantra":

It is the non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), the meaning of which is "attaining the state of a Vajradhara. For this reason, it says: "One should realize through intense application," which means with great diligence and without the mind wandering elsewhere. Regarding the phrase "as long as the activities of heat": first there is the heat of wisdom (*prajñā*); second, it becomes accompanied by smoke; third, a flickering light arises; fourth—

Blazing like a lamp, the fifth is constant luminosity; it is like a cloudless sky. This very point was clearly taught: the slight clarity of appearance is called "heat" (*ūṣmagata*). When that same radiance of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) becomes moderately clear, it is called "the peak" (*mūrdhan*). At the time when external objects appear and the radiance of primordial wisdom increases, there is the mere cognition of aspects (*vijñaptimātra*).

The uninterrupted continuity of luminosity, which is liberated from the collection of conceptualizations during the stage of *gyi gnas skabs*, is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). That very state, when the qualities of a Buddha have reached their peak, is the meaning of what is called "the supreme dharma" (*agradharma*). As for the passage beginning with "whoever hates," etc., it means that through being deluded and associating with sinful companions, one is corrupted and led downward, resulting in rebirth in the Avīci hell. The yogin...

Regarding the phrase "beginning with the one called Byor che mchog," the expression "that region is thoroughly examined" means that one should also offer worship to its branches. The term "de rung ni" (it is suitable) has the meaning of "abiding in the heart of the yogin. This concludes the twenty-ninth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanopāya-ālambana*.

This is the detailed explanation. Furthermore, the phrase "Moreover" (*atha punar*) refers to one other than Heruka; it means the wrathful king known as Amṛtakuṇḍalin. His *abhisamaya* (clear realization) is as follows: "The utterance" (*udīraṇa*) refers to the extensive arrangement of the vowels and consonants according to their proper sequence. "The portion of the earth" (*pṛthivībhāga*) and so forth refers to the offering of the *bali* (food offering) to all the elemental spirits (*bhūta*). "The universal transformation" (*parāvṛtti*)...

The seed-syllable is the form of the letter *Hūṃ*; immutability is bliss. Abiding in space, it is without location. Then, having donned the armor, all is empty and without support. The three syllables known as the "Clay Drum" (*rdza rnga*) are the three bodies (*kāya*) through the differentiation of body, speech, and mind. Perfectly supported by eight lines that are intensely encircled by wind, the ninth line abides in the center.

The stainless manifestation of emptiness is proclaimed; Āli and Kāli are made equal and pervasive. Possessing the nature of the four joys, It is the indestructible great drum of Dharma, The twelve branches of the excellent speech, The complete syllables of the Dharma. Then, through the process of enumeration, One correctly relies upon the selflessness of phenomena. Renowned as having four faces, It utterly subdues the four māras. Mounted upon the wind...

"Generating [the winds] and correctly gathering the three realms, one thoroughly understands the reality of the winds. Arising sequentially from the *āli* and *kāli*, which are not mountains, they are the letters of the expression and the expressed; these conceptualizations are like echoes. Take the thirty-second vowel," and so forth—this is as it is described and easy to understand. *Oṃ sumbhani sumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Oṃ gr̥hṇa gr̥hṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gr̥hṇāpaya gr̥hṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vajra rāja hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is called "Victorious Over the Three Realms. Adorned with these four mantra-words, for the purpose of protecting the maṇḍala and utterly subduing all malevolent spirits, it is endowed with the four wrathful deities. In an instant...

Regarding the phrase "The Eightfold Transformation of the Body" (*sku brgyad 'gyur*), one should emanate two bodies for each mantra. These consist of eight [deities] with the faces of a *khva* (vulture) and so forth, up to the perimeter of the great wheel that is extremely fierce and dispels all obstructors; they have one face and two arms, holding a copper knife (*zangs gri*) and a *khaṭvāṅga*, with three eyes blazing with red light rays, and are fierce and terrifying.

The one who has reached the prime of youth, with a youthful and transformed face, is girt by a tiger-skin loincloth; his lower body is wrapped in a kīla-shape, sharp and blazing, emitting rays of light like the fire at the end of an eon that destroys the world. Then, having caused the hosts of obstructors in the eight directions and intermediate points to enter into the bell, [one performs] the emergence from the ritual procedure and from the ritual procedure...

To repel [obstacles], one should brandish the wrathful kīlas with this mantra: *Oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ | kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān hūṃ phaṭ | hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ vajrakīlaya vajradhara ājñāpayati kāyavākcittavajrakīlaya hūṃ phaṭ*. Gazing fixedly with a wrathful look, one should strike them with the vajra hammer.

*Bya'o, oṃ vajramuṅgara vajrakīlaya āloṭāya hūṃ phaṭ.* Upon the wheel generated by the syllable *bhrūṃ*, there are Vajracaṇḍa, Vajrasūrya, Vajraśekhara, Vajravikṣepa, Vajrayakṣa, Vajrakṛṣṇa, Vajramahābala, Vajrabhairava, and likewise Śikhicakravartin.

"From the purification of the ten wisdoms—renowned as the 'Excellent Harm-giver' (Oṃ tu gnod mdzes)—namely, the wisdoms of suffering, origin, cessation, and path; of exhaustion, non-arising, phenomena, subsequent knowledge, conventional reality, and literal sound—one should emanate the ten wrathful deities. In the center, through the complete transformation of Vajrasattva, one should generate oneself as Vajra-Hūṃkāra."

His body is blue and possesses great ferocity; he is majestic, radiant, and terrifying, inspiring awe. His right and left faces are yellow and green respectively; they are heroic and ugly, with furrowed brows and a snarling expression. His eyes are red and round, with a fierce, blazing garland of wrathful flames swirling around him. *Vajra-hūṃ*—*Hūṃ*.

Adorned with ornaments of human bone, wearing a garland of flowers upon his head, he is the nature of the emanation of the five Buddhas. With two hands he holds a vajra and a bell, and performs the mudrā of Trailokyavijaya. Through wisdom and meditative absorption, with his remaining hands he holds a hook, a sword, and a skull-cup with its mouth wide open. Seated upon a throne with his right leg extended, [he tramples] Bhairava and...

At the time of the ritual, one visualizes [the deities] beneath the lotus feet. On the eastern petal is Vajracaṇḍa, blue in color, with a yellow face on the right and a green face on the left. His right hands hold a vajra, a club, and make the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*); his left hands hold a skull-cup (*kapāla*) and a *khaṭvāṅga*. With two arms, he embraces a consort who resembles himself. In the northern direction is Sūrya.

In the center is STE (Vajrasattva), red in color, embracing Prajñā who resembles Ljang gu rang; he holds a vajra, a staff, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga. In the western direction is Rdo rje gtsug tor (Vajroṣṇīṣa), red in color, embracing Prajñā who resembles Ljang gu rang; he holds a red lotus and...

He holds a *thod pa* (skull-cup) and a *khaṭvāṅga*. Vajrakuṇḍalī is in the southern direction; his color is like that of emerald (*ljang gu rang*), he embraces Prajñā, and his right and left hands are yellow and white, holding a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*). In the southeast corner is Vajrayakṣa, smoke-colored, with his right and left hands being yellow and emerald-green respectively.

He embraces his own consort with wisdom, and holds a trident, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*. In the southwest is black Vajra, red in color; his right and left hands are yellow and green, and he enters into union with his own consort while holding a battle-axe, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*. In the northwest is Mahābala-vajra, [red] in color...

In the southeast is Vajrabhairava, blue in color, with his right and left hands yellow and green respectively; he embraces his own Prajñā and holds a trident, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*. In the northeast is Vajrabhairava, blue in color, with his right and left hands yellow and green respectively; he embraces his own Prajñā and holds a sword, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*.

Above is Dzinpa’o (the Holder), the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin); he is white in color, with his right and left hands blue and green respectively, embracing his own Prajñā while holding a wheel, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga. Below is Gnod mdzes rdo rje (Vajra Yamāntaka); he is blue, with his right and left hands yellow and green respectively, embracing his own Prajñā while holding a vajra and a club.

They hold the noose of the *śiṅ-dang* nāga and make the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*). All the wrathful deities likewise abide upon various lotuses and sun disks, treading with their right legs extended upon the hundred world-protectors—namely, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vaiśravaṇa, as well as Agni, Rākṣasa, and Vāyu.

The deity is Īśvara; above him is Brahmā, the lord of the gods; and below is Viśvakarman. At their hearts, they should be visualized in both their natural and reverse orders. All the wrathful deities have dark-brown hair blazing upward, with furrowed brows, faces contorted by fierce frowns, short statures, protruding bellies, and three red, round eyes.

He has a garland of human heads for a necklace and is adorned with ornaments of human bone; he has a blue serpent of infinite extent as a crest-jewel, and his earrings are made from the radiating light of a red *jog po* [serpent]. He is decorated with a white lotus used as a necklace, and he holds a yellow *stobs rgyu* [serpent] as a sacrificial banner. With a yellow *dung skyong* [serpent], he forms a bracelet. The Kulika...

The supreme among the various [ornaments] is perfectly arranged as a breast-ornament (*hāra*); a white lotus serves as a waist-band; and since the color of Vaiśravaṇa resembles the root of a lotus, he forms the anklets. In an instant, his body, speech, and mind are thus adorned.

Through the empowerment of the water of bodhicitta, one possesses a crown arising from one’s own buddha-family, from which blazing vajras radiate fierce, shimmering light. Emanating from one’s own body, they pervade the expanse of space, filling the ten directions with the turbulent energy of the blazing wrathful families.

Then, the wheel of the command (*ājñācakra*) revolves swiftly; by means of knowledge of that very [reality], it is rotated counter-clockwise. Having stabilized the deities with the mind, thereafter there will be no obstacles. All malevolent spirits will die merely by finding this utterly pure Tathāgata; the enemy of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*) will be destroyed. There is no doubt that those who transgress this will be struck down.

Through the performance of the activities of the Teaching, such as the fierce rites of the glorious Vajra-Hūṃkāra, together with the maṇḍala and the ritual substances, may the fruit of all siddhis arise.

This concludes the explanation of the thirtieth chapter from the *Introduction to the Means of Accomplishment*, the commentary on the difficult points of the *Śrī Heruka*. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then, all the great flesh," and so forth: "all" refers to the afflictions such as hatred and the rest; by the power of the samayas, these are destroyed. If one asks what happens by that, it says "born of the vajra," which means the Vajra...

This is the wisdom of non-duality. That which arises from it is the body of the Vajradhara. "This" refers to these [beings]; "by all the malevolent ones" refers to the terrifying and unbearable [forces] such as hatred and so forth. This is a summary of what is called "born of the vajra. Thus, since [the substances] such as dogs and so forth are both food and burnt offerings, they are called "food" (*bza' ba*).

"One should perform the burnt offering (homa) and the torma (bali) ritual. Regarding the phrase "to be performed by one free from conceptualization," it is because [the mind] is luminous by its own nature. Furthermore, having attained that which is without flaw, it is to be performed by the Vajrayogin; otherwise, it would result in causing harm to sentient beings. As it has been said: "Merely by harming sentient beings, the siddhi of the mudrā will not be attained."

"Whichever mind is non-conceptual, in the fiercely roaring hearth, where the fire of total solitude blazes, one should perform the burnt offering of all conceptualizations—flesh and great flesh—as well as whatever is censured by people, [the blood] arising from the limbs of living beings, and various kinds of liquor; this is what is meant. 'All' refers to the three worlds. In those various places, whatever has been overcome..."

That which was spoken by the Blessed One is "without remainder," meaning it is called "attainment" (*siddhi*). "The entire kingdom" refers to the state of being a Vajradhara. Regarding the passage beginning with, "Conch shells, tortoises, and pearls—though all three arise from causes," the "causes" are non-virtuous actions, and they have truly arisen from those. By that, among the six realms of existence, [one attains] the human realm through merit.

"Manifesting as noble beings, who would disparage this very skull, which is the embodiment of the gnosis of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? Thus it is said; the meaning is that it is indeed not to be disparaged. Birth accompanied by the fruit of virtuous actions—that is, human birth—arises from a great accumulation of merit and is therefore extremely difficult to obtain. [It is the basis for] gnosis and liberation...

Because it is accomplished, it is the skull of the one whose body is the *dharmadhātu*—that is, the human [skull]. Since it is the locus of beautiful form and qualities, it is "thoroughly adorned with the five mudrās. It is said: "The bone garland is indeed the excellent ornament that purifies. Therefore, it says: "The heroes explain the *īśvara*. Regarding the term "sign" (*saṃketa*), it refers to the barbarians; it is the Buddha’s mudrā. This is the hero.

Regarding the phrase "this is its abode," it signifies that the true meaning of manifest enlightenment—the nature of bliss arising from the five channels as the essence of the five elements and the five Buddhas—is revealed as the reality of all stable and moving beings without exception. The left side represents wisdom (*prajñā*), which is the very nature of being devoid of intrinsic existence (*niḥsvabhāva*). That itself...

The thorough inquiry into the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) serves to indicate the non-dual suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. That which is called "the gathering of all friends" refers to the manifest awakening to bliss through the non-duality of Śrī Heruka and Vārāhī; it is oriented toward the essence and inclined toward nirvāṇa. Then, one becomes the master, the Vajradhara himself.

The glorious father of all Buddhas, Arranged according to the sequence of the six families, Is recited with the left hand positioned [as follows]: Having joined the *āli* and *kāli* together, In the order of the syllables of the *varga* groups: The thumb is the *niṣṭhā* (little finger); The index finger is the *pāpa* (ring finger); The middle finger is the *dīrgha* (middle finger); The ring finger is the *tala* (forefinger); The last is the *kaniṣṭhikā* (thumb). Regarding the passage beginning with "Vajrasattva," the meaning is easy to understand.

"Dpa' bo" (Vīra) refers to Akṣobhya. One should address the mantra syllable by its specific family name according to where it resides and empower it through that application, saying: "O [Name], Vajra Tathāgata! In this regard, the sequence of the families is as follows: *Ā ĀḤ KA TSA TA TA PA YA ŚA*. These are the various manifestations of the King Vairocana.

The nine vowels (*gyi yi ge*) are the nature of the letter *a*. The second group of consonants—*ka kha ga gha ṅa*, *ca cha ja jha ña*, *ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa*, *ta tha da dha na*, *pa pha ba bha ma*—is that of Ratnarāja (Jewel King). The third group of consonants—*ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha kṣa*—is that of Amitābha (Immeasurable Light). The fourth group of consonants—*ai ai e o au aṃ aḥ*—is that of Amoghasiddhi (Unfailing Success). *ao aoo aam aaḥ*.

The class of *Nga nya na ma'i* belongs to the fifth [family], Akṣobhya. Thus, these constitute the arising, destruction, and abiding of the entire world. Accordingly, one should apply the names and sequences of the Vajras of all the Buddhas as follows: the sixth, Vajrasattva, is the crown-protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*). Furthermore, the cause is adorned by the fruit, and the fruit also...

Regarding the phrase "Extending the Causes": Vajrahāsa (Vajra Laughter), Vajralāsyā (Vajra Grace), Vajranṛtyā (Vajra Dance), and Vajrarati (Vajra Joy) are the names belonging to the Vairocana family. Prajñāṅkuravajra (Vajra of the Sprout of Wisdom), Vajrāṅkuravajra (Vajra of the Vajra Sprout), Paramānandavajra (Vajra of Supreme Bliss), Sukhānandavajra (Vajra of Blissful Joy), and Āsphālanavajra (Vajra of Striking) are the names belonging to the Karma family.

*Vajrasukhāṅkuśa*, *Padmavajra*, *Vajrapadmāṅkuśa*, and *Ānandavajra* are names belonging to the Ratna family (*ratnakula*). *Jñānavajra*, *Cintāmaṇivajra*, *Anaṅgavajra*, and *Avalokiteśvaravajra* are names belonging to the Padma family (*padmakula*).

The vajra of great bliss, the vajra of passion, the vajra of space, the vajra of wisdom, and the vajras of the perfections are the names of the family of hatred; they are blessed as the Sukhāvatī realm of the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. Likewise, these also become the names of Mahāmudrā: Vajra...

Vajrahṛdayā, Vajraśastrā, Vajrāmemā, Vajranairātmyā, and Vajralocanā—these belong to the family of Vairocana. Vajradākinī, Vajragaurī, Vajramālā, and Vajrasakhī are the names of those belonging to the Ratna (Jewel) family. [Also] Vajravīryā and Vajrāṅkuśī.

Dang, Vajra-Ḍośalā, Vajramālā, and Vajrahāsā are the names of those belonging to the Lotus family (*padmakula*). Vajrāñjali, Vajrapuṣpā, Vajrapadma, Vajrasambhavā, and Vajralāsyā are the names of those belonging to the Action family (*karmakula*). Vajrarāgā, Vajratārā, and Vajramālā...

Vajrāveśā, Vajramatī, Vajra-kaṅkālā, Vajralalanā, Vajradhūpā, and Vajrahastā are the names for the great siddhi-mudrās of those belonging to the family of hatred (*dveṣa*). These are to be arranged in the hands: the left [hand] arises from wisdom (*prajñā*) and is the cause that generates movement; it consists of the five fingers and the five elements.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The earth is called the eyes," and so forth: it is well-established as *la-tā*, *gu-ru*, *gtso-mo* (the principal lady), *byis-pa* (the infant), and *dar-ma* (the youth). The perfections (*pāramitās*) are four; emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the nursemaid. These five elements are without beginning or end; they are the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), the blissful holder (*dhṛti*). That which is the absence of intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*); the characteristic of entities here is method (*upāya*).

"Arising is also arising, and raining is also raining; this is the compassion of Heruka. Therefore, skillful means is designated as the male, while emptiness is the female form. Through the inconceivable and spontaneously accomplished dharma of passion, one acts as the support; by relying upon that very [means], one should take [the consort] from the womb. With the second Vajradhara in front, perform the ritual union."

O noble being, you should be honored; having gathered various offerings, I shall then grant you permission. Until reaching the heart of enlightenment, throughout all the wheels of the directions without exception, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma for the supreme among sentient beings. Through the logic of wisdom and skillful means, like a wish-fulfilling jewel, completely abandoning all weariness and assembly, today—

Having set out for the sake of the benefit of beings, having received empowerment and authorization, and having performed the duties with great joy, one who brings happiness to all beings should speak with gentle words: "Today my life, along with its fruit, has borne fruit; today my human existence has become meaningful. Today I have realized my own nature; today I have enjoyed true bliss. The speech of the ḍākinīs is inconceivable."

"Today I have obtained the tantra; today the deities are pleased with me; today I possess the siddhis; today I am born into the family of the Buddhas; today I have become a son of the Buddhas. Having completed all the activities for the disciple, the phrase "from behind" means subsequently; as for the request to depart, it is performed with flowers, incense, unguents, song, dance, and offerings.

"By means of them, having thus performed the withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*), one should partake of the food together," means that [this is done] together with those who have been empowered in this very [rite]. "This is not to be explained" means that the perfect gift (*samyak-dāna*) is to be kept strictly secret. If one asks, "What is the result of that? it is said: "Through the union of all heroes, it is the supreme bliss of the ḍākinīs. This is the *Śrīheruka*.

This concludes the explanation of the thirty-first chapter from the *Dka’ ’grel* (Pañjikā), the *Sādhanopāyamaṇḍalavidhi*. Furthermore, that which is to be explained next concerns the section beginning with: "The fire offering for the meal-time. Regarding this, it is said: "By whatever actions sentient beings are tormented in the unbearable hells, by means of those very [actions] when endowed with great methods, yogins will certainly be liberated. As for the term 'wealthy' (*phyug*), it refers to..."

"Such as 'Bu' and so forth" means that they are the purity of the five Buddhas, and these must be accomplished without fault. If one asks, "In what way are humans wealthy? it says, "The castes," and so forth. Since the word "wealthy" (*phyug*) implies excellence, among the castes, the supreme caste is taken as "wealthy" because it possesses all virtuous qualities. This refers to the sequence previously taught.

"BA NI" means the seventh birth is extremely clear; or else, it is the common [attainment], which is to obtain freedom from being afflicted by disease and from sores, scabs, and the like. Or else, "as previously taught" refers to the action according to how it was demonstrated by the gestures of the hand. Regarding the mandalas for accomplishing the siddhis in the *sthāna*, *upasthāna*, and *kṣetra*: having prepared the great circle (*maṇḍala*) in front, with devotion...

Having performed [the preliminaries] and taken hold [of the vow], I, the practitioner of the glorious Heruka, shall accomplish the maṇḍala of the assembly. Regarding the statement, "The heart-essence of Kṛṣṇaśvana is endowed with black māṣa beans," this means that for the purpose of accomplishing the great vetāla, one first makes perfect offerings through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the five types of offerings, recites the essence mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) one hundred thousand times, and then—externally...

One should undertake the practice with diligence. Having obtained a corpse—or any other suitable substance—that is fresh, unimpaired, and beautiful in form, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the waning moon, one should go to a secluded region, such as a mountain peak or a charnel ground, and draw the maṇḍala using the powdered remains of all the substances found in a charnel ground according to the proper sequence: it should be square with four gates.

Adorned with eight pillars and horse-treadings, with an eight-petaled lotus drawn in the center and marked by a multicolored sun, one should then perform the practice together with a supreme spiritual companion of great fortitude. Having arranged flowers and incense in abundance and beautified the site with victory banners, one should present extensive offerings and tormas, and cleanse the area with scented water mixed with the five nectars.

Having prepared the base, one should anoint it with a large quantity of sesame oil and worship it with *utpala* flowers. One should fill a single or eight vases with blood, fat, and marrow. The necks [of the vases] should be bound with cemetery cloth. There should be incense consisting of a great amount of resin, along with a body-powder made from the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)—such as fat and blood—and the wool of the *arka* tree.

Anoint a wooden branch seven times with lac resin. Light a large sesame oil lamp and smear its smoke into his eyes. Perform the protection with the two garments and the meditative visualizations of the ritual dagger (kīla) and the enclosure exactly as before. Then, while sounding the bell and the hand-drum and uttering the syllable *HŪṂ*, offer a torma consisting of rice mixed with human flesh and blood, along with blood.

One should give [the offerings] to the deities. Then, having placed the head toward the east in the center of the mandala, the Hero (vīra) should sit facing east at its heart, with an *ākarṣa* vessel placed to his left. Furthermore, there should be porridge mixed with the milk of a black dog or a black cow, combined with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), as well as black meat, rice, and a broth consisting of flesh and blood.

Having properly placed the skull-cup upon the skull-bowl of the charnel ground, slightly open its mouth, and direct it toward the fire kindled with wood and other materials as the bestower of supreme [attainments], one should then meditate on the command-wheel of glorious Heruka at its center and perform the fire offering (*homa*) one hundred and eight or eight hundred times with the heart mantra. [One should offer] to glorious Heruka and the ḍākinīs of Vajravārāhī...

Even if one sees oneself surrounded by as many māyā-birds as there are in the world, laughing loudly "ha ha," or surrounded by jackals howling, or seeing the hosts of rākṣasas uttering terrifying cries in the ten directions, one should not be afraid. With firm perseverance, one should remain in meditative equipoise; having stationed the companions of accomplishment to the right, one should ring the bell and [hold] the vajra in hand.

One should exercise mastery. If one fumigates with incense continuously, then that corpse will rise and say, "What shall I do? One should offer *argha* to it and say: "Excellent! O Great Hero, Vajrasattva of noble asceticism! I am the accomplished one; grant me the siddhi of well-being! Grant whatever the practitioner desires from among the single [attainments], and then return to your own abode."

Surrounded by a retinue of heroes and rākṣasas, the practitioner is endowed with glory; in that very instant, the three worlds will be known. He shall also become a divine body, a great hero possessing a desirable form. Throughout the three worlds without exception, he is like a Fortunate Tathāgata. Like the expanse of space, he is utterly free from aging and death. Desire...

"The entry into the siddhis of the elements, wandering throughout all existence, the very state of heavy ash, and the remainder, the dry head and the weapon"—this is the explanation based on the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). Here, the word "head" (*mgo bo*) refers to earth; "ash" (*thal ba*) refers to water; "dry head" (*mgo skam*) refers to fire; and "weapon" (*mtshon cha*) refers to wind. These constitute the mandala of the four great elements.

Regarding the phrase "the great mountain Meru should be made the center of the mandala," this refers to Mount Meru, the king of mountains. The sequence for its visualization is as follows: from the complete transformation of the syllable *yām*, there arises a blue wind mandala shaped like a bow, marked with banners and consecrated by the syllable *yām*. Its depth is immeasurable, extending for six hundred thousand yojanas. Above that, from the complete transformation of the syllable *rām*, there arises fire...

Visualize the supreme mandala as a three-sided red triangle, blazing with flickering garlands of fire and radiant like ten million suns. Its depth is three thousand four hundred and fifty *rkang* (cubits), and its width is twenty-one thousand and eleven *rkang*. Above the fire is water, perfectly arisen from the syllable *BĀM*, clear and cool like snow.

A circle marked with a white *bum pa* (vase) and possessing garlands of light; above that, from the complete transformation of the syllable *Lāṃ*, there arises a golden mandala, square in shape, eight hundred thousand units in height and twelve hundred thousand units in width—a mandala of earth—whereby all that remains thereafter also turns into gold. Upon that is the syllable *Khaṃ*, which becomes a three-pronged crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*). At the center of the crossed-vajra...

From the three syllables of *bala* arises Mount Meru, eighty-four thousand *yojana* in height, square in shape, composed of the four kinds of precious substances, and having the form of a parasol on its upper portion; it is eighty thousand *yojana* in width. To its eastern direction, from the complete transformation of the syllable *āḥ*, arises Pūrvavideha, eight thousand *yojana* in extent, and nine thousand *yojana* at its narrowest, like a half-moon.

It has the form of *pa*. To the north, from the complete transformation of the syllable *ai*, is Aparagoyānī, ten thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, square in shape; to the west, from the complete transformation of the syllable *au*, is Godānīya, nine thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, having the form of the full moon; to the south, from the complete transformation of the syllable *ae*, is Jambudvīpa...

The Gling ste mountain range is seven thousand *yojana* in length and breadth; it is wide in the northern direction and slopes downward toward the south. On both sides of those [mountains], in each of the four directions—east, south, west, and north—are the syllables *ai ai*, *au au*, *ri rī*, and *li lī*. By means of these syllables, [the deities] Śarīra and Śarīraparvata, Āḍambara and Aparāḍambara, Cañcala and Varatrasa, and Śabda [are established].

Mi-snyan and Sgra-mi-snyan are its moons; each of those eight minor continents is further surrounded by five hundred [smaller] islands. Above that, from the complete transformation of the syllable *Rāṃ*, there arises a sun maṇḍala. Above that, from the complete transformation of the syllable *Hūṃ*, there arises a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*). At its center is also *Hūṃ*; from that, one should visualize a vajra-kīla and a fence. *Vajra-hūṃ*.

One should perform the meditation on the wheel of Amoghasiddhi. From the complete transformation of the syllable *Hūṃ* arises Samantabhadra. From that, the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*)—triangular, white, and standing upright—is the nature of the inner space; upon a red lotus, from the complete transformation of the syllable *Bhrūṃ* and the wheel, there appears yellow Vairocana, with one face and four arms, holding a sword...

She is adorned with a crown of skulls and a silk scarf (*dar*), and holds a *khaṭvāṅga* decorated with a wheel and a hand-drum in her right hand, and a bell and a skull-cup in her left. Standing in the posture with the right leg extended, she embraces the blue Yamī. Yamī, who is also blue, has one face and four arms; she holds a hand-drum and a copper knife in her right hands, and a bell and a skull-cup in her left hands.

You have matted hair, loose locks, and are adorned with the five mudrās. Thus, one should visualize the celestial mansion at the summit of Mount Meru, which arises from Vairocana together with his consort; it is as vast as space, composed of the five precious substances, excellent, and endowed with qualities such as being four-cornered, and possesses vajra pillars and *tvaranas*.

It is adorned with half-lotuses and garlands of flowers hanging down, and is embellished with vajra threads that are the concordant result of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*. In its center are the *ālikāli* [vowels and consonants], above which are the two syllables *hūṃ* and *āṃ*; from the complete transformation of these at the centers of the vajra and the bell, there arises Vajrasattva with three faces.

Six-Armed Mahākāla is like the stainless sky at dawn, holding [the consort] as clearly as ten million moons. His right and left faces are blue and red; he embraces [his consort] while holding a vajra and a bell. In his [other] right hands, he holds a hand-drum (*damaru*) and a human head, and in his left hands, he holds a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga*. He is adorned with Akṣobhya upon his crown. This is the mantra-base.

One should visualize the syllable *baṃ*; in the center is wind, and likewise fire. In the center of that are the *āli-kāli* vowels and consonants, and in their center is the line of emptiness. Perfectly joined with great bliss, it is the supreme non-duality of the non-dual. By means of being exhorted by sound, all sentient beings arrive; through the yoga of the Buddhas' grace, the realms of sentient beings are thoroughly purified—the maṇḍala arising from bliss.

TE, BHRŪṂ ĀṂ HRĪṂ HOḤ HŪṂ HIḤ. To empower the mental continuum, one should emanate from the seed-syllable AI: Vairocana, Vajrasūrya, Padmanarteśvara, Vajrarāja, Akṣobhya, and likewise Heruka. OṂ HŪṂ ĀṂ ĀḤ KHĀṂ HAṂ: [the purifiers of] delusion, hatred, and likewise envy, attachment, and so forth.

The seed syllables *Saṃ*, *Vaṃ*, *Laṃ*, *Rāṃ*, *Āḥ*, and *Hūṃ* belong to Ser sna (Pāṇḍaravāsinī), Dbang phyug rdo rje (Īśvaravajrā), Sparśa-vajrā, Rasa-vajrā, Gandha-vajrā, and Dharmadhātu-vajrā. The seed syllables *Lāṃ*, *Māṃ*, *Pāṃ*, and *Tāṃ* belong to Spyan ma (Locanā), Māmakī, Gos dkar mo (Pāṇḍaravāsinī), and Sgrol ma (Tārā). Oṃ Āḥ!

By reciting "HŪṂ," one should complete the body, speech, and mind of the three realms of existence. Through meditative concentration, one should visualize the aggregates, sense bases, and elements in whatever form is desired—such as having one face, two arms, and so forth—thereby completing all three realms of existence without exception. Then, within the mandala of space, there are the syllables OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ.

Interspersed with two red syllables, like a gandharva being, the five syllables are summoned from the direction of space with a mind of aspiration. They enter the heart center, and through the blazing fire of great passion generated by the subsequent engagement of method and wisdom, the two bodies melt into the lotus.

It becomes like a reflection in the samādhi of the Great Abode, which is as stainless as space and the source of all phenomena. Following that, from the light rays emanating from the nature of great love, compassion, joy, and equanimity—generated by the aspiration prayers practiced since beginningless time—there appear goddesses with wide-open eyes.

Those who possess [the realization] that is like a reflection in the sky invoke the Protector with this song: "Kye! O Bliss of the Three Worlds, please remain here! Ā la la la la ho! Behold the abode of Padma! O Great Bliss, King of Vajra Holders, Observe the vows of the Victors! Ā la la la la ho! You are the supreme among all the renunciant ones; behold the essence of the Sugatas! O Beautiful One..."

"Bliss at this time is the essence within the three realms! Ā la la la la ho! O Lord of Bliss, grant, grant, grant! O Lord of the Victors, Dharmakāya! As soon as he was exhorted by this song, [the child] emerged from the heart of the vajra arisen from the syllable *Hūṃ*; this is the "sequence of birth from the womb. Alternatively, it is said to be "like that of a tortoise," meaning that a tortoise is born from its five openings.

PA'O. Regarding its sequence: meditating on the form of the deity of yoga in a single instant is the arising of unimpeded primordial wisdom. The Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of method and wisdom—great compassion that is effortless and uninterrupted—is called "the tortoise" (*kūrma*), because it is fixed and immutable. [This refers to] the four-armed and four-faced...

The phrase "Fourthly," and so forth, should be applied to both stages [of generation and completion]. Regarding the description "white complexion," one should understand this as the specific procedure for the Vajradhara [mandala], and all the deities should be visualized. Desiring the siddhi for the sake of siddhi, the wise person should not remain for even a moment with thoughts directed toward anything else; through such distinguished qualities, [the goal is attained].

The yogin shall attain the siddhi of all desires. This concludes the explanation of the thirty-second chapter from the *Śrī Heruka-pañjikā-sādhanālaṃkāra*. Then, having understood everything, [it is said]: "The supreme among all applications is the mudrā of supreme bliss; it is the great method for attaining siddhi."

This is the *ḍākinīsamaya*. Therefore, there is no superior sādhana for the practitioner than this, because it accumulates great merit and so forth. For that reason, one should construct the maṇḍala of the assembly (*gaṇa-maṇḍala*), just as it was spoken in the *Āryadevapratibhāṣasaṃkṣiptacaryāpradīpa*. As for the food, snacks, and so forth, they are to be taken literally. Then, the male...

Regarding the phrase "to those beginning with Nyarab sbyin" (Nyārabdha), etc., "one's own lap" refers to one's own limbs. Regarding "the heroes are to be worshipped," it means that the heroes are to be offered. Regarding "those beginning with 'Ma'" (Mother), the word "or" indicates whoever is fortunate; otherwise, they would become impure. All of these are to be set aside for the purpose of worshipping oneself.

"From bonds, one shall be liberated" means that one is to be liberated from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), because liberation occurs through the abandonment of those predispositions. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Master, well-established in the body," one should perform everything while visualizing oneself in the form of Vajradhara; subsequently, all heroes and heroines should be enjoyed. Having arisen from the state of non-appearance, [one proceeds] as a couple.

Through the sequence of the elements of entry, one will manifest the body of a Buddha and abide adorned with all the qualities of the vajra-like samādhi. Regarding the phrase "moving beneath the earth" and so forth: for the sake of sentient beings, whatever one desires—such as pacification and the rest—all will be accomplished by his mere command; of this there is no doubt.

This concludes the explanation of the thirty-third chapter from the *Pa'o*, the commentary on the difficult points (*pañjikā*) and the ritual manual (*sādhanā*) of the glorious Heruka, concerning the introductory narrative. Now, regarding the phrase "the extensive ritual of the wheel within the lattice of the ḍākinīs": by performing all those applications of yantras and mantras exactly as they have been taught, there is no doubt that accomplishment will be attained. [The ritual manual] is in the mind...

"Because it is supported, it is the attainment of the state of *ābadhūtī*. Regarding its meditation, it is said: "The heroes and yoginīs are joined within the center of the lotus. Here, "center" refers to the heart of the central lotus; they are joined there.
