Because it stirs away the sins of conceptualization, it is the *ābadhūtī*, having the form of blazing fire; its lord is also *Ā*.

One recites "BA DHŪ TI. Its locus is the "well-established" (*pratiṣṭhita*), which means that upon which something rests. By this, it is likewise said for the yogin as well. Where? It says, "between the eyebrows," meaning it is surrounded by the sixteen lines of the *āli* between the moon and the lotus. Regarding the phrase "the mouth of the wandering hero" (*vīracāri-mukha*), "wandering" (*cārin*) means terrifying; [it refers to] the Blessed One...

"Regarding the phrase *dās kyi zhal du'o*: by that cause, one should offer to the Fire God (*agni-deva*) who has arisen from the nature of the first vowel; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase *'di dag ces bya ba ni*: it means 'by these substances. Regarding the phrase *bsreg bya lnga*: it means 'by the purities of the five Tathāgatas. Regarding the phrase *bsreg bya dgu*: it means 'each [of those] nine,' thus making forty-five."

The meaning is that one should perform the fire offering (*homa*). Then, "the blazing garland ocean" refers to that which possesses intense radiance. "One should contemplate" means by means of mantra. If one asks what should be done, it says "the wheel. "The mandala of all gates" refers to the mandala of the three realms without exception—the self-arisen supreme deity. "The hero of heroes," and so forth, refers to the self...

"By means of the yoga of one's own chosen deity. "The abode of the hero" refers to the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) together with its surroundings. "On the petals are the four female messengers" means that on the four petals of the central lotus are the four [deities] beginning with the ḍākinī. "The Cakravartin hero, in non-duality, bestows the khaṇḍaroha externally as he pleases" means that having visualized it according to his desire, he—

"One should perform the fire offering with superior aspiration. What is "external"? It refers to those such as the face of a crow. By whose form? It says, "by one's own form," meaning that by means of the mantra, one should visualize it in the form of the gateway and the four corners of the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) exactly as they are. "Should be shown" means "should be meditated upon. Where? "In the center of the wheel. The wheel—

Regarding the statement, "In this teaching of today, it is that which accomplishes all siddhis": one should meditate on the maṇḍala of the mind, which is the nature of the three realms, within the *bindu* of the seed-syllable of the marks upon the white lotus at the heart of the Jñānasattva. This is described as: "Adorned with millions of rays of light, densely gathered by clouds of Buddhas; the condensed yoga of the *bindu*, subtle..."

Meditate clearly on the yoga of *mo'i*. Within the signs of the stages of the families, from the syllable *Hūṃ* arises a maṇḍala as vast as the expanse of space, the abode of the Victorious Ones, a treasury of jewels, great bliss, composed of extremely subtle atoms, and a garland of light rays of primordial wisdom. From this, infinite forms of various kinds [emanate], and all sentient beings without exception become the commitment of the Vajra Ḍākinī.

When the vital breaths and efforts are thoroughly restrained through the blessing of the mantra, and the mind is held with extreme stability, there is no doubt that within seven days one will directly perceive [the deities] moving, shaking, descending, vibrating, surging, and leaping. Regarding the teaching of these wheels, it says: "O Vajragarbha of great compassion, O Ocean of Knowledge," and so forth.

Just as in the first chapter of the *Niṣpannayogāvalī*, which teaches the wheel (*cakra*), one should not entertain any doubt here either. Regarding the phrase "the master of the union of the two messengers" (*dūtyadvayayogātman*): having obtained the scriptural tradition of mantra, which is extremely difficult to find, and being fully endowed with recitation and meditation, one will certainly attain accomplishment here. This concludes the *Pañjikā* on the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, titled the *Sādhanopāya*.

This concludes the explanation of the thirty-fourth chapter from the *Kyi gleng gzhi* (The Introduction). Now, regarding the phrase "the supreme ritual action is to be illustrated according to the sequence": "sequence" (*rim*) refers to a continuous succession; it means that the tradition transmitted from one master to another must be maintained without impairment. Regarding the phrase "the self of the non-dual offering": this refers to the non-dual offering, which is the method (*upāya*).

"Dang" means non-dual wisdom (*prajñā*). Through the mantra that is the essence of its application, the supreme activity (*karmottama*) is to be accomplished. "Activities are to be applied individually" refers to pacification (*śānti*) and so forth. "The mantras that bring about accomplishment" refers to the eight classes (*aṣṭakula*). Regarding the phrase "their divisions in due order," the letters consist of the vowels and the thirty consonants.

The three channels are the yoginīs who are the very nature of the channels. By the word "and so forth," the twenty-four heroes are included, as well as their mantras. Regarding the phrase "completely circled by the force of the arrow" and so on: the "arrow" is the wind; by its force they move, and by that they circle—that is, they definitely engage in coming and going. Their mutual convergence...

"Mantra" (*sngags*) refers to the conjunction of *ālikāli*; "conjunction" means they are distinguished by their respective locations. "Distinguished by location" means they are arranged at the heart, throat, navel, and head. Regarding the phrase "having grasped those seed-syllable garlands, *hūṃ* abides at the end": wherever [the deities] are summoned and inserted, the syllable *hūṃ* abides there. The meaning of this is as follows: the left...

On both the right and left sides, one should arrange the twelve vowels facing upward; those facing downward are the two strings beginning with the letter *ka*, which should be placed in their midst. As it has also been said: "On both the left and right sides, The twelve vowels abide; They are correctly explained as facing upward, With *ka* and the others clearly interspersed."

When the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) is ceased, cessation is the twofold binding of movement. That which is called "the object of accomplishment" has become the *siddhi*; it is the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) that is without support. "Not even a single step is taken" means that because there is no movement by means of the winds, the destination to be traveled does not exist; for that very [destination] has become of one taste with its own nature.

Regarding the phrase "and having joined the union," and so forth: "having joined the union" is explained as the two moons. On both the left and right sides, there is a vajra linked-chain (vajra-laguḍa) tied together, abiding eternally at the upper aperture, possessing garlands of blazing light.

The union (*saṃpuṭa*) is the application of supreme joy as a continuous flow within the collection of the path of liberation. Alternatively, the mutual embracing of the two hands is described as the "vajra-chain binding" (*vajra-laguḍabandha*). The union of method and wisdom is explained as "union" (*saṃpuṭa*). Regarding the phrase "the very opening of the vajra," and so forth, it refers to the insertion of the vajra into the lotus. As for "circling" (*parivarta*):

The "Stirring" refers to the vajra and lotus being made to move like a small bee on a flower; by means of circling, this is the "Stirring. Through the nature of bliss and joy, the tongue is placed within the lotus, using the hook of desire as a goad.

"Summoning all the Tathāgatas, the unshakeable one who performs shaking is Vajra; he is renowned as the *mathanī* (churning stick). Regarding 'striking with the food-vajra,' it is the assembly (*melāpaka*) of the Tathāgatas. Regarding 'having joined an arrow to the breath,' the 'arrow' refers to sound (*śabda*). Regarding 'joining it to the limb called *khatvāṅga*,' the *khatvāṅga* is the body of the deity; because its limb is like space (*ākāśa*), it is called *kha*."

Regarding the line, "O Tathāgata, within the vessel of the skull-cup offering, the offering liquid is certainly applied to the mouth," it is as follows: the mantra practitioner should visualize [the syllable] at the navel; in the center of the wind is a fire mandala. Upon that is a multicolored lotus, and upon that is a skull-cup completely filled with the bodhicitta-nectar of primordial wisdom (*jñāna-mṛta*). In its center are the *āli-kāli* vowels and consonants, which possess the nature of the five primordial wisdoms, and the syllable *Hūṃ*.

Regarding the blessing: through the yoga of Vajrasattva arising from the syllable *Bāṃ*, one is peaceful and possesses the state of compassion; like the stainless autumn sky, one radiates many garlands of light rays like the moon, treading with one's feet upon the four Māras, and is the great bliss inseparable from Vārāhī. Upon the moon at the crown of the head is the indestructible [syllable], exceedingly [radiant] like an *ātasa* flower.

A stream of milk flows day and night from the breasts of the consort. Upon the lotus below, adorned with the sun and moon, one should visualize her at the center of the hub. Within the center of the wind is a fire mandala; one should not view her as formless, but apply the mind in a state of perfect tranquility. Furthermore, from the syllable *Lāṃ* at the head, there is a great vajra mandala, and the remainder of the naga Śeṣa is Great Bliss.

Adorned by the three beautiful celestial maidens, visualize that from the central *bindu* (drop), a stream flows like falling rain. The syllable *Ai* is explained as a stream of nectar, which descends into the two eyes. It is equal to a white *kunda* flower or the moon, adorned with the ornaments of Indra. Above, it is shrouded by clouds and adorned with lightning and thunderbolts, pervading the center of space.

By meditating on the continuous flow of nectar-rivers pouring forth, one brings peace to the very limits of the city. If one visualizes [the deity] seated upon the object of accomplishment, poisons, fevers, and the like will be dispelled by mere meditation alone. If one constantly meditates on the colors and forms of the central mandala, even if one’s lifespan is exhausted, it will indeed become long; one should join the two lips in a single union.

There is no aging and no death; one shall not be afflicted by diseases and the like. Even the great poison of those seized by the eight classes of great *nāgas* will be rendered non-poisonous through this arrangement; it shall even revive those who have died from poison. One shall triumph over untimely death and become completely liberated from disease. Like the moon of the autumn season, a crescent moon is drawn upon the thumb of the left hand.

By spreading out the syllable *Bām* and correctly gathering the nectar, one gradually overcomes untimely death. Then, the ritual for protection proceeds as follows: visualizing the reversal of Vajrapāṇi’s protection, one is the principal deity of the self-protection and reversal, with a white face and right faces that are blue, red, and yellow, while the left faces are greenish-blue, red, and smoke-colored; the upper face is large and white.

Seated upon a moon disc and adorned with various ornaments, beautified by white garments, and in the posture of the right leg extended, she tramples underfoot the Lord of Death, Māra, and his retinue. Wearing the great crown of the five Buddhas, she is supreme in restoring the dead to life; possessing three eyes, peaceful yet joyful with an expression of compassion, her first hand, in the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*), brandishes a vajra.

Holding a bell together with a lotus and a wheel; likewise, holding a sword, a battle-axe, a staff, and a skull-cup; a hook that bestows fearlessness; furthermore, a bow and an arrow drawn to the ear; a *khaṭvāṅga*, a drum, a vase filled with nectar, a conch together with a lotus, and the fifteenth and sixteenth [mudrās] confer empowerment.

This is the mudrā of Bai. One should visualize a wheel at its center: having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, at its hub is a twelve-spoked viśvavajra; at the hub of the viśvavajra is the syllable *Hūṃ*, and at the hub of that [syllable] is the syllable *Bāṃ*. At the hub of the syllable *Bāṃ*, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished interspersed with three syllables, together with the protective mantra (*rakṣā*). Within the spokes is space.

The four female deities (*gro ma bzhi*) are to be arranged here in a counter-clockwise direction, combined with *dām*, *lām*, *khām*, *rūm*, *ri*, *rī*, *li*, and *lī*. As for the arrangement of the lotus petals, they correspond respectively to the mandala of the Mind: *khām*, *prām*, *kām*, *tzām*, *kām*, *prām*, *bām*, and *mām* are in the east, north, west, and south. In the southeast and other intermediate directions, *sām*, *bām*, *āṃ*, *khām*, *bām*, *lām*, *bām*, and *trām* are combined with the syllable *hūṃ*. Of these—

On the exterior, one should draw a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*), with the sixteen vowel syllables written upon its hub. On the four corners, one should draw the four faces of Yamāntaka. Then, one should draw a sixteen-petaled lotus; on the pericarp, one should write *kāṃ khāṃ gāṃ ghāṃ ṅāṃ*, and *cāṃ chāṃ jām*. On the sixteen petals, one should write the hundred-syllable mantra of the Venerable Lord (*Bhagavat*).

Outside of that, draw a sixteen-spoked wheel. On the spokes of the wheel, write counter-clockwise as before: *Ām Ām Bām Mām Mām Bām, Bām Sum, Bām Sām, Mām Hām, Bām Khām Mām Tsām, Rām Khām Khām Hām Sām Mām Tsām, Ām Sām, Hām Sām Bām Mām Bām Tsām Bām Mām*. These should be written with the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning, interspersed with *Hrīḥ* and the name of the person for whom the rite is performed.

One should write [the syllables] *dzaḥ*, *nyaṃ*, *taṃ*, *thaṃ*, *daṃ*, *dhāṃ*, *naṃ*; *taṃ*, *thāṃ*, *daṃ*, *dhāṃ*, *naṃ*; *paṃ*, *phāṃ*, *baṃ*, *bhāṃ*, *maṃ* joined with names upon the necks outside of that. Outside of that, there is a four-cornered [mandala] with four doors, surrounded by five walls; and at the four doors and the intermediate directions, one should place *kāṃ*, *auṃ*, *syāṃ*, *śūṃ*, *yāṃ*, *yāṃ*, *yāṃ*, *yāṃ*, *yāṃ*, *rāṃ*, *lāṃ* in their proper order.

WĀM ŚĀM ŚĀM SVĀ HĀ. The name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) should be joined with *HŪṂ* and *HŪṂ PHAṬ*. Above the door, a vajra with its points closed should be drawn; above that, the eight-syllable mantra should be written. On the outside, upon the sash, this protection and averting [mantra] should be written: *NAMA:*...

SAMANTA KĀYA VĀK CITTA VAJRA NĪ | OṂ HŪṂ VAJRA HERUKA CAKRAVARTI SARVA LOKIKA LOKOTTARA NĪ | YANTRA MANTRA TANTRA BUBHRA YOGATINĪYE NA KE NA TSITA KRTANE | SARVA NĪ ĀKADDHYA ĀKADDHYA | GṚHṆA GṚHṆA BHAKṢAYA BHAKṢAYA | TRĀSAYA TRĀSAYA | HANA HANA | DAHA DAHA | PĀTAYA PĀTAYA | KṢMĀṂ KṢMĀṂ | JÑAUṂ ||

DZNYŪM, MA THA MA THA, BIDDHVĀM SA YA BIDDHVĀM SA YA, SHA TA SA HA SRA DHA, SHA TA SA HA SRA DHA, BI TZURṆĀ YA, BI TZURṆĀ YA, OṂ PHAṬ VAJRA HERUKA AUṢṆĪŚA CAKRĀVARTI ṢE KHĀṂ MU KHĀṂ TSAKṢU BANDHA BANDHA HŪṂ HŪṂ, SNGAGS PA CHE GE MO RAKṢA KURU HŪṂ OṂ SVĀHĀ. Write the wheel (cakra) within the belly of the letter KṢĀ; furthermore, write KṢĀ within the belly of the letter THĀ.

Outside, one should write the *ālikāli*. Outside of that, it should be encircled by a garland of vajras. Having performed the consecration according to the ritual procedure, one should recite the mantra for reviving the deceased: *Oṃ matri sāñjivani mahāmeye tri mikhi dzi ba prabeśaya sarvavajrapadma samayayoge mahābodhicittaṃ bhedhoma vartehūṃ hūṃ hūṃ.*

AA AA SVĀ HĀ; by reciting this one hundred and eight times, untimely death is averted. Then, one should take self-arisen substances: the dust from the footprint of a *ḍombī* or a Brahmin, elephant dust, *bodhicitta*, *tsil chen*, incense smoke, and lotus water. These should be mixed with *vajra* water and formed into a circle using the *mālā-mantra*. It should then be wound with a white thread. Following the empowerment and the authentic offerings, there is the *bali* offering.

One should perform the extensive ritual; having manifested oneself as the actual Śrī Heruka, one should recite the mantra: *Oṃ Hrīḥ Ha Ha Āḥ Mukha Śāntiṃ Kuru Śāntiṃ Kuru Hūṃ Hūṃ Dhama Dhama Phaṭ*. If it is placed inside ghee, honey, and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), [the afflicted person] will become free from illness along with their disease. Alternatively, if it is always bound upon the head of a yogin, the yoginīs...

One will attain the supreme [attainment], become free from obstacles, and when entering into battle, one will be victorious over all. Oṃ vajra heruka samaya manu pālaya herukatve no patiṣṭha dṛḍho me bhava, supoṣyo me bhava, anurakto me bhava, sustoṣyo me bhava, sarvasiddhiṃ me prayaccha, sarvakarmasu ca me, cittaṃ śreyaḥ.

KU RU HŪṂ, HA HA HA HA HOḤ! BHAGA BĀṆA VAJRA HERUKA PADMA BHĀM KṚTTA TE DHE KU YAD! At that time, one should proclaim the misdeeds of that person who does not abandon their sins, saying: "O Guru and Muni, please [purify] this! Then, from one's own body—which abides as the Great Wrathful One blazing like the terrifying fire of a charnel ground—one emanates [light] and enters the heart of the object of practice through the lotus of union.

Having separated [the consciousness] through the nature of compassion, one should cause its protective deity to enter into one’s own body. Then, grasping the deity of consciousness with the thumb and ring finger, place it within an *amṛtakośa* (jujube) fruit; imagine that it is carried to the pure land of Sukhāvatī, where it attains the body of Akṣobhya and performs offerings. Then, recite together with the name: *Oṃ Phaṭ Ā Mu Kaṃ Bhakṣa Phaṭ Kha*.

Visualize that [the victim] is surrounded by ḍākinīs and devoured; then, drawing [the victim] in with wrathful hooks, one should extract the central channel from the center of the wrathful palace of *hūṃ*. Having drawn out the heart, marrow, flesh, and blood, and having cut them into pieces, one should swirl them around like a bundle of feathers. In the same way, there are many hosts of wrathful deities and ḍākinīs with various kinds of weapons.

One should visualize that [the obstacles] are being severed and struck down from above, and that the ḍākinīs, enraged and with gaping mouths, cause terror. By practicing this for seven days, even a wise Vajra-holder would fall; this rite should be performed with great intensity at midday or midnight. With hair loose and naked, one should look toward the direction of Yama in a state of wrath, [holding] a staff...

Abiding upon the breast, one should recite the mantra of the Fire of Time (*Kālacakra*): *HŪṂ PHAṬ RĀṂ RĀṂ RĀṂ ĀMUKAṂ PAÑCAJĪVITAṂ NARTAKA RĪ RĀṂ RĀṂ RĀṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ*. By this mere recitation, the object of accomplishment will not survive for even a single moment. Within fourteen days and nights, even if he were a Vajradhara, there is no doubt that he will die. Thereafter, one should perform pacification for him as long as his sins remain.

Until the vajra [is struck], this mantra should be recited: *Oṃ svāhā ā ā bām ām mukapāpa ciraṃto bhūtātaye vaśanti rbhavatu bām ām ām āṃ oṃ svāhā*. If one wears white garments, anoints the body with white fragrances, drinks milk, and performs the recitation in an empty temple, peace will be attained. This concludes the third chapter from the *Śrī Heruka-pañjikā-nibandha*, the Introduction to the Means of Accomplishment (*Sādhanopadeśa*).

This is the explanation of the fifth chapter. Now, the phrase "Then" refers to the sequence following the subduing of untimely death. "That which is to be worshipped is itself the worship," meaning it is the action seal (*karmamudrā*). This very thing is the great worship of all the Tathāgatas. Why is this so? Because it is said, "Mantra is renowned as the invocation of worship. Here, "mantra" refers to non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*).

Its purification is that even the utterance of syllables is mantra; therefore, this is renowned as "offering. Regarding the statement on its cause of engagement, it says, "swiftly accomplishing siddhi," and so forth. Since one swiftly accomplishes siddhi through this offering, it should be understood that those who desire siddhi perform it for that purpose. Regarding the two signs, the mantra is supreme...

Regarding the term *sbyar* (union): by the syllable *hūṃ*, Vajra is constantly generated; by the syllable *āḥ*, Padma is generated; by the syllable *bāṃ*, the *kuliśa* (thunderbolt) is generated; and by *phaṭ*, the aperture is closed, signifying primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). The *ḍākinī* is Vajravārāhī; the *vīra* is Śrī Heruka. This is the engagement through the nature of non-duality. Regarding the phrase "the yoginīs are to be churned," it refers to meditative equipoise.

[This] is the entry [into the practice]. The "wise one" is so called because he is skilled in his actions. The "pure body" refers to being completely liberated from subject and object. "One's own desire" means one's own wish; having selected one from among those who possess noble lineage and ethical discipline—such as a mother or daughter—one should welcome her as a hero. "Distinctly separate" means...

"All those belonging to the maṇḍala assemblies are individually distinguished; they are applied with a fixed certainty that is free from error. This means that they are treated as if they were born of yoginīs. Why is this? "In order to sever the afflictions and to benefit sentient beings, one should visualize them as the actual performance of ritual actions. Regarding this, it is for the purpose of severing the afflictions and for the sake of sustaining sentient beings. As for "actions," it is thus.

The Tathāgatas have the characteristic of complete purity, and the meditation on them as appearing as substantial entities is for the sake of abandoning error. Regarding the phrase "having distinguished that very [reality] by means of differentiation," "that very [reality]" refers to the five families, such as the ignorance-vajra and so forth, which are the purities of the eye and the other sense organs. "They should be applied to the path of the channels" means that through the mantras of the channels, one should apply the excellence of that very reality.
It is to be joined by means of the non-dual self-awareness whose very nature is like an illusion, such that as it is externally, so it is internally.

Thus it is said. "By this" means by means of the application of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "Together with the gods, asuras, and humans" means that they are to be held in the mudrā; such is the meaning. This concludes the explanation of the thirty-sixth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanāvatāra*. Then, furthermore:

"Explain" means the great method for those of lesser yogic capacity. "Exorcism" refers to exorcising by means of mantras accompanied by excellent medicines. "Subjugation" refers to the subduing of all women—that is, practicing together with all those who are deceitful, fickle, and difficult to tame. Regarding the enjoyment of the qualities of sensual desire, [it is] their mutual union.

"Mantra" (*mantra*) refers to the statement of the branches of the *sādhana*. "Mutually" (*paraspara*) means outer and inner. Those very twenty-four ḍākinīs are called "mantra" because they resemble mantras. "United with the ḍākinī as one" means that both have been condensed. Alternatively, "mantra" refers to the special vowel-syllables. If one asks what those are like:

First, if one visualizes the vowel-consonant together with the bindu upon a lotus, it will blaze forth in an instant and move near to all objects. Furthermore: "The supreme of all bliss, the indestructible dharmadhātu, Perfectly endowed with AU and the bindu, Having condensed the mantras and tantras, It pervades all the three realms. In food and drink..."

The passage ending with "the one possessed of purity" (*yang dag ldan*) is clear. By means of that very ritual, after drinking mustard oil, one should vomit at the conclusion of the recitation; this and so forth is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "sesame oil" (*til mar*) and so on, the body is smeared with a paste made by grinding *śāli* rice with oil. The phrase "ghee cake" (*snum khur*) and so forth is also easy to understand. After eating black sesame, [one consumes] salt...

"One should cause [the victim] to vomit by means of this very ritual," and so forth, is clear. Regarding "beef" and so on, this refers to the inner fire offering (*antar-homa*): within the hearth-pit itself, one should visualize the deity in the center of a lotus, about the size of a thumb-joint. With two arms and a red-colored body, seated upon a solar seat, and well-established through the radiance of light—furthermore...

Regarding "one should draw [the object] by means of the breath and burn it within the measure of the *nāsikya*," this refers to the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of that [practice], which becomes the mastery of summoning through the mind. The phrase "at that very moment" and so forth is easy to understand. Regarding "it should be kept secret with great effort," "secret" (*guhya*) refers to the concealment; in the context of the characteristics of practicing the commitments (*samaya*), one must exert oneself and strive intensely to keep it secret. It is not [to be disclosed].

It is that which makes [the meaning] clear. For example, just as a supreme jewel placed in the hand of a blind person would not be seen by one of inferior fortune, so too this extraordinary ritual will not be perceived by those of meager merit. Furthermore, even for a practitioner who has squandered their merit, it will be obtained by pleasing the guru, but not otherwise. This concludes the third chapter from the *Introduction to the Means of Accomplishment*, the commentary on the difficult points of the *Śrī Heruka*.

This is the explanation of the twenty-seventh chapter. Now, regarding the term "sign" (*saṃketa*), it refers to the designation of signs. Similarly, concerning the phrase "whatever are the characteristics of the body of the ḍākinī," the ḍākinīs are twenty-four in number. "Body" refers to the yogic bodies of the yoginīs. Regarding the phrase "the limbs of the heroes are divided," this refers to the twenty locations such as Pullīramalaya and so forth.

"RTZA BZHI'O" (The Four Channels). This teaches the arrangement of the wheels (*cakra*). Regarding the phrase "de bzhin" (thus) and so forth, it means that the arrangement is according to how one meditates. Regarding the phrase "dpa' bo'i dbang phyug mi dri" (the Lord of Heroes, Mi-dri) and so forth, it means that one should not reveal his form to anyone; this and the following are easy to understand. "Gsang ba srung" (Guarding the Secret) means that one should keep oneself concealed. "De dang" (With that) refers to the measure.

"Whoever" refers to the practitioner of the glorious Heruka yoga. "Seeing merit" means that by means of that merit, one will be liberated. If one asks what [is seen], it is "well-born"; here, the sixth case ending is used in the sense of the fifth. By this, liberation from the lower realms is shown. Abiding in the state exactly as it is refers to the yoginī.

"Secret Person" (Guhyapuruṣa) refers to one who is equal in nature to those who protect the commitments (*samaya*); it means being together with such a person. This concludes the explanation of the thirty-eighth chapter from the *Pīṭhāvatāra*, the commentary on the difficult points of the *Śrī Heruka*. The phrase "Then" (*atha*) refers to what follows the play (*līlā*); it indicates that the teaching is given after having realized that all things are illusory. *Mantra*...

The phrase "by means of what" (*kyis*) refers to the exhortation of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). When it is said that "mantra protects the mind," it is taught that one should exhort the reality (*tattva*). As for what results from this, the passage beginning with "then one should look at this correctly" and so forth means that it will bestow the supreme [attainment]; the meaning is easy to understand. This concludes the chapter on the introduction to the *Sādhanopāya* commentary on the *Śrī Heruka*.

This is the explanation of the *Sum cu rtsa dgu pa* (The Thirty-Nine). Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then" (*atha*) and so forth: "humans" refers to those who belong to the world upon the surface of the earth. "The Hero" (*vīra*) is the glorious Cakrasaṃvara. "His mantra" is the eight-line [mantra]. "Their yoga" is that which possesses the excellence of his form. If one asks what its function is, it is said: "Together with the lamp and the intoxicant..."

"Thus it is said," and so forth; this means that the inner fire offering (*homa*) should be performed. This concludes the explanation of the fortieth chapter from the *Commentary on the Difficult Points* (*Pañjikā*) of the *Śrī Heruka*, based on the introduction to the *Sādhana*. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then, as for the supreme ritual action, by which one who knows [it] accomplishes [it]," the word "by which" refers to the mantra; it is difficult to obtain and secret.

It has become so. If one asks how this is known, it should be understood from the *Explanatory Tantra* (*Vyākhyātantra*) through the command of the Guru. As it is said: "Wherever there may be an activity, if there is no specific ritual for that particular action, the wise practitioner should rely upon the rituals taught in the General Tantras. It further says: "The Vajra, the Horse’s Gallop, the Lord of Death (*Yama*), as well as the Zombie (*vetāla*), and others..."

Pervaded by the *sṛṇi* (goad), reversing the stages and their sequences, firmly blocking the gateway of emptiness, possessing the vajra and skull-cup, distinguished by a garland of mantras—these twelve great yantras will bestow the supreme recollection upon the practitioner who accomplishes the siddhis. Then, having fashioned the binding of the clay drum, one should manifest the laughter itself for the powerful one.

For each of the individual preparatory rites of the clockwise circumambulation of the left [hand], [recite]: Oṃ sumbha ni sumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavān vidyārāja hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | In the center of the right eye is the deity, which corresponds to the specific ritual activity. Then again: Oṃ sumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ. This is the second.

*La ni hūṃ phaṭ*, *ni de hūṃ ta gri*; on the third is *hūṃ hnā sum hūṃ hnā grīṇā*; on the fourth is *hūṃ de hūṃ de hūṃ de hūṃ*; on the fifth is *ho bhagavāna hūṃ grīṇā pāya*; on the sixth is *ānaya phaṭ vidveṣaya phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ*; on the seventh is *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ rāja hūṃ hnā grī oṃ*. Through this application, [there is] longevity, as well as [the power over] falling and this very [state].

Furthermore, one should perform the following: at the location of the syllable *Hūṃ*, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as if struck by a blazing vajra-strike; and upon the center of the vajra, one should also write *Hūṃ*. One should then bury it immediately in the ground at a cremation site in either a skull-cup from a hero slain in battle or an empty brahmin’s vessel. Then, for the first [syllable], it is *Oṃ ni hūṃ*; the fourth is empty; *Oṃ gṛ hūṃ*; for the second, it is *Bha*; the ninth is empty; the third...

*Śūnyam*, *haṃ śūnyam*, the third syllable is *hā hūṃ saṃ śūnyam*, *hā phaṭ hā*. In the fourth is *śūnyam*; in the fifth is *oṃ bhaga hūṃ śūnyam*, *oṃ parya parya*. In the sixth is *rāja*, *śūnyam*, *ānaya*, *śūnyam*, *hā śūnyam*. In the seventh syllable is *ho hūṃ bāṃ vidyā*, *śūnyam*, *hā hūṃ hūṃ grī*. These are to be arranged according to the movement of a horse.

Then, having recited the mantra, if the practitioner is oppressed by a *vetāla* that causes obstacles to the victim—a person riding a camel or a horse—the two shall be separated. One should place the camel and the horse in a flask according to the ritual procedure and bury them at the door of the victim’s house or in a place where a corpse has been cremated. In that regard, one should place poison, blood, and mustard seeds into a skull, and [use] a human-bone needle and a cloth from a charnel ground.

One should recite over a skull-cup filled with the flesh of a heroic man while facing westward, and thus two wheels should be drawn. On the eighth or fourteenth day of the waning moon, at midnight, one should perform this ritual sequence. For the purpose of killing, it is performed by being seized and devoured by the Lord of Death (Yama). For the hungry ghosts (preta), it is by the hungry ghosts. For the zombies (vetāla), it is by the zombies. For the rākṣasas, it is by the rākṣasas. For the empty ones, it is by the empty ones.

"Draw a lotus at the feet of the Lord; the vajra should be drawn at the perimeter. Skulls should be drawn at the four boundaries. If one acts with wrath toward all these according to the observed ritual procedures, then that terrible and unbearable [deity] will likewise appear. If one asks, 'How are those yantras accomplished? for that reason it is said: 'For the practitioner who seeks siddhi, they will undoubtedly be accomplished through mere recollection.'"* *Sanskrit: *padmapāde likhet tasya vajreṇāntaṃ vibhājayet | kapālāni caturdikṣu likhitavyāni | karmavidhidarśanena sarveṣv eteṣu krodhaṃ kuryāt | tathā tad bhīṣaṇam asahyaṃ ca | kathaṃ te yantrāḥ sidhyantīti cet, ata āha—sādhakasya siddhisādhanasya smaraṇāt sidhyanti nissaṃśayam iti ||* *Note: The text provided appears to be a commentary on a section of a tantric manual (likely from the Guhyasamāja or similar cycle). The translation reflects the technical terminology of ritual practice.*

Regarding the passage beginning with "If so, all the abodes of the gurus, etc., are pervaded by all the ḍākinīs," the term "all" refers to the thirty-two sites, including the outer villages (*grong mtha’*) and the neighboring villages (*nye ba’i grong mtha’*). The "gurus of all" those [sites] are the twenty-four lands (*viṣaya*). The "space" (*mkha’) of all those abodes of the gurus and so forth..."

The meaning is that [the secret] pervades all gro mas, and it is they who express the secret, and no others. If one wonders what those whose arrangement constitutes the ritual procedure are like, it is said: "Manifestly arising in place after place, possessing gnosis, the birthplace," and so forth. Here, "gnosis" (ye shes) refers to great bliss; "possessing gnosis" means being endowed with that.

The immeasurable birthplace of each [individual] is one's own birthplace, which is the ocean of the bodhicitta. What is it that is generated by that? It is stated here: "That is explained as the ḍākinī," and so forth. Regarding this, the twenty-four elements are the ḍākinīs; they arise perfectly as the very vajra-body of the yoginī. The vajra-maṇḍala...

Regarding the phrase "the principal of the maṇḍala" (*maṇḍalādhipati*) and so forth: "Vajra" means indivisible, which is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). Being the principal therein refers to the principal of the vajra-maṇḍala; [the deities] are born from those very [principles]. Their abodes are stated as "Kulutā" and so forth, beginning from the wheel of body (*kāyacakra*) up to the end of the wheel of mind (*cittacakra*). As it is:

In order to summarize the applications, [the Blessed One] spoke these words beginning with "The daughters of these regions," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the heroes and the non-dual yoginīs," this refers to entering into meditative union (*samāpatti*). As for the expression "entering by the force of the mind" (*manovegena praviṣṭāni*), "force of the mind" means *manovega*; these twenty-four [yoginīs], having become exceedingly swift, possess the nature of perfect gathering.

Regarding the statement, "The yoginīs speak in signs," it begins with the words, "The six yoginīs," and so forth. If one asks what the specific distinctions of these signs are, it is stated here: "Kuluta, the mātṛs of the land of Mya-ngan," and so on. By way of illustration through twenty-one thousand [verses], one should understand there to be twenty-one thousand and seventy-two thousand [signs]. That...

If one asks with what they are to be combined, it is said here: "The remaining others, however many there may be, are the yoginīs of the wheel of the glorious Heruka. This means that everything is subsumed within the nature of the twenty-four [sites]. This concludes the explanation of the forty-first chapter from the *Padminī*, a commentary on the difficult points of the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-tantra*, concerning the introductory section on the means of accomplishment (*sādhanopāya*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Then the hero Me-tog-chu" (Flower Water): "Flower" refers to honey, which is to be drunk by the hero. Regarding the phrase "the mantra is to be recollected," it refers to the eight forms of the syllable *ha*. Having found a girl with beautiful eyes... Regarding the phrase "together with the mudrā" and so forth, it is easy to understand. As for the phrase "by this recitation of the three mantras": *Oṃ sarvavajrakāmini*...

*Sarva bhakṣāṃ śo dhaya guhyavajriṇi svāhā*. Regarding this, "short" (*'thung*) refers to oneself. "Likewise" (*de bzhin*) means that it is also directed toward her. "Touching" (*reg*) refers to the great supreme lotus, like a red water-born flower; there, with a mind intent on accomplishing oneself, one should join one's own vajra. "Laughing" (*bzhad pa*) consists of eight types.

It is not so; "the great principal one" refers to the mantra of intoxication by liquor. This is because all Tathāgatas are gathered within the body-maṇḍala of the practitioner, and likewise, all women are included within the body-maṇḍala of Sparśavajrā. As for who Sparśavajrā is, she is the practice of the ultimate truth and the laughter of the deities.

Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the mudrā" (*phyag rgyas bsgrub*): "accomplishing" (*bsgrub*) refers to that which is to be accomplished, namely, great primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Such a "mudrā" refers to the action-mudrā (*karmamudrā*). If one asks what it is like, [it is described as] "the one who possesses the renowned gaze and the leftward gesture. Here, "gaze" (*blta ba*) means the eyes; "leftward gesture" (*bsnyems pa*) means the left side. It refers to one who is constantly endowed with this gesture for its purpose. By this...

"BA" means "by this. Regarding the phrases "at night" or "likewise during the day," these refer to one who possesses a mind that has entered into that [state]. From such familiarization, the signs of Mahāmudrā arise, as indicated by the passage beginning with "Whatever secret of form and action," and so forth. "Nyön" refers to Vajrapāṇi; thus the Blessed One spoke those words to him. This is the manifestation of the siddhi.

The secret signs of this hero are as follows: subtle form, the abandonment of touch, pervasiveness, perfect attainment, intense luminosity, stability, mastery, and the state of being at will. At that time, one will not be afflicted by hunger or thirst, and even the functions of speaking, urinating, and so forth will cease. These...

"All are equal to a dream, and not even the slightest distinction is perceived. Regarding the phrase "tears always flow from them," the word "two" here should be understood as referring to the two eyes; it means that alas, these sentient beings do not meditate for even a single moment upon such sublime skillful means, yet are born in this refuge-less saṃsāra, which is filled with the masses of suffering that are unbearable.

Because compassion arises constantly for this [world] which is agitated by the fear of birth, old age, death, and so forth, and which is characterized by movement from its state; "that food produced from oneself" refers to taking that nectar of bliss from the lotus. "One does not meditate on the vajra" means to act in the manner of one who has been born, with the intention of transcending the three realms.

Regarding the phrase "worship by becoming naked," this refers to gazing at the breasts, the armpits, the thighs, and the lotus mandala. This is taught through the assembly of mudrās; one should experience the taste of all the sense faculties therein. "Exhaling" means to cause the winds of wisdom to descend. "Shaking" means to move the body of the one to be accomplished.

*BA'O* and *dgod* (laughter) refer to assuming the body of laughter. *Gar* (dance) refers to engaging through the movements of dance. *Ngom tsar* (wonder) means causing ordinary beings to be filled with amazement. *Sna tshogs* (various) refers to all yogins. *Dang po* (first) means that this shall be explained; such is the meaning. *HA HĀ HE HĒ HO HŌ HAM*.

"HAḤ"—this is called the eightfold laughter. This concludes the explanation of the forty-second chapter from the *Śrī Herukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanāvatāra*. Then, regarding the passage beginning with "Avalokiteśvara," one might ask: for what purpose does Avalokiteśvara explain the yoginīs? To this, it is said: "The Hero and non-duality..."

"Mi" means that because Avalokiteśvara proceeds non-dually with the yoginīs, as a hero does with women; he is thus both the hero and the non-dual woman. To whom, then, will he look with his eyes? To this it is said: "Of the divisions of the abodes. Here, "abodes" refers to Pullīramalaya, Mālava, and so forth. The "divisions" of these are the abodes.

Regarding "the La-sogs-pa," this means knowing which specific ritual is to be applied in each particular case. If one asks, "By doing what does one know this? it says, "Always delighting in meditation" (*bhāvanā-nityābhirata*); that is, for one who possesses meditation and focused vision, [the deity] will look upon them with a compassionate gaze. As for where they should dwell, it says "at the crossroads of the path" (*catuṣpatha*) and so forth, which is easy to understand. How so?

"In the joyful abode of the Lotus Source, just as flocks of swans gather, the ḍākinīs who abide by the samaya will behold [the practitioner] even from afar. This is because they are moved by the compassion of the Great Compassionate One. For the yogin, worshiping with the mudrā while naked is "naked worship. Because one is liberated through that very action, it is called "naked mudrā worship."

"By its very nature, it is completely liberated," it is said. Regarding the phrase "covered by other garments," "garments" refers to tiger skins and the like; "others" refers to bone ornaments placed upon the limbs. "Desires do not stain [it]" means: "Just as water does not stain a lotus, and just as the sun does not scorch the sky. Likewise, [the hair...]

Regarding the phrase "having become liberated and naked," it means that one should perform all activities with devotion toward that [deity]. Alternatively, it means that one should diligently undertake all activities, such as the trainings and empowerments. Regarding the phrase "the root mantra and likewise the Tathāgatas," the "root mantra" refers to the recitation. "By entering while binding the directions" means with great care.

The meaning is that if even the deities who offer worship by entering through mantras resembling a bow, an arrow, and fire do not see the fire, what need is there to mention humans? Regarding the power of accomplishing and reciting those mantras, it is said: "Filling the hollow of the palm with flowers, one scatters them upward into the sky," meaning that the flowers in the hollow of the palm remain in the sky and [do not fall to] the earth.

"One does not see any downfall," or alternatively, "the flower in the heart" means that even up to a thousand or a hundred thousand beings who roam in the sky will be brought under one's control. "One will know the movement of the stars" means that all things are known through stainless primordial wisdom (*vimalajñāna*). "In various lands, as well as in wildernesses," and so forth, is easy to understand. Regarding the body...

Regarding the phrase "The First Application," and so forth: one should perform the external activities with the manner that will be explained below. As for "at the foot of a tree," one should visualize a six-petaled lotus at the heart. That which arises from the nature of the seven syllables is as follows:

"One will become inseparable from the holder of the gathered emanations; even the holders of the earth [the *kṣetrapālas*] do not go elsewhere. Regarding the phrase "having arranged my own body," this refers to the *cakra*: having sprinkled the ground with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and placed *kuśa* grass upon it, one performs the recitation (*japa*) one hundred and eight times. Then, if one lies down according to the ritual procedure, the *ḍākinī*-wheel is emanated, and together with the three worlds, they merge and...

"Having entered, [the words] beginning with 'equal to the Blessed One' and so forth will all appear. Likewise, regarding the mantra 'a sword, water,' and so forth, it refers to a virtuous maiden; if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over the eyes of the maiden at the time of the afternoon shift, it will show what will happen at dawn. Inside the house, light a lamp and [place] a full vessel."

If one demonstrates [the ritual] using a sword, a mirror, or an actual lamp for the deity worship of the *ras ris* (painted image), it will reveal what is hidden here. Furthermore, if one anoints a pebble with sesame oil and rubs it with a fingernail, and then demonstrates [the ritual], it will reveal who has stolen wealth, as well as [any] destruction, loss, and so forth. Then follows the seven-syllable mantra of the Hero and the procedure for arranging the wheel.

Regarding the phrase "the sun itself" and so forth: "the sun" refers to midday. With a wrathful mind, one should write the name of the victim in the proper sequence using human blood and a brush made of human bone, according to the previously explained method, upon a cloth from a charnel ground, a skull, or the leaf of an *arka* tree; having placed this within the effigy and smeared it with marrow, again and again...

Warm it and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times. For those afflicted by infectious diseases, write the syllable *yi* at the heart. For those with abdominal pain, write it on the forehead. For those suffering from hiccups, write it upon a mandala of wind and clouds. For those with piercing pains, draw a three-pointed spear. For poison and skin diseases, write it upon a *makara*. For those seized by planetary spirits, write it upon an image of the planet.

"One should arrange the wheel in its proper sequence; this indeed generates and sustains all illnesses. Regarding the phrase 'the syllables in the form of crystal,' one should draw and arrange them in the center of a moon disc upon a lotus petal or the left hand using white sandalwood paste and so forth, and then show it to the one afflicted by illness. By the mere act of looking at it, one will be instantly and completely liberated from disease."

"Transformed like the moon of the autumn season, the flowing stream of nectar descends into the heart, the *ūrṇā*, the throat, and the head. Having visualized the syllables as the form of the moon, they radiate out in the ten directions. One should perform the fire offering (*homa*) with substances such as *pālāśa* wood, as previously explained. When one recognizes by the characteristics that [the patient] is afflicted by the disease of jaundice, one should strike them with the first breath."

It brings about the pacification of all diseases, poisons, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "diseases and malevolent spirits" and so on: it means that if these [spirits] are dispelled by mere recollection and even their shadows do not remain, what need is there to mention [their removal] by showing one's hand? As for the phrase "if one is bound head-first in battle," it means that one should draw these wheels upon the left hand using either *ldong ros* or *yungs* (mustard), or alternatively, upon a copper plate.

"Turn all the weapons against the bodies of those who have drawn their swords! Having recited the mantra one thousand times, [the enemy] is bound and placed inside a vajra fist. Then, by recollecting the King of Secret Mantras: "As long as the fist is not released, even if the enemy holds a weapon in hand, they will be unable to discharge that weapon so long as the fist is not released."

"By this, one shall be victorious over the land; by the spreading of the *rgyan-po*, one shall become victorious. Furthermore, having placed a wheel upon the corpse of one who has died from an obstacle, and having raised it up, if one faces it toward the west rather than toward oneself and writes this, by the mere act of writing it, one will be victorious over the *rgyan-po*. In all cases, through the mantra of perfect meditative equipoise, the Wheel of Authority is thoroughly established throughout the three realms."

When applied, it is capable of bringing benefit or harm to those below the earth, upon the earth, and in the higher realms. This concludes the explanation of the forty-third chapter from the *Introduction to the Sadhana* of the commentary on the glorious *Heruka*. Next, as for the "female messenger" (*dūti*), she is the messenger of karma; she consists of the seven syllables and the six yoginīs. As for the seven syllables, they reside upon the petals of various lotuses.

The syllables of the ritual procedure for the six yoginīs should be arranged upon the spokes of the wheel in accordance with the activity [to be performed]. Having interspersed them with the name of the person to be accomplished, they will accomplish that very thing instantly. One should mix together red sandalwood powder, as well as *ske tse*, *lan tsa*, and earth from the footprint of the practitioner, and bind [the object] with it. With both hands, [one should hold] the wheel of the yoginīs.

Having pleased [the deity] by means of meditative cultivation and entering into equipoise, one should perform a fire offering at midnight in a cremation-ground fire or a fire from the burning of a corpse. Having fashioned an image of the person to be accomplished from their ashes, and having placed it facing forward with a wheel drawn on a *gro ga* leaf inserted within it, one should summon that person, visualize them as being rendered unconscious, and recite [the mantra] one hundred times while pronouncing the name of the individual.

The meaning is that if one recites the *ṛtva-aṣṭaka* mantra, that person will be summoned. As for the phrase "the object to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) and so forth, it is easy to understand. Regarding the statement "this application is successful": having taken that very dust and mixed it with iron filings, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished along with their invocation; then, having drawn a wheel on a cloth from a charnel ground, one binds it and recites the mantra seven times while making offerings.

If one digs about eight finger-widths into the ground at the crossroads of the *la lam gyi bzhi mdor* and hides [the powder] there, whoever [is targeted] will be bound immediately. If it is taken out and washed with cow’s milk, they will return to normal. Taking that very powder and preparing it with the five limbs of a corpse, one writes the name of the person to be subjugated along with a wheel upon a cloth from a corpse in the proper sequence; having rolled it up and recited the mantra one hundred times, [one buries it] in a cemetery.

If it is concealed by the *krodha* [wrathful deities], one will certainly go mad immediately; for its restoration, however, if one extracts it and washes with cow’s milk, one will be liberated. This application is successful—so it is said. This concludes the explanation of the forty-fourth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanāvatāra*. Then, regarding the phrase "the supreme among ritual actions":

*Sos pa ni* means "according to the literal sound. *Ba yi 'o mas* means "it should be washed with cow's milk. *Linga* refers to that which is self-arisen. Regarding the phrase "in that way" and so forth: having performed this by drinking milk for seven days, every single day, then when three days have passed, one should go to the river—that is, where it flows toward the ocean—and worship the mandala of the Yoginī, and then issue the command.

It will become the siddhi of speech; what has been spoken will become certain. Regarding the phrase "in a hundred wombs," one should write the previously explained wheels, alternating their names with the flavors, starting from the tongue of flavor (*rasanā*) up to the grape (*drākṣā*). "Abiding in the belly" means placing them there. In whose belly? In that which has been fashioned as its image—namely, red sandalwood and so forth—exactly according to the literal description. Of that...

The thread emerges from the birth-place; or else, one should visualize it at the linga. Pressing the thread with the thumb of the left hand’s fist, the wise one should move the little finger for three sessions, and so forth—this is clear. Regarding the phrase "if heated," it should be connected with the words "as long as the *tsilma* has not dissolved. "Of the animal" refers to the corpse. [End of] the ritual action.

"Phonya mo'i" means "subsequent pacification," which refers to burning [the corpse] together with both the woman and the man. "'Dzin" (hold) means that one should call out her name by means of the mantra and command three times: "Always perform my task! Then, one should take a branch of the *karavīra* tree about the size of half an arm-span and address the girl by her own name, saying, "Come here, so-and-so! Come here, so-and-so!"

Reciting, "Lead [him] here quickly! one should circumambulate while making this request. Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the center," it means dwelling in the center of the joined birth-place. Regarding the phrase "red flower," it means that this rite should be performed at the time when the moon is waning. This concludes the explanation of the forty-fifth chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanāvatāra*. Then, yi...

Regarding the phrase "the five *ha*s," this refers to the sequence ending with *ha hi hu he ho*. It is the expression of the activity (*karma*); the sixth [syllable] is transformed into the center, appearing as Heruka. It becomes the five-pronged vajra in the center of the sun, empowered by the five syllables *ha*. As for the "five syllables *ha*," this is easy to understand. Regarding the term "hare" (*śaśin*), the seed-syllable residing within the hare's skull should be grasped. The glorious He...

This concludes the explanation of the forty-sixth chapter from the introductory section on the sadhana of the *Rukajapa-nāma-pañjikā*. Furthermore, that which is to be explained next is the "Essence of All Ḍākinīs. This refers to the section immediately following the chapter just mentioned. "Essence" (*hṛdaya*) means mantra; it is the essence of all ḍākinīs. "This" refers to what appears below.

The phrase "arisen from the cause of human bone" and so forth is clear. "From the nature of earth" refers to the clay wiped from the hands of a potter. Then, as for the procedure to be performed: one should take the dung of a cow whose calf has died, fashion it into an image, insert the mantra into its heart, cover its eyes with a piece of cloth, and drive it into the bed with a stake. If it is removed, [the patient] will be liberated.

It is so. Then, regarding the passage beginning with "If one wishes to transform a man into a woman," and so forth: the fruit of the *kākāṇḍī* is the fruit of Mahākāla. As for "hunger," this refers to the mouth; one should take the seed of a man [placed] in the skull of a woman according to the previously explained ritual, and mix it with the blood of a rabbit. Regarding "binding the hands," this means grasping it with the fist.

One should recite until one becomes weary during the twelve *nāśya* [mantras]. If one clears it from the head, one will return to a normal state. Then, regarding the phrase "if one desires to turn a man into a donkey," the term "king’s staff" (*rājadaṇḍa*) refers to gold. "Having performed the fire sacrifice" (*homa*) means in a hearth for all ritual actions (*sarvakarmika*). If one clears it from the head, one returns to a normal state. Regarding the phrase "if one desires to turn something into a non-substance":

The preceding was easy to understand. This concludes the explanation of the forty-seventh chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanālaṃkāra*. Furthermore, that which is to be explained next is as follows: "Whatever is the auspiciousness of all ḍākinīs" refers to the activity of what has been spoken.

*Oṃ sarvabuddhadākinye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.* Regarding the statement "by reciting this mantra, accomplishment is attained," it means that one performs all activities without depending on preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and so forth. Immediately after speaking these secret mantras, he spoke in brief the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the mandala of the abodes: *Ḍākinī*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Maṇi, the abode of all," the so-called "Excellent Mountain" refers to Mount Meru, which consists of the seven types of precious substances and has eight peaks, adorned with an abundance of flowers, fruits, and the like. Above that, within this celestial palace (vimāna), upon vases made of gold, silver, and other materials, are the syllables *ha ha he he*, resembling the *kundam* flower and the moon.

By that mudrā of laughter, the four skull-cups at the intermediate petals are consecrated. On the four petals of the cardinal directions are the four [deities] beginning with Ḍākinī. On the three wheels are the heroes and heroines. The four beginning with Khaṇḍarohā are the gates. Yamamathani and the others are at the intermediate points; this is the summary. Vajrasattva...

Regarding the phrase "Vairocana": this refers to the enumeration of the remaining [deities] starting from the wheel of body up to the end of the wheel of mind. "One should always meditate on the nature of the wheels" teaches the inner yoga. "By the ritual previously explained" means by the ritual taught in the first and third chapters. "With zeal" means one should perform the offerings.

This is the meaning. This concludes the explanation of the forty-eighth chapter from the *Padminī-nāma-ṭīkā*, the commentary on the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-tantra* concerning the ritual procedures for the accomplishment of prosperity (*śrī*). Furthermore, regarding what is to be explained next, the phrase "as long as the ritual for accomplishing prosperity" (*yāvac-chrī-sādhana-vidhi*)—here the word "prosperity" (*śrī*) signifies the supreme, which is obtained because it is irreproachable—the section beginning with "from one birth" (*ekajāti*) and so forth refers to [the state] from one birth...

This refers to reciting continuously until exhaustion. Regarding the phrase "itself" and so forth: it possesses the hair from the body of another, namely a beast. If one mixes its hair, nails, teeth, skin, and fur—these five limbs—and holds them in the hands or at the neck, one will become like that [beast]. If one releases them, one returns to one's natural state. It is said: "One who delights in hardship and affliction..."

"Action" (*karma*) refers to that which causes harm and, by way of removing [obstacles], is said to be contrary to the path of *siddhi*. This concludes the explanation of the forty-ninth chapter from the introduction to the *Herukābhidhāna-pañjikā*, the Method for Accomplishment. Then, regarding the passage beginning with "Next, the ritual of fire-offering" (*tato homavidhiḥ*), it is according to the outer and inner applications as they are. By whom...

If one asks, "How is it to be burned? it is by means of the *homa* mantra from the forty-seventh chapter. As for the remainder, it is *durvā*. That which is called *kusmāṇḍa* is its seed-syllable (*bīja*). Regarding the phrase "on the leaf of the householder's *tāmalī*," this refers to the leaf of the *bāsaka*; with that, one should perform the *homa*. The application (*prayoga*) for this is stated as follows: on a *tāmalī* leaf, using charcoal from a burnt corpse, [one should place] the letter *ga* inside...

Having drawn the object to be accomplished at dawn and bound it, place it inside a fish-belly, fill it with *durvā* grass, rice husks, and so forth, seal it with a lid, and cover it with clay. If one buries it face-down within the outer earth so that no air can enter, the mouth will become bound. Furthermore, regarding what is to be explained next: this refers to the "Great Joy" (*pramuditā*) and the other [bodhisattva grounds].

This concludes the explanation of the fiftieth chapter from the *Introduction to the Sadhana* of the *Pañjikā* titled *Śrī Heruka*. Furthermore, what is to be explained next is the passage beginning with "The system of the text is extremely difficult to find," which here also consists of Vajrapāṇi being addressed and speaking. Apart from devotion toward the Great Guru, who is the instruction of all the Buddhas, it is difficult even for those practicing austerities to find it.

Because it has thus become, it is extremely difficult to find. As for how the suchness (*tattva*) of phenomena has become so, it is the movement of the union that abides perfectly in the two states of bliss; through Mahāmudrā, one becomes a manifestly perfected Buddha. Furthermore, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should follow the sequence of practicing by internalizing [this] with superior clarity, without any loss.

From the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) onward, through the extremely clear ritual procedures for the sadhana and conduct of the [deities], until reaching the culmination of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), one becomes equal to the glorious Heruka through manifest meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This is the "Buddha-Enlightenment Hand" arising from the *Ḍākinījālasamvara*, the union with all Buddhas, the perfection of the samādhi originating from the *Ḍākinījālasamvara*.

The Vast Activity: The Command of the Yoginī Concerning the Abiding State, including the guidance and practical application; together with the response, it is before the eyes of the Buddha. Having become supreme among the supreme, the oral instructions transmitted from one to another—through hearing, reflection, and meditation—the cultivation of insight and primordial wisdom through the constant connection of uninterrupted yoga brings the fortunate ones to full maturity and complete perfection.

Because it was taught for the sake of that fortunate vessel, Subhāṣita, whatever comes here is the system of the treatise. Whatever was spoken in all the tantras, that which abides as the great secret of all Buddhas, and that which consists of three hundred million [verses], has come down in the *Prapañca-tantra*. Therefore, the afflictions of the ultimate completion stage—the meditation on the fourteen realities based upon the generation stage—[are addressed therein].

"Free from fear" or "possessing diligence" means being a hero (*vīra*), for one is enthusiastic toward virtue. To "make it manifest" refers to what is taught here by symbols (*saṃketa*). "By me" refers to the Vajradhara; "hidden" means concealed. Where? In other tantras—namely, those of Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Anuttarayoga. "Clothing" refers to a tiger skin. Alternatively, [it may be interpreted as] definitively...

Because it is that which is to be established, it is "clothed," meaning the celestial palace (*vimāna*). The five mudrās refer to the five wheels and so forth; alternatively, they refer to the five wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). What is called "the limb of wisdom" (*prajñāṅga*) refers to the *khaṭvāṅga*; alternatively, it refers to the neck being embraced by wisdom. What is called "resembling a stake" (*kīlākāra*) refers to the wrathful stake (*krodhakīla*), the vajra-point, the pinnacle, and the arrow.

"Such as lattices and mirror-lattices," and so forth. "Reciting *ālikāli*" means visualizing them in the form of the moon and the sun. Regarding the phrase "preceded by the emptiness of causes and so forth": "causes" refers to the creative factors; "and so forth" refers to those causes and the like, such as the activity of generation. The "emptiness" of these is the fourth [wisdom], the wisdom of accomplished activity (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

The so-called "preliminary practice" (*sngon 'gro*) is the third [wisdom], the wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Regarding the phrase "entering from sound and so forth," "entering" refers to the causal Vajradhara. The cause of entering is "sound," which is the syllable *HŪṂ* of the fourth stage. The term "and so forth" refers to the space between the moon, the sun, and the consort. "As long as one possesses the condensed application" refers to those three.

This is the yoga of accomplishing the activity, which consists of the visualization of the Gongbu (Gong bu) form; it is the complete consecration of the Vajradhara by means of the utterly pure gnosis called "Satisfying with Nectar" (*Amṛtasaṃtarpaka*). "Passing into Nirvāṇa" is a summary term. The "hand-offering" (*pāṇipūjā*) has already been explained. Even if such a state is not accomplished due to negligence, then—

It is said, "Regarding the phrase 'the yogins who are the time of the deceased,' and so forth," which is easy to understand. This concludes the explanation of the fifty-first chapter from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna-pañjikā-sādhanālaṃkāra*.
Through the kindness of various gurus in person and by examining the systems of numerous masters, [this has been composed].
In order to bring myself to mind, I have written this narrative of the sādhana with supreme clarity and radiant devotion;
it concerns the yoga of the two non-dual [deities].
By whatever virtue has arisen from completing this commentary on the *Dka’ ’grel*,
may it serve the purpose of yogins.
The *Maṇḍalopāyikā-nidāna*, a commentary on the difficult points of the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, composed by the great master Lavapa, is complete. Furthermore,
from the presence of the venerable Saṃbhavajñānāloka,
the Sun of Secrets:
The *Dka’ ’grel* (Pañjikā) by La wa pa was explained with great diligence.
It was translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian preceptor Sūryagupta and the Tibetan translator ’Gos lhas btsas.
